questions.stem: Which of the following is true about renal tubular transport?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is true about renal tubular transport?

options.label: A
options.text: Maximum reabsorption in the distal tubule

options.label: C
options.text: H+ is absorbed in the proximal tubule

options.label: D
options.text: Amino acid is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule

questions.answerText: Amino acid is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
questions.solution: e. Explanation: In the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) , most of the filtered substances, including amino acids , are reabsorbed. Nearly 100% of the amino acids that are filtered by the glomerulus are actively reabsorbed here using specialized transporters. Amino acid is reabsorption: Location : Amino acids are primarily reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of the nephron. Reabsorption : Nearly 100% of filtered amino acids are reabsorbed by active transport mechanisms in the PCT. Mechanism : Amino acids are transported from the tubular lumen into the renal cells through specific sodium-dependent co-transporters . Significance : This process ensures that essential amino acids are retained in the body and not lost in urine. Maximum reabsorption in the distal tubule (Option A) : The proximal tubule is the primary site for reabsorption of most substances (like glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate). The distal tubule is more involved in fine-tuning reabsorption and secretion, particularly for ions like sodium, potassium, and calcium. Urea is absorbed 100% in PCT (Option B) : Urea is not absorbed 100% in the PCT. It is partially reabsorbed in the PCT, but most urea reabsorption occurs in the loop of Henle and distal tubule . Urea has a role in the kidney’s ability to concentrate urine. H+ is absorbed in the proximal tubule (Option C) : Hydrogen ions (H+) are not absorbed in the PCT; instead, they are secreted into the tubule to help regulate acid-base balance. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
e.

Explanation:

  • In the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), most of the filtered substances, including amino acids, are reabsorbed. Nearly 100% of the amino acids that are filtered by the glomerulus are actively reabsorbed here using specialized transporters.

Amino acid is reabsorption:

  • Location: Amino acids are primarily reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of the nephron.
  • Reabsorption: Nearly 100% of filtered amino acids are reabsorbed by active transport mechanisms in the PCT.
  • Mechanism: Amino acids are transported from the tubular lumen into the renal cells through specific sodium-dependent co-transporters.
  • Significance: This process ensures that essential amino acids are retained in the body and not lost in urine.

 

Maximum reabsorption in the distal tubule (Option A): The proximal tubule is the primary site for reabsorption of most substances (like glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate). The distal tubule is more involved in fine-tuning reabsorption and secretion, particularly for ions like sodium, potassium, and calcium.

Urea is absorbed 100% in PCT (Option B): Urea is not absorbed 100% in the PCT. It is partially reabsorbed in the PCT, but most urea reabsorption occurs in the loop of Henle and distal tubule. Urea has a role in the kidney’s ability to concentrate urine.

H+ is absorbed in the proximal tubule (Option C): Hydrogen ions (H+) are not absorbed in the PCT; instead, they are secreted into the tubule to help regulate acid-base balance.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors is responsible for increasing gastric motility?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following factors is responsible for increasing gastric motility?

options.label: A
options.text: Presence of fatty food in the stomach

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of tryptophan in the stomach

options.label: D
options.text: The presence of acid in the stomach

questions.solution: stric motility. This occurs because the stretch activates mechanoreceptors in the stomach wall, which then trigger the release of signals that promote motility, helping the stomach to mix and propel its contents. Factors responsible for increasing gastric motility: Factor Effect on Gastric Motility Explanation Distension of the stomach Increases gastric motility Stretching of the stomach wall activates mechanoreceptors, stimulating motility. Gastrin Increases gastric motility Hormone released in response to food, especially proteins, that stimulates gastric motility. Acetylcholine (ACh) Increases gastric motility Released by the parasympathetic nervous system, promoting smooth muscle contraction. Peptides and amino acids Increases gastric motility Presence of partially digested proteins or amino acids triggers gastrin release. Gastric emptying reflex Increases gastric motility Reflex activated when food enters the duodenum, regulating the rate of gastric emptying. Increased secretion of digestive enzymes Increases gastric motility The release of gastric juices and digestive enzymes aids in the mixing and movement of food. Presence of fatty food in the stomach (Option A) : Fatty food in the stomach actually slows gastric motility because it triggers the release of cholecystokinin (CCK) , which inhibits gastric emptying. Presence of tryptophan in the stomach (Option C) : While tryptophan is an amino acid, it is not a direct factor in increasing gastric motility. Its role is more related to the synthesis of serotonin, which can affect various aspects of gastrointestinal function, but not directly promote motility in the stomach. The presence of acid in the stomach (Option D) : The presence of acid in the stomach does not directly increase gastric motility. It is more involved in digestion and the regulation of gastric secretion. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A child accidentally took a bottle full of iron tablets. Which of the drugs is used as an antidote for iron poisoning?
questions.stemHtml: A child accidentally took a bottle full of iron tablets. Which of the drugs is used as an antidote for iron poisoning?
questions.solution: class="customMeta" data-dictid="072b8af16e1692777196f21b086f92">poisoning can occur when a person ingests a toxic amount of iron tablets or other iron-containing substances. Deferoxamine is a chelating agent that is used as the antidote for Acute iron poisoning. Mechanism: Binds iron in the body and forms a stable complex that can be excreted through urine and faeces. Deferoxamine helps to remove excess iron from the body and prevent its toxic effects. Luspatercept (Option A) is a medication used for the treatment of anemia in certain blood disorders and is not indicated for the treatment of iron poisoning. Deferiprone (Option C) is an oral chelating agent used to treat iron overload in disorders like thalassemia. However, deferoxamine is the preferred antidote for acute iron poisoning. DMSA (Dimercaptosuccinic acid) (Option D) is another chelating agent used for heavy metal poisoning, but it is not the preferred antidote for iron poisoning. It is more commonly used for lead or mercury poisoning. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Adrenaline acting via beta 2 receptors causes bronchodilation, whereas histamine acts through H1 receptors to cause bronchoconstriction. Which type of antagonism is it?
questions.stemHtml: Adrenaline acting via beta 2 receptors causes bronchodilation, whereas histamine acts through H1 receptors to cause bronchoconstriction. Which type of antagonism is it?
questions.solution: s="customMeta" data-dictid="99de407a1516927771818ac910ab5f">antagonism refers to the interaction between two substances or pathways that have opposing physiological effects. In this case, adrenaline (also known as epinephrine) acting through beta 2 receptors causes bronchodilation, while histamine acting through H1 receptors causes bronchoconstriction. Type of Antagonist Description Example Physiological Antagonist Involves two agents that produce opposite effects on the same physiological function without interacting directly with each other or the same receptor. Histamine causes bronchoconstriction, while adrenaline causes bronchodilatation Chemical Antagonist (Option B) Direct interaction between two drugs to form an inactive product. Heparin works by enhancing the activity of antithrombin III, which inhibits blood clotting. Protamine sulfate binds to the negatively charged heparin, neutralizing its anticoagulant effect. Non-Competitive Antagonist (Option C) Prevents the action of an agonist without competing with it for the binding site. Irreversible binding to the receptor reduces the maximum effect of the agonist. Phenoxybenzamine binds to α-adrenergic receptors, reducing the effect of adrenaline. Competitive Antagonist (Option D) Competes with agonists for the same binding site, reducing the potency of the agonist. Reversible binding to the same receptor site as the agonist. Propranolol (β-blocker) binds to β-adrenergic receptors, reducing the effect of adrenaline. @Neet_pg_bot

    • Type of Antagonist

    Description

    Example

    Physiological Antagonist

    Involves two agents that produce opposite effects on the same physiological function without interacting directly with each other or the same receptor.

    Histamine causes bronchoconstriction, while adrenaline causes bronchodilatation

    Chemical Antagonist

    (Option B)

    Direct interaction between two drugs to form an inactive product.
    • Heparin works by enhancing the activity of antithrombin III, which inhibits blood clotting.
    • Protamine sulfate binds to the negatively charged heparin, neutralizing its anticoagulant effect.

    Non-Competitive Antagonist

    (Option C)
    • Prevents the action of an agonist without competing with it for the binding site.
    • Irreversible binding to the receptor reduces the maximum effect of the agonist.

    Phenoxybenzamine binds to α-adrenergic receptors, reducing the effect of adrenaline.

    Competitive Antagonist

    (Option D)
    • Competes with agonists for the same binding site, reducing the potency of the agonist.
    • Reversible binding to the same receptor site as the agonist.

    Propranolol (β-blocker) binds to β-adrenergic receptors, reducing the effect of adrenaline.

questions.solutionHtml:
mMeta" data-dictid="6bffb538c616927771895e03011a28">hypoglycemic agent which can lead to lactic acidosis.

Metformin

MOA
  • Stimulates the AMP-dependent protein kinase (AMPK) in the presence of insulin.
  • It inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and non-oxidative glucose metabolism and increases insulin sensitivity.
  • Inhibits the mitochondrial glycerol phosphate dehydrogenase
  • Reduces peripheral resistance to insulin in muscle and adipose tissues

Dose

500 mg OD to 2550 mg/day (max)

Uses

First-line oral hypoglycemic for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

DOC: Prophylaxis in prediabetes or impaired glucose tolerance

Metabolic syndrome

DOC: Diabetes due to insulin resistance

  • In PCOS: Metformin also promotes ovulation
  • Clozapine-induced DM/glucose intolerance.
  • Cushing syndrome
  • Gestational diabetes

Other benefits

  • Weight loss in obese patients and weight neutrality in thin patients.
  • There is no risk of hypoglycemia (No effect during the normoglycemic state).
  • Reduction of lipogenesis (decrease triglyceride and LDL levels).
  • Decreases micro- and macrovascular complications of DM
    • Micro: diabetic neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy
    • Macro: MI and stroke

Side effects
  • Nausea/Vomiting/Diarrhoea
  • Megaloblastic anaemia: reduces vitamin B12 absorption from GIT
  • Lactic acidosis
  • Avoid metformin in Renal disorder, liver disease, COPD, CHF, dehydration, and sepsis (hypoxia increases lactic acid production).

Incorrect Options:

Tolbutamide (Option A) is a sulfonylurea used to manage type 2 diabetes mellitus by stimulating insulin release from the pancreas. Its major side effect is hypoglycemia, and it is not associated with lactic acidosis.

Glipizide (Option B), a sulfonylurea for type 2 diabetes, primarily causes hypoglycemia and is not linked to lactic acidosis.

Pioglitazone (Option C), a thiazolidinedione for type 2 diabetes, improves insulin sensitivity. Lactic acidosis is a rare side effect, typically associated with significant kidney or liver dysfunction.

questions.stem: Beta-blockers are ideally avoided in which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: Beta-blockers are ideally avoided in which of the following?
questions.solution: deally avoided in diabetes mellitus with hypertension due to. Potential to mask symptoms of hypoglycemia and patients fail to recognise key symptoms of a hypoglycemic state and neglect getting appropriate treatment. Increased risk of hypoglycemic episodes, as glycogenolysis in the heart, skeletal muscles, and liver that occurs due to sympathetic stimulation is attenuated. Uses of beta-blockers Drug of choice Migraine prophylaxis (Option D) Essential tremors (Option A) Aortic dissection if they also have hypertension Other Uses Hypertension-second-line drugs Stable angina: Decrease the frequency of attacks and increase exercise tolerance. (Option C) Cardiac arrhythmias: Used in both supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias. Congestive heart failure: Decreases mortality. Thyrotoxicosis: Propranolol controls the sympathetic symptoms Glaucoma: Timolol and Betaxolol are used. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (Improves cardiac output). Myocardial infarction (Ml): Secondary prophylaxis of Ml and myocardial salvage during evolution of Ml (decreases mortality). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
deally avoided in diabetes mellitus with hypertension due to.
  • Potential to mask symptoms of hypoglycemia and patients fail to recognise key symptoms of a hypoglycemic state and neglect getting appropriate treatment.
  • Increased risk of hypoglycemic episodes, as glycogenolysis in the heart, skeletal muscles, and liver that occurs due to sympathetic stimulation is attenuated.

Uses of beta-blockers

Drug of choice
  • Migraine prophylaxis (Option D)
  • Essential tremors (Option A)
  • Aortic dissection if they also have hypertension

Other Uses
  • Hypertension-second-line drugs
  • Stable angina: Decrease the frequency of attacks and increase exercise tolerance. (Option C)
  • Cardiac arrhythmias: Used in both supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias.
  • Congestive heart failure: Decreases mortality.
  • Thyrotoxicosis: Propranolol controls the sympathetic symptoms
  • Glaucoma: Timolol and Betaxolol are used.
  • Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (Improves cardiac output).
  • Myocardial infarction (Ml): Secondary prophylaxis of Ml and myocardial salvage during evolution of Ml (decreases mortality).

questions.stem: Renin is secreted by?
questions.stemHtml: Renin is secreted by?
questions.solution: p> Renin is secreted by the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells , which are specialized smooth muscle cells located in the walls of the afferent arterioles of the kidney, near the glomerulus. These cells release renin in response to various stimuli, such as low blood pressure, low sodium levels, or sympathetic nervous system activation. Location of JG Cells : JG cells are specialized smooth muscle cells located in the afferent arteriole of the kidney, just before it enters the glomerulus. These cells are part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) , which is responsible for regulating blood pressure and filtration rate. Renin Secretion Trigger : The JG cells secrete renin in response to several stimuli: Low blood pressure (detected through baroreceptors in the JG cells). Low sodium concentration in the distal tubule, which is sensed by the macula densa . Sympathetic nervous system activation , which triggers the release of renin through β-adrenergic stimulation. Function of Renin : Renin is an enzyme that initiates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) . It converts angiotensinogen (released by the liver) into angiotensin I , which is later converted to angiotensin II in the lungs. Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by constricting blood vessels and stimulating the release of aldosterone, which increases sodium and water reabsorption in the kidneys. Lacis cells (Option A) : These are extraglomerular mesangial cells located near the JGA. While they are part of the JGA and play a role in supporting the JG cells, they do not secrete renin . Macula densa (Option B) : The macula densa cells are located in the distal convoluted tubule and detect sodium concentration in the filtrate. While they signal the JG cells to release renin when sodium levels are low, they do not secrete renin themselves. Intraglomerular mesangial cells (Option D) : These cells are located within the glomerulus and provide structural support. They do not secrete renin. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
p>
  • Renin is secreted by the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells, which are specialized smooth muscle cells located in the walls of the afferent arterioles of the kidney, near the glomerulus.
  • These cells release renin in response to various stimuli, such as low blood pressure, low sodium levels, or sympathetic nervous system activation.

Location of JG Cells:

  • JG cells are specialized smooth muscle cells located in the afferent arteriole of the kidney, just before it enters the glomerulus.
  • These cells are part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), which is responsible for regulating blood pressure and filtration rate.

Renin Secretion Trigger:

The JG cells secrete renin in response to several stimuli:

  • Low blood pressure (detected through baroreceptors in the JG cells).
  • Low sodium concentration in the distal tubule, which is sensed by the macula densa.
  • Sympathetic nervous system activation, which triggers the release of renin through β-adrenergic stimulation.

Function of Renin:

  • Renin is an enzyme that initiates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).
  • It converts angiotensinogen (released by the liver) into angiotensin I, which is later converted to angiotensin II in the lungs.
  • Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by constricting blood vessels and stimulating the release of aldosterone, which increases sodium and water reabsorption in the kidneys.

 

Lacis cells (Option A): These are extraglomerular mesangial cells located near the JGA. While they are part of the JGA and play a role in supporting the JG cells, they do not secrete renin.

Macula densa (Option B): The macula densa cells are located in the distal convoluted tubule and detect sodium concentration in the filtrate. While they signal the JG cells to release renin when sodium levels are low, they do not secrete renin themselves.

Intraglomerular mesangial cells (Option D): These cells are located within the glomerulus and provide structural support. They do not secrete renin.

questions.stem: Center controlling vomiting?
questions.stemHtml: Center controlling vomiting?
questions.solution: The Area postrema is located in the medulla oblongata and is part of the vomiting center in the brain. It plays a crucial role in detecting toxins or irritants in the blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and triggering the vomiting reflex. This area has a "blood-brain barrier" that is less restrictive, allowing it to respond to circulating substances that may induce vomiting. Vomiting pathway: The vomiting pathway involves a complex coordination between multiple centers in the brain and peripheral structures. Here's a simplified pathway for vomiting (emesis) : 1. Triggering Factors: Chemoreceptor Trigger Zone (CTZ) : Located in the area postrema in the medulla, it detects toxins, drugs, or metabolic changes in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Gastrointestinal Irritation : Distension, irritation, or inflammation in the stomach, intestines, or esophagus can send signals to the brain. Vestibular System : Motion sickness or vertigo activates the vestibular system in the inner ear, sending signals to the vomiting center. Higher Centers : Emotional stress, pain, or sights/smells (via the cortex and limbic system ) can also induce vomiting. 2. Signal Transmission to the Vomiting Center: Chemoreceptor Trigger Zone (CTZ) and Gastrointestinal signals : These stimuli are relayed to the vomiting center in the medulla oblongata . The vomiting center integrates signals from multiple sources, including the CTZ , vestibular system , and cerebral cortex . 3. Activation of the Vomiting Center: The vomiting center (located in the medulla oblongata ) coordinates the motor activities required for vomiting, such as contraction of the abdominal muscles and diaphragm, relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, and retroperistalsis in the stomach. Neurotransmitters involved in this process include serotonin (5-HT) , dopamine , histamine , and acetylcholine . 4. The Vomiting Reflex: Deep inspiration : The diaphragm contracts to create negative pressure. Closure of the glottis : Prevents aspiration of vomitus into the lungs. Relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter : Allows the contents of the stomach to move upwards. Contraction of abdominal muscles : Increases intra-abdominal pressure and forces stomach contents into the esophagus. Ejection of gastric contents : Vomiting is completed with the expulsion of stomach contents. Apneustic center (Option A) : The apneustic center, located in the pons , is involved in the regulation of breathing patterns , not vomiting. Pneumotaxic center (Option B) : This center, also located in the pons , helps control the rate and pattern of breathing , not vomiting. Pre-Bötzinger complex (Option D) : Located in the medulla , this area is primarily responsible for generating rhythmic breathing and does not play a direct role in controlling vomiting. @Neet_pg_bot

  • This area has a "blood-brain barrier" that is less restrictive, allowing it to respond to circulating substances that may induce vomiting.

    • Vomiting pathway:

    The vomiting pathway involves a complex coordination between multiple centers in the brain and peripheral structures. Here's a simplified pathway for vomiting (emesis):

    1. Triggering Factors:

    • Chemoreceptor Trigger Zone (CTZ): Located in the area postrema in the medulla, it detects toxins, drugs, or metabolic changes in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
    • Gastrointestinal Irritation: Distension, irritation, or inflammation in the stomach, intestines, or esophagus can send signals to the brain.
    • Vestibular System: Motion sickness or vertigo activates the vestibular system in the inner ear, sending signals to the vomiting center.
    • Higher Centers: Emotional stress, pain, or sights/smells (via the cortex and limbic system) can also induce vomiting.

    2. Signal Transmission to the Vomiting Center:

    • Chemoreceptor Trigger Zone (CTZ) and Gastrointestinal signals: These stimuli are relayed to the vomiting center in the medulla oblongata.
    • The vomiting center integrates signals from multiple sources, including the CTZ, vestibular system, and cerebral cortex.

    3. Activation of the Vomiting Center:

    • The vomiting center (located in the medulla oblongata) coordinates the motor activities required for vomiting, such as contraction of the abdominal muscles and diaphragm, relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, and retroperistalsis in the stomach.
    • Neurotransmitters involved in this process include serotonin (5-HT), dopamine, histamine, and acetylcholine.

    4. The Vomiting Reflex:

    • Deep inspiration: The diaphragm contracts to create negative pressure.
    • Closure of the glottis: Prevents aspiration of vomitus into the lungs.
    • Relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter: Allows the contents of the stomach to move upwards.
    • Contraction of abdominal muscles: Increases intra-abdominal pressure and forces stomach contents into the esophagus.
    • Ejection of gastric contents: Vomiting is completed with the expulsion of stomach contents.

     

    Apneustic center (Option A): The apneustic center, located in the pons, is involved in the regulation of breathing patterns, not vomiting.

    Pneumotaxic center (Option B): This center, also located in the pons, helps control the rate and pattern of breathing, not vomiting.

    Pre-Bötzinger complex (Option D): Located in the medulla, this area is primarily responsible for generating rhythmic breathing and does not play a direct role in controlling vomiting.

questions.stem: In the cardiac muscle, the inhibition of Na +K +ATPase results in?
questions.stemHtml: In the cardiac muscle, the inhibition of Na +K +ATPase results in?
questions.solution: ys a crucial role in maintaining the resting membrane potential of cardiac muscle cells by actively pumping 3 Na⁺ ions out of the cell and 2 K⁺ ions in . This maintains a high concentration of Na⁺ outside the cell and a high concentration of K⁺ inside the cell, contributing to a negative resting membrane potential. Inhibition of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump leads to a reduction in the gradient of sodium and potassium across the membrane. As a result: Na⁺ accumulates inside the cell , making the inside less negative (more positive). This causes depolarization , as the normal negative resting membrane potential is reduced or lost. PHASES OPENING AND CLOSURE OF CHANNELS Phase 0- Depolarization Opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels Phase 1- Initial rapid repolarization Closure of Na+ channels Opening of K+ channel Phase 2- Plateau phase Slower but prolonged opening of L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels K+ channel also remains open. Phase 3- Late rapid repolarization Closure of the Ca2+ channels Slow, delayed increase of K+ efflux Phase 4- Baseline Resting Membrane Potential About −80 to −90 millivolts. Hyperpolarization and then depolarization (Option A) : Inhibition of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase generally causes depolarization , not hyperpolarization, because the loss of the Na⁺ and K⁺ gradient makes the cell less negative inside. Hyperpolarization (option C) : Hyperpolarization would result from an increase in the efflux of K⁺ or an increase in the influx of Cl⁻, but Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition causes depolarization . Repolarization (Option D) : Repolarization refers to the return of the membrane potential to its resting negative value, which doesn't occur with Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition. Instead, depolarization occurs. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What would be the subsequent diagnostic step for a 16-year-old girl who was brought to the hospital by her mother due to primary amenorrhea, where the evaluation revealed the presence of axillary and pubic hair along with normal secondary sexual characteristics, and an ultrasound scan indicated the absence of a uterus?
questions.stemHtml: What would be the subsequent diagnostic step for a 16-year-old girl who was brought to the hospital by her mother due to primary amenorrhea, where the evaluation revealed the presence of axillary and pubic hair along with normal secondary sexual characteristics, and an ultrasound scan indicated the absence of a uterus?
questions.solution: p> Karyotyping is the most appropriate next step in the diagnosis of primary amenorrhea with the absence of a uterus. The presence of axillary and pubic hair, along with normal secondary sexual characteristics, suggests the presence of functional ovaries. However, the absence of the uterus raises the suspicion of a chromosomal abnormality, such as Turner syndrome (45,X), which is a common cause of primary amenorrhea with the absence of the uterus. Karyotyping helps in identifying any chromosomal abnormalities. Incorrect Options: Testosterone levels (Option A) are more relevant in cases of androgen excess or virilization, which is not indicated in this scenario. Estrogen measurement (Option C): Since the patient has primary amenorrhea and the absence of uterus, the focus should be on evaluating chromosomal abnormalities rather than measuring estrogen levels. LH and FSH measurement (Option D) can be helpful in the diagnosis of primary amenorrhea, but karyotyping takes priority in this case. LH and FSH levels can provide information about the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and help differentiate between various causes of primary amenorrhea. @Neet_pg_bot

These enzymes are responsible for breaking down a variety of biological polymers, such as proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, into their constituent monomers. Lysosomes contain around 50 types of hydrolytic enzymes, including proteases , lipases , nucleases , and glycosidases . These enzymes function in an acidic environment (pH 4.5 to 5.0) and are crucial for intracellular digestion, autophagy, and the degradation of cellular waste. He had normal handwriting skills, and could understand what was being asked of him to which he responded by nodding. Where could be the lesion for this clinical condition?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presented to the ER with a history of a road traffic accident. On examination his vitals were stable, but he could not speak. He had normal handwriting skills, and could understand what was being asked of him to which he responded by nodding. Where could be the lesion for this clinical condition?

options.label: D
options.text: Occlusion of left internal carotid artery

questions.solution: Broca's aphasia, which is characterized by non-fluent speech . The patient can understand speech and perform normal motor activities (such as handwriting), but cannot speak . Broca's area , located in the left frontal lobe (in the posterior part of the frontal gyrus), is responsible for speech production. A lesion in this area leads to difficulty in speech production , but comprehension remains intact. This explains why the patient can understand what is being asked and respond by nodding, but cannot speak. Brodmann Areas: Definition Numbered regions of the cerebral cortex identified by Korbinian Brodmann, based on neuronal structure and arrangement. Linked to sensory processing, motor control, and cognitive functions. Key Brodmann Areas and Functions Brodmann Area Function 1, 2, 3 Primary somatosensory cortex; processes tactile information. 4 Primary motor cortex; controls voluntary movements. 5, 7 Somatosensory association areas; integrate sensory input. 6 Premotor/supplementary motor areas; plan movements. 17 Primary visual cortex; processes visual data. 18, 19 Visual association areas; advanced visual processing. 22 Wernicke's area; facilitates language comprehension. 44, 45 Broca's area; involved in speech production. Wernicke’s area (Option B) : Lesions in Wernicke’s area , located in the left temporal lobe , cause fluent but nonsensical speech (Wernicke’s aphasia). The patient would have difficulty understanding spoken language, which is not the case here. Primary motor cortex (Option C) : A lesion in the primary motor cortex would cause motor deficits , such as weakness or paralysis, but would not specifically affect speech production in isolation. Occlusion of left internal carotid artery (Option D) : Occlusion of the left internal carotid artery can cause a stroke that might affect various brain regions, but it would likely cause more widespread neurological deficits, including motor and sensory impairments, not just selective speech impairment like in Broca's aphasia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Identify this movement that takes place in the intestine.
questions.stemHtml: Identify this movement that takes place in the intestine.
questions.solution: ictid="9e2d8a3f5a16927771932c2348ec52">muscular contraction that occurs in the smooth muscle layers of the digestive tract, including the intestines. It propels food and chyme forward through the gastrointestinal tract in a unidirectional manner. This is the movement responsible for pushing the contents of the intestine through the digestive system. Peristalsis: Reflex response is initiated by the stretching of the gut wall due to the contents of the lumen. Location: It occurs throughout the gastrointestinal tract, from the esophagus to the rectum. Mechanism: Stretching triggers circular contraction behind the stimulus and relaxation in front of it. The wave of contraction moves in an oral-to-caudal direction. Propels the contents of the lumen forward at rates of 2 to 25 cm/s. Regulation: Peristaltic activity is influenced by autonomic input but occurs independently of extrinsic innervation. Local stretch releases serotonin, activating sensory neurons that stimulate the myenteric plexus. Cholinergic neurons in the myenteric plexus: In retrograde direction: release substance P and acetylcholine, causing contraction behind the bolus. In anterograde direction: activate the neurons releasing nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP), causing relaxation ahead of the bolus Functional Integration: Peristalsis is an example of the integrated activity of the enteric nervous system. Neurotransmitters Involved in Peristalsis Neurotransmitter Role Mechanism Acetylcholine (ACh) Stimulates contraction Acts on muscarinic receptors, increases motility Substance P Promotes ascending contraction Released by mucosal stimulation, enhances orad contraction Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) Promotes relaxation Acts on smooth muscle to induce relaxation during peristalsis Serotonin (5-HT) Regulates motility and initiates reflex Released from enterochromaffin cells, activates 5-HT receptors Nitric Oxide (NO) Mediates relaxation Released by inhibitory neurons, assists VIP in relaxation Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) Influences sensory signaling Modulated by serotonin, aids in coordinating reflexes @Neet_pg_bot

It propels food and chyme forward through the gastrointestinal tract in a unidirectional manner. This is the movement responsible for pushing the contents of the intestine through the digestive system.

Peristalsis:

  • Reflex response is initiated by the stretching of the gut wall due to the contents of the lumen.

Location:

  • It occurs throughout the gastrointestinal tract, from the esophagus to the rectum.

Mechanism:

  • Stretching triggers circular contraction behind the stimulus and relaxation in front of it.
  • The wave of contraction moves in an oral-to-caudal direction.
  • Propels the contents of the lumen forward at rates of 2 to 25 cm/s.

Regulation:

  • Peristaltic activity is influenced by autonomic input but occurs independently of extrinsic innervation.
  • Local stretch releases serotonin, activating sensory neurons that stimulate the myenteric plexus.
  • Cholinergic neurons in the myenteric plexus:
    • In retrograde direction: release substance P and acetylcholine, causing contraction behind the bolus.
    • In anterograde direction: activate the neurons releasing nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP), causing relaxation ahead of the bolus

Functional Integration:

  • Peristalsis is an example of the integrated activity of the enteric nervous system.

Mechanism

questions.stemHtml: What is the most probable diagnosis for a 65-year-old woman who arrives at the outpatient department with symptoms of breathlessness and fatigue? She has no previous medical history of reactive airway disease or heart disease, but she has undergone breast cancer treatment including breast conservation surgery and chemoradiation. On examination, engorged neck veins and jugular venous pressure (JVP) indicate a rapid x and y descent. The chest x-ray findings are as follows.
questions.solution: ditis. Explanation: Constrictive pericarditis is a condition where the pericardium (the sac surrounding the heart) becomes thickened, fibrotic, and less flexible. This restricts the heart's ability to expand fully during diastole, leading to heart failure-like symptoms such as breathlessness and fatigue . It often occurs after chest irradiation or cardiac surgery , both of which the patient has experienced due to breast cancer treatment. The symptoms of engorged neck veins and a rapid x and y descent in the JVP are typical findings in constrictive pericarditis. These signs reflect impaired diastolic filling and rapid early filling of the heart during diastole due to the rigid pericardium. The chest X-ray findings would typically show pericardial calcification , which is a classic feature of constrictive pericarditis. Cardiac tamponade (Option B) : This condition involves accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac , leading to pressure on the heart. While it can also cause symptoms like engorged neck veins , jugular venous distension , and breathlessness , the JVP typically shows a prominent "blunted" y descent (rather than the rapid x and y descent seen in constrictive pericarditis). 777190396ae8b625">inhibitor suppresses gastric acid secretion by inhibiting the H+/K+ ATPase pump located in the parietal cells of the stomach.

Proton pump inhibitor

MOA

It inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase pump located in the parietal cells of the stomach, thus reducing acid secretion in the stomach.

Potency of PPI
  • Rabeprazole > Lansoprazole > Rabeprazole > Omeprazole > Pantoprazole
  • All PPIs have equal efficacy.

Properties

  • Acid production reduction persists for 2 to 4 days even after stopping the drug and resumes later.
  • Duration of action is typically 2 to 4 days.
    • Omeprazole is the fastest acting PPI.
    • PPIs are acid labile; Enteric coating can protect from acid degradation.
    • They should be taken on an empty stomach when only ~I0% of proton pumps are active, followed 1 hour later by a meal to activate the H+/K+/ATPase at a time when plasma concentration of the PPI is maximal.

Side effects

  • Chronic use of PPIs can lead to hypergastrinemia, which can further result in:
    • ECL hyperplasia
    • Fundic gland polyposis
    • Atrophic gastritis
  • Gastrointestinal upset (nausea, constipation, diarrhoea)
  • Increased microbial growth leads to a higher risk of bacterial infection
  • Increased risk of bone fractures due to hypocalcemia (reduced absorption of calcium)

questions.stem: What is the treatment of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: What is the treatment of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?
questions.solution: > Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that can be used to treat Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, a condition characterised by excessive gastric acid secretion due to gastrin-secreting tumours (gastrinomas). Its treatment is aimed at controlling acid hypersecretion to prevent complications such as peptic ulcers. Omeprazole helps alleviate the symptoms and complications associated with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Other PPls such as pantoprazole, lansoprazole, and esomeprazole may also be used. Incorrect Options: Cimetidine (Option A) is an H2 receptor antagonist, reduces stomach acid production and can provide symptomatic relief for GERD and peptic ulcers. However, it is not the first-line treatment for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, which requires more potent acid-suppressing medications due to excessive gastrin-induced acid secretion. Misoprostol (Option C) is a prostaglandin analogue that has cytoprotective properties and can help prevent gastric ulcers caused by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). While it may be used for certain conditions involving gastric ulcers, it is not typically considered a primary treatment for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Aluminium hydroxide (Option D) is an antacid that neutralizes stomach acid, providing temporary relief from symptoms like heartburn and indigestion. However, it does not address the underlying cause of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and can cause constipation with excessive use. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Mechanism of action of a drug
questions.solution: odynamics deals with the mechanism of action of a drug. The primary focus of pharmacodynamics is the study of how a drug produces its therapeutic effects at the molecular or cellular level. It refers to the specific biochemical and physiological interactions between a drug and its target molecules in the body. Incorrect Options: Mode of excretion of a drug (Option A) refers to the process by which a drug is eliminated from the body. It involves the removal of drugs or their metabolites from the bloodstream through various routes, such as renal excretion (via urine), hepatic excretion (via bile), or pulmonary excretion (via breath). This process is part of pharmacokinetics. Transport of drugs across the biological membranes (Option C) is related to pharmacokinetics, which deals with the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of drugs (often referred to as ADME). The latency of onset (Option D) refers to the time a drug takes to produce its pharmacological effect after administration. This is influenced by factors such as drug formulation, route, absorption rate, and distribution. While pharmacodynamics can indirectly affect the onset, the primary focus of this discipline is on the drug's mechanism of action. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: A

questions.solution: g> The dicrotic notch (incisura) is a small downward deflection seen in the arterial pressure waveform just after the systolic peak . It occurs due to sudden closure of the aortic and pulmonary (semilunar) valves at the end of ventricular systole . This closure causes a brief backflow of blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery, which is then halted, leading to a pressure rebound in the arteries. questions.stem: What do chaperones assist in?
questions.stemHtml: What do chaperones assist in?
questions.solution: g>Explanation: Chaperones are proteins that assist in the correct folding of other proteins. When a protein is synthesized, it may adopt various three-dimensional structures, and only one of these structures will have biological activity. Chaperones prevent the incorrect folding of proteins and ensure they achieve the correct structure necessary for proper function. They are crucial in the assembly of tertiary and quaternary protein structures. Chaperones, such as heat shock proteins (HSPs), are also produced in response to stress, including heat, toxins, or radiation, and help in maintaining protein integrity under these conditions. Misfolded proteins can lead to diseases, including prion diseases and chaperonopathies. Incorrect Options: Ubiquitinization of proteins (Option A): Ubiquitinization refers to the process where a small protein called ubiquitin is attached to other proteins, typically marking them for degradation by the proteasome. This is unrelated to the function of chaperones, which focus on helping proteins fold correctly, not tagging them for destruction. Protein modification (Option B) involves chemical changes to a protein after its synthesis, such as phosphorylation, glycosylation, or acetylation. While chaperones help proteins fold correctly, they do not directly modify them in terms of adding chemical groups or altering their structure after they are fully folded. Protein cleavage (Option D) is the process of breaking down proteins into smaller peptides, often by enzymes like proteases. This process is not related to the role of chaperones, which help proteins fold into their correct structures rather than breaking them down or cleaving them into smaller parts. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is primarily located in the cytoplasm. The enzyme exists in various isoforms, with LDH-5 being the most abundant in the cytoplasm. About 99% of LDH activity is found in the cytoplasm, where it plays a critical role in the conversion of lactate to pyruvate and vice versa, part of the cell's metabolic processes. While a small fraction of LDH can be found in the nucleus (involved in DNA binding and transcription), the vast majority of LDH activity occurs in the cytoplasm. Lysosomes are involved in cellular digestion and degradation processes, and while some enzymes may be active there, LDH is not typically one of them. It is primarily cytoplasmic Golgi complex (Option D) is responsible for modifying, sorting, and packaging proteins for secretion or use within the cell, but it is not a location where LDH is predominantly found. questions.stem: What is the probable vitamin deficiency in a patient who displays symptoms of diarrhea, memory impairment, and a distinctive rash as described?
questions.stemHtml: What is the probable vitamin deficiency in a patient who displays symptoms of diarrhea, memory impairment, and a distinctive rash as described?
questions.solution: rong> is characterized by the classic triad of symptoms: Dermatitis Bright red erythema- in sun-exposed areas (face, ankles, feet) Casal’s necklace - ↑pigmentation around the neck Diarrhoea, and Dementia. The patient's symptoms, combined with a diet high in maize and sorghum, both known to contribute to niacin and tryptophan deficiencies suggest pellagra as the most likely diagnosis. Sorghum has high leucine content which inhibits the QPRTase enzyme required for synthesis of Niacin from tryptophan. Additionally, Maize is low in tryptophan. {{caption_text}} Causes of pellagra: Dietary Deficiency- Maize and Sorghum based diet Impaired Tryptophan Metabolism Factors Affecting Tryptophan to Niacin Conversion: Vitamin B6 Deficiency Medications: Isoniazid (INH), OCPs Hormonal Influences: Estrogen metabolites hinder tryptophan metabolism. Genetic Disorders: Inherited conditions like Hartnup disease can impede tryptophan absorption in the intestines and reabsorption in the kidneys Carcinoid Syndrome Other Contributing Factors: Alcoholism: Interferes with nutrient absorption, including niacin and tryptophan. Malabsorption Syndromes Incorrect Options: Thiamine (Option A) deficiency causes beriberi or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome , with symptoms like confusion, ataxia, and neuropathy, but not diarrhea or rash . Clinical Presentation:

  • Acute Gouty Attack- Sudden onset of intense joint pain, typically affecting the big toe, but can also involve other joints such as the ankle, knee, wrist, or elbow

Diagnosis:

  • Medical History- History of recurrent joint pain, sudden onset, and self-limiting nature of attacks.

  • Long-term Management- Lifestyle modifications (dietary changes, weight loss), medications to lower uric acid levels (allopurinol, febuxostat) to prevent further attacks.

 

Serum Uric Acid Level (Option A): While elevated serum uric acid levels are often seen in individuals with gout, they are not sufficient to confirm the diagnosis on their own.

Urine Uric Acid Levels (Option C): Urine uric acid levels are not typically used as a diagnostic test for gout. Although increased urinary excretion of uric acid may be observed in some cases of gout, it is not a specific or reliable marker for diagnosing the condition.

X-Ray Changes (Option D): X-ray changes, such as the presence of joint erosions or bone damage, may occur in advanced stages of gout or if there have been recurrent episodes of inflammation over time.

questions.solution: ong>Explanation: The patient is presenting with delusions of persecution, where she believes that others are conspiring against her, which is a key characteristic of this type of delusion. Delusions of persecution involve the belief that one is being targeted, harmed, or harassed by others, often without any evidence. In this case, the student believes that the principal, teachers, and other students are part of a conspiracy to harm her academically. Types of delusions Delusion Description Delusion of Persecution Belief of being harassed, persecuted, or mistreated by others. Most common type of delusion. (Option C) Delusion of Reference The belief that surrounding people are talking about them or spying on them. It is a form of delusion of persecution. (Option D ruled out) Delusion of Grandiosity Exaggerated belief in one's own importance, power, or identity. Belief in being a significant figure who can help others or may claim to hear the voices of God, which reinforces their belief in their elevated status. Seen in mania (as Mood-congruent delusion) Nihilistic Delusion Belief that the body/part of body/world or everything related to it has ceased to exist. Also known as the delusion of negation. seen in depression (most commonly) as ( Mood-congruent delusion) Cotard syndrome: Patient with depression having delusions of nihilism (specifically related to parts of the body). Delusion of guilt The patient firmly believes that he is a sinner, though not having committed any sin. Seen in depression (as Mood-congruent delusion) Delusion of Poverty The patient is convinced that he is poor and in a state of destitution, although he is not.   • Belief in being a significant figure who can help others or may claim to hear the voices of God, which reinforces their belief in their elevated status.
  • Seen in mania (as Mood-congruent delusion)

Nihilistic Delusion
  • Belief that the body/part of body/world or everything related to it has ceased to exist.
  • Also known as the delusion of negation.
  • seen in depression (most commonly) as (Mood-congruent delusion)
  • Cotard syndrome: Patient with depression having delusions of nihilism (specifically related to parts of the body).

Delusion of guilt
  • The patient firmly believes that he is a sinner, though not having committed any sin.
  • Seen in depression (as Mood-congruent delusion)

Delusion of Poverty
  • The patient is convinced that he is poor and in a state of destitution, although he is not.

Delusion of enormity
  • The patient believes that their action can produce catastrophe.
  • Eg, the patient refuses to urinate because he believes that it may flood the world.

Delusion of Infidelity
  • The belief that one's partner is unfaithful.
  • Associated factor: prolonged alcohol use
  • Also known as Othello syndrome/Morbid jealousy

De clerambault’s syndrome/ Erotomania
  • The patient (often a single woman) believes that a person of higher status is in love with her.
  • May be a feature of paranoid schizophrenia.

Hypochondriacal delusion/Delusion of ill health
  • Characteristically seen in depression, it may also be seen in schizophrenia.

Various forms of Hypochondriacal delusion:

Delusion of Infestation/ Parasitosis/ Ekbom syndrome:

  • The patient falsely believes that he is infested with insects,he does not experience sensation.
  • It affects both men and women equally and becomes more common with age.
  • ‘Empty matchbox sign’ may be present (when the patient attempts to catch the insect to show it to the clinician).

Delusional dysmorphophobia:

  • The patient believes that his body/part of his body is deformed and wants it to be corrected.

Delusional halitosis:

  • The belief that the patient has a malodorous body odour.

Incorrect Options:

Thought insertion (Option A) is a type of delusion where a person believes that someone else is forcing thoughts into their mind. The individual may feel that their thoughts are not their own and are being controlled by an external force. This symptom is commonly associated with schizophrenia but can also occur in other medical and psychiatric conditions.

Delusion of control (Option B) is characterized by the belief that an external force or agency is controlling or manipulating one's thoughts, actions, or body. The individual may feel as though they are not in control of their own behaviour and are being compelled to act against their will. This symptom is often seen in schizophrenia.

Disorder

Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD)

Conduct Disorder

Definition

The persistent pattern of negativistic, defiant, disobedient, and hostile behaviour toward authority figures.

(Option A ruled out)

A persistent pattern of behaviour involving aggression, violating others' rights, and disregarding social norms.

(Option B)

Diagnostic Criteria (DSM-5)

  • Duration: ≥6 months.

  • Symptoms (≥4):

    • Losing temper.

    • Easily annoyed/sensitive.

    • Angry/resentful.

    • Argues with authority figures.

    • Refuses requests/rules.

    • Deliberately annoys others.

    • Blames others for their own mistakes/behaviors.

    • Spiteful/vindictive (at least 2x in 6 months).

    • No severely aggressive or delinquent behaviours.

  • Duration: ≥12 months, with 1 symptom present in the last 6 months.

  • Symptoms (≥3):

    • Physical aggression or threats.

    • Destruction of property.

    • Deceitfulness or theft.

    • Harming animals.

    • Violation of rules (e.g., truancy, running away).

Types (DSM-5)

  • Angry/Irritable Mood: Frequent temper loss, persistent irritability.

  • Argumentative/Defiant Behavior: Argues, refuses to comply, blames others.

  • Vindictiveness: Spiteful/vindictive actions ≥2x in 6 months.

  • Childhood-onset: Symptoms before age 10.

  • Adolescent-Onset: Symptoms after age 10.

  • Unspecified-Onset: Age of onset unknown

Severity Specifiers

  • Mild: Symptoms in 1 setting.

  • Moderate: Symptoms in 2 settings.

  • Severe: Symptoms in ≥3 settings.

  • Mild: Few conduct problems, minor harm.

  • Moderate: Intermediate symptoms.

  • Severe: Many symptoms, significant harm caused.

Treatment

  • Family Interventions: Parent training in child management, reinforcing positive behaviour.

  • Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): Parents are taught to discourage the child's oppositional behaviour by not paying much attention to it.

  • Parenting Techniques: Focus on reducing harsh punishment and increasing positive interactions.

  • Psychosocial Interventions: Early intervention, CBT, school-based programs.

  • Pharmacologic Interventions: Antipsychotics (risperidone, quetiapine), SSRIs for impulsivity/irritability, sodium valproate.

Antisocial personality disorder (Option C) is diagnosed in adults (18 years and older), making it inappropriate to diagnose in a 13-year-old. While the child’s behaviour may resemble ASPD, the diagnosis requires a history of symptoms extending into adulthood.

Disruptive mood dysregulation (Option D) primarily involves severe temper outbursts and a consistently irritable mood, not the antisocial behaviours observed here. The child’s actions, such as stealing and bullying, suggest Conduct Disorder rather than mood regulation issues.

questions.solution: " data-dictid="e7032bae7f1692777195d693722e54">platelet count and JAK 2 mutation with increased megakaryocytes in the bone marrow aspiration point to the diagnosis of essential thrombocythemia. Essential Thrombocythemia (ET) This is a type of myeloproliferative neoplasm. Aetiology: Caused by mutations in JAK2, CALR, or MPL genes, known as "driver mutations." Other mutations associated: SH2B3, TP53, IDH2, 20q-, etc. Pathophysiology: JAK2V617F mutation (valine to phenylalanine) activates hematopoietic cytokine receptors, leading to myeloproliferation. CALR mutations result in abnormal protein, affecting cellular proliferation and differentiation. MPL mutations affect thrombopoietin receptor function, increasing thrombocytosis risk. Extreme thrombocytosis (>1 million platelets) can lead to bleeding episodes due to acquired von Willebrand disease. Symptoms & Risks: Characterized by high platelet count and megakaryocytic hyperplasia in bone marrow. Risks include thrombosis, haemorrhage, and potential progression to myelofibrosis or leukemic transformation. Diagnosis: Platelet count >450,000 and presence of JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation. Bone marrow examination may show megakaryocytic hyperplasia. Management: Cytoreduction may be necessary to manage thrombocytosis and prevent complications like thrombosis. Regular monitoring of platelet count and mutation status is key for management. Polycythemia vera (Option A) is a myeloproliferative disorder and patients have uncontrolled RBC production. These patients may have raised WBC and platelets due to stimulation of megakaryocyte and myeloid lineages but the most definite feature is the elevated RBC mass. Primary myelofibrosis (Option C): This is a myeloproliferative neoplasm leading to the deposition of fibrous connective tissue in the bone marrow resulting in bone marrow failure. Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (Option D): Characterized by the presence of the BCR-ABL1 gene, it is a type of myeloproliferative disorder mainly involving the overproduction of granulocytes. It is defined by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, which results from a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (t(9;22)(q34;q11.2)). @Neet_pg_bot

Essential Thrombocythemia (ET)

  • This is a type of myeloproliferative neoplasm.

Aetiology:

  • Caused by mutations in JAK2, CALR, or MPL genes, known as "driver mutations."
  • Other mutations associated: SH2B3, TP53, IDH2, 20q-, etc.

Pathophysiology:

  • JAK2V617F mutation (valine to phenylalanine) activates hematopoietic cytokine receptors, leading to myeloproliferation.
  • CALR mutations result in abnormal protein, affecting cellular proliferation and differentiation.
  • MPL mutations affect thrombopoietin receptor function, increasing thrombocytosis risk.
  • Extreme thrombocytosis (>1 million platelets) can lead to bleeding episodes due to acquired von Willebrand disease.

Symptoms & Risks:

  • Characterized by high platelet count and megakaryocytic hyperplasia in bone marrow.
  • Risks include thrombosis, haemorrhage, and potential progression to myelofibrosis or leukemic transformation.

Diagnosis:

  • Platelet count >450,000 and presence of JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation.
  • Bone marrow examination may show megakaryocytic hyperplasia.

Management:

  • Cytoreduction may be necessary to manage thrombocytosis and prevent complications like thrombosis.
  • Regular monitoring of platelet count and mutation status is key for management.

 

Polycythemia vera (Option A) is a myeloproliferative disorder and patients have uncontrolled RBC production. These patients may have raised WBC and platelets due to stimulation of megakaryocyte and myeloid lineages but the most definite feature is the elevated RBC mass.

Primary myelofibrosis (Option C): This is a myeloproliferative neoplasm leading to the deposition of fibrous connective tissue in the bone marrow resulting in bone marrow failure.

Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (Option D): Characterized by the presence of the BCR-ABL1 gene, it is a type of myeloproliferative disorder mainly involving the overproduction of granulocytes. It is defined by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, which results from a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (t(9;22)(q34;q11.2)).

span> her hands and doubts of them being contaminated, which are features of Obsessive Compulsive Disorder.

Obsessions

Compulsions
  • Intrusive and unwanted repetitive thoughts, urges, or impulses.
  • Most common: Contamination
  • Repetitive actions or thoughts carried out in a strict, regulation-bound manner or reaction to obsessions.
  • Performed to relieve anxiety or fear.

Major symptom patterns:

Symptom Pattern

Description

Contamination/Cleansing

Obsession with contamination, followed by washing/avoidance.

Pathological Doubt/Checking

Obsession with doubt, followed by compulsive checking.

Intrusive/Forbidden Thoughts

Intrusive thoughts of aggression or sexual acts, without compulsion.

Symmetry/Ordering

Need for symmetry or precision, leading to compulsive slowness.

Other Symptoms

Religious obsessions and compulsive hoarding.

 

Treatment

Description

Pharmacotherapy

First line: SSRIs (preferred), Clomipramine. Treatment for 1-2 years.

Augmenting agents: Antipsychotics (Risperidone, Aripiprazole), Memantine, Riluzole, Ketamine, Lamotrigine, N-acetylcysteine (NAC).

Other therapies: Desensitization, Thought-stopping, Flooding, Aversive conditioning, Psychodynamic psychotherapy, and Family therapy.

CBT is preferred in younger patients. Combination of CBT and pharmacotherapy is useful.

Somatic Therapies

Anterior cingulotomy, Capsulotomy, Deep brain stimulation with electrodes.

Phobia (Option A) involves a morbid and irrational fear with acute anxiety and panic-like symptoms.

Forced thinking (Option B) is seen in the pre-ictal stage and is relieved after a seizure.

Generalized anxiety disorder (Option D) involves continuous, free-floating anxiety and is not situation-dependent.

Macrovascular Complications of Diabetes Mellitus Major causes of morbidity and mortality in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Involves large blood vessels, leading to: Coronary circulation: Myocardial ischaemia/infarction. Cerebral circulation: Transient ischaemic attack, stroke. Peripheral circulation: Claudication, ischaemia. Key Points: Excess mortality : Mainly due to myocardial infarction and stroke. Accelerated atherosclerosis : Earlier onset and more severe in diabetics. Amplified risk factors : Smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia. Metabolic syndrome : Common in type 2 diabetes, with additional cardiovascular risk factors due to insulin resistance. Criteria for metabolic syndrome are Hypertension High Fasting glucose Elevated TG Low HDL Central obesity Statistics: Condition Increased Rate in Diabetics Cardiovascular death 1.7 times higher Myocardial infarction 1.8 times greater Stroke hospitalisation 1.5 times higher Non-traumatic amputations 60% occur in diabetics First cardiovascular event (type 1) 3 times higher in women, 2.3 times higher in men Mechanisms linking hyperglycemia to macrovascular disease: Increased vascular permeability : Due to high blood glucose. Lipoprotein deposition : Hyperinsulinemia and hypertension increase atherogenic lipoprotein deposits in large vessels. Risk Management: Glycaemic control : Reduces both microvascular and macrovascular complications. Blood pressure control : ACE inhibitors/ARBs are protective. Dyslipidemia management : Statins are recommended to lower cardiovascular risks. Lifestyle modifications : Smoking cessation, weight management, and regular physical activity are crucial. Diabetic Microvascular Complications Diabetic microangiopathy affects small blood vessels in diabetes, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. Key clinical syndromes include: Diabetic retinopathy (Option D) Diabetic nephropathy (Option C) Diabetic neuropathy Foot ulcer (Option B) is a microvascular complication of diabetes. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ery disease

Explanation:

  • The macrovascular complication that develops in the advanced stages of diabetes is coronary artery disease.

Macrovascular Complications of Diabetes Mellitus

  • Major causes of morbidity and mortality in type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
  • Involves large blood vessels, leading to:
    • Coronary circulation: Myocardial ischaemia/infarction.
    • Cerebral circulation: Transient ischaemic attack, stroke.
    • Peripheral circulation: Claudication, ischaemia.

Key Points:

  • Excess mortality: Mainly due to myocardial infarction and stroke.
  • Accelerated atherosclerosis: Earlier onset and more severe in diabetics.
  • Amplified risk factors: Smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia.
  • Metabolic syndrome: Common in type 2 diabetes, with additional cardiovascular risk factors due to insulin resistance. Criteria for metabolic syndrome are
    • Hypertension
    • High Fasting glucose
    • Elevated TG
    • Low HDL
    • Central obesity

Statistics:

Condition

Increased Rate in Diabetics

Cardiovascular death

1.7 times higher

Myocardial infarction

1.8 times greater

Stroke hospitalisation

1.5 times higher

Non-traumatic amputations

60% occur in diabetics

First cardiovascular event (type 1)

3 times higher in women, 2.3 times higher in men

Mechanisms linking hyperglycemia to macrovascular disease:

  • Increased vascular permeability: Due to high blood glucose.
  • Lipoprotein deposition: Hyperinsulinemia and hypertension increase atherogenic lipoprotein deposits in large vessels.

Risk Management:

  • Glycaemic control: Reduces both microvascular and macrovascular complications.
  • Blood pressure control: ACE inhibitors/ARBs are protective.
  • Dyslipidemia management: Statins are recommended to lower cardiovascular risks.
  • Lifestyle modifications: Smoking cessation, weight management, and regular physical activity are crucial.

Diabetic Microvascular Complications

  • Diabetic microangiopathy affects small blood vessels in diabetes, leading to significant morbidity and mortality.
  • Key clinical syndromes include:
    • Diabetic retinopathy (Option D)
    • Diabetic nephropathy (Option C)
    • Diabetic neuropathy

Foot ulcer (Option B) is a microvascular complication of diabetes.

Causes: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitides are the primary causes. questions.solutionHtml:
>purpuric rash which is seen in meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitides.
  • Neisseria meningitidis is a gram negative diplococci.
  • Fulminant meningococcemia presents with a very high fever and hemorrhagic rash.

Acute Bacterial Meningitis

  • Definition: Acute purulent infection in the subarachnoid space (SAS) leading to CNS inflammation.
  • Causes:
    • Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitides are the primary causes.
    • Listeria monocytogenes is a significant risk in adults over 50, especially in those with diabetes, alcoholism, or weakened immune systems.
  • Presentation: Can be acute and fulminant or subacute, with the classic triad of symptoms:
    • Fever
    • Headache
    • Nuchal rigidity (stiff neck)

Clinical features

Description

Consciousness

Decreased level of consciousness occurs in >75% of cases, ranging from lethargy to coma.

Kernig's Sign

Positive when passive extension of the knee elicits pain; indicative of meningeal irritation.

Brudzinski's Sign

Positive when passive flexion of the neck results in spontaneous flexion of the hips and knees; also indicative of meningeal irritation.

Pupils

May present as dilated and poorly reactive due to increased intracranial pressure (ICP).

Posturing

Possible decerebrate posturing as a sign of severe CNS dysfunction.

Signs of Increased ICP

Includes elevated CSF opening pressure (>180 mmH2O), papilledema, and potential cerebral herniation (1–8% incidence).

Additional Symptoms

Nausea, vomiting, photophobia; seizures in 15–40% (focal or generalized).

Meningococcemia Rash

Erythematous maculopapular rash that quickly becomes petechial, commonly on the trunk and lower extremities.

 

Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option B) is a gram-negative rod-shaped bacteria.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option C) is a gram-positive, spherical bacteria.

E. Coli (Option D) is a gram-negative rod-shaped bacteria.

questions.stemHtml: A 72-year-old former pilot visits a neurologist, accompanied by his wife, exhibiting symptoms of rapidly advancing dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, and visual impairments. The provided FLAIR MRI scans can assist in confirming the diagnosis. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.solution: l> The clinical scenario and the FLAIR MRI in the scenario showing the “ hockey stick ” sign is found in variant type Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) is a rare, rapidly progressing brain disorder affecting coordination, memory, and mental functions. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) findings Electroencephalography (EEG) Periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWC) These can be either lateralized in earlier stages or generalized in later stages. {{caption_text}} MRI findings DWI or FLAIR MRI has a sensitivity of 98% and specificity of 93% DWI: Increased intensity in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and cortex Cortical ribboning {{caption_text}} Hockey stick or pulvinar sign is seen in variant , infectious, or acquired CJD In the initial stages, the MRI is normal in Alzheimer’s (Option A) , and in the later stages shows temporal and parietal atrophy. There is no history of stroke; hence vascular dementia (Option B) is unlikely to be the diagnosis The hockey stick sign is not and indicator of sporadic CJD (Option C) . @Neet_pg_bot

l>
  • The clinical scenario and the FLAIR MRI in the scenario showing the “hockey stick” sign is found in variant type Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD).
  • Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) is a rare, rapidly progressing brain disorder affecting coordination, memory, and mental functions.

    • Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) findings

     

     

     

     

     

    Electroencephalography (EEG)
    • Periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWC)
    • These can be either lateralized in earlier stages or generalized in later stages.

     

     

     

     

     

     

     

    MRI findings
    • DWI or FLAIR MRI has a sensitivity of 98% and specificity of 93%
    • DWI: Increased intensity in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and cortex
    • Cortical ribboning
    • Hockey stick or pulvinar sign is seen in variant, infectious, or acquired CJD

     

    In the initial stages, the MRI is normal in Alzheimer’s (Option A), and in the later stages shows temporal and parietal atrophy.

    There is no history of stroke; hence vascular dementia (Option B) is unlikely to be the diagnosis

    The hockey stick sign is not and indicator of sporadic CJD (Option C).

Complications of HIV/AIDS

Gastrointestinal tract

Candidiasis

  • Oral, Esophageal and Tracheal candidiasis
  • Presents with odynophagia
  • Treatment: IV fluconazole

Black hairy tongue

  • Due to the Ebstein-Barr virus.

Chronic diarrhoea

  • Due to Cryptosporidium or Isospora Belli
  • Investigation: Microscopy reveals
    • Cyst < 10 μm - Cryptosporidium
    • Larger cyst - Isospora belli
  • Treatment
    • Cryptosporidium: Nitazoxanide
    • Isospora: Cotrimoxazole

Neoplastic diseases

Kaposi sarcoma
  • Due to HHV-8
  • Vascular tumours on the skin, mucus membrane or organs

Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma

  • Immunoblastic lymphoma
  • Burkitt’s lymphoma
  • Primary CNS lymphoma

Respiratory system

Pneumocystis pneumonia

  • Due to pneumocystis jirovecii
  • Presents with non-productive cough, fever and weight loss
  • Investigation
    • CXR: Bilateral perihilar opacities
    • Beta-1,3-glucan test positive
    • Broncho-alveolar Lavage (BAL): Giemsa staining or methenamine staining shows oval-shaped fungi.
  • Treatment: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

Others

Renal

HIV associated Nephropathy

CVS

Myocardial infarction, cardiomyopathy

 

WHO clinical staging of HIV

Stage 1

  • Asymptomatic
  • Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy

Stage 2

  • Unexplained moderate weight loss (< 10% of body weight)
  • Recurrent upper respiratory tract infections
  • Herpes zoster
  • Angular cheilitis
  • Recurrent oral ulceration
  • Papular pruritic eruptions
  • Seborrhoeic dermatitis
  • Fungal nail infections

Stage 3

  • Unexplained severe weight loss (> 10% of body weight)
  • Unexplained chronic diarrhoea for > 1 month
  • Unexplained persistent fever (> 37.5°C for > 1 month)

Persistent oral candidiasis

  • Oral hairy leucoplakia
  • Pulmonary tuberculosis
  • Severe bacterial infections
  • Acute necrotising ulcerative stomatitis, gingivitis or periodontitis
  • Unexplained anaemia (< 80 g/L (8 g/dL)), neutropenia (< 0.5 × 109 /L)
  • and/or chronic thrombocytopenia (< 50 × 109 /L)

Stage 4

  • Candidiasis of oesophagus, trachea, bronchi or lungs
  • Cervical carcinoma – invasive
  • Cryptococcosis – extrapulmonary
  • Cryptosporidiosis, chronic (> 1 month)
  • Cytomegalovirus disease (outside liver, spleen and nodes)
  • Herpes simplex chronic (> 1 month) ulcers or visceral
  • HIV encephalopathy
  • HIV wasting syndrome
  • Cystoisosporiasis (formerly known as isosporiasis), chronic (> 1 month)
  • Kaposi’s sarcoma
  • Lymphoma (cerebral or B-cell non-Hodgkin)
  • Mycobacterial infection, non-tuberculous, extrapulmonary or disseminated
  • Mycosis – disseminated endemic (e.g. coccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis (formerly penicilliosis), histoplasmosis)
  • Pneumocystis pneumonia
  • Pneumonia, recurrent bacterial
  • Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
  • Toxoplasmosis – cerebral
  • Tuberculosis – extrapulmonary (CDC includes pulmonary)
  • Sepsis, recurrent (including non-typhoidal Salmonella) (CDC only includes Salmonella)
  • Symptomatic HIV-associated nephropathy
  • Symptomatic HIV-associated cardiomyopathy
  • Leishmaniasis, atypical disseminated

Options A, B, and D are incorrect.

questions.stem: As seen below, a 49-year-old man presents with flu-like symptoms and a palmoplantar rash. On examination, he has epitrochlear lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: As seen below, a 49-year-old man presents with flu-like symptoms and a palmoplantar rash. On examination, he has epitrochlear lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: The classical rash and other symptoms point to the diagnosis of secondary syphilis . Classic Manifestations of secondary syphilis: Mucocutaneous or cutaneous lesions and generalized non-tender lymphadenopathy. The primary chancre may still be present in ~15% of cases, more common in HIV-infected individuals. Skin Rash: Macular, papular, papulosquamous, and occasionally pustular syphilides. Lesions may be subtle, and 25% of patients with a visible rash may not recognize it. Lesions initially present as pale red or pink, non-pruritic macules on the trunk/extremities. Progress to papular lesions, often affecting palms and soles. Severe necrotic lesions (lues maligna) may occur in HIV patients. Hair and Mucosal Involvement: Patchy alopecia of the scalp, eyebrows, or beard in 5% of cases. Condylomata lata (moist, infectious lesions) may form in intertriginous areas (e.g., perianal, vulva, scrotum) in 10% of cases. Mucous patches (painless silver-grey erosions) occur in 10-15% of patients, commonly in the oral or genital mucosa. Constitutional Symptoms: Sore throat (15–30%), fever (5–8%), weight loss (2–20%), malaise (25%), anorexia (2–10%), headache (10%), and meningismus (5%). Acute meningitis occurs in 1-2% of cases, with up to 40% of early syphilis cases showing CSF abnormalities. Ocular and Otic Involvement: Ocular symptoms: pupillary abnormalities, optic neuritis, iritis, or uveitis; may lead to permanent blindness if untreated. Otic symptoms: sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, or tinnitus. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are crucial for preventing long-term damage. Less Common Complications: Hepatitis, nephropathy, gastrointestinal issues (e.g., hypertrophic gastritis, proctitis), arthritis, and periostitis. Hepatic involvement is common but typically asymptomatic. Renal involvement results from immune complex deposition, leading to proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome. Resolution: Most secondary syphilis manifestations resolve spontaneously within 1–6 months. Options A, C and D are incorrect. @Neet_pg_bot

    • Condylomata lata (moist, infectious lesions) may form in intertriginous areas (e.g., perianal, vulva, scrotum) in 10% of cases.
    • Mucous patches (painless silver-grey erosions) occur in 10-15% of patients, commonly in the oral or genital mucosa.

    Constitutional Symptoms:

    • Sore throat (15–30%), fever (5–8%), weight loss (2–20%), malaise (25%), anorexia (2–10%), headache (10%), and meningismus (5%).

questions.stem: What is the condition in which the cherry red spot, as shown in the image below, is observed?
questions.stemHtml: What is the condition in which the cherry red spot, as shown in the image below, is observed?
questions.solution: f7">occlusion (CRAO) Explanation: The presentation of sudden, painless vision loss with a cherry-red spot at the macula is suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) The central retinal artery is blocked, causing widespread retinal ischemia. Sometimes, if a cilioretinal artery is present, it can continue to supply the macula, preserving central vision even when the central retinal artery is occluded. Clinical features: Symptoms: Sudden, painless, profound vision loss Painless, except in GCA: GCA-associated CRAO may present with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and/or pain around the temple Clinical Signs: Visual Acuity (VA): severely reduced, often to counting fingers or worse Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD): Profound and sometimes total (amaurotic pupil) Fundus Examination: Retinal Whitening: Pale and opaque retina , particularly in the posterior pole Cherry-Red Spot): Bright red area at the fovea due to the contrast between pale retina and underlying choroidal circulation {{caption_text}} Cattle truck appearance: Due to segmentation of blood column in retinal veins {{caption_text}} Attenuated Arteries: Narrowed and segmented retinal arterioles Optic Disc Changes: Pale optic disc over time due to optic atrophy from prolonged ischemia is seen in chronic cases. Fluorescein Angiography (FA) Arterial Filling : Delayed Masking of Background Fluorescence : Edematous retina blocks normal fluorescence from the choroid Patent Cilioretinal Artery : Area of normal perfusion if a cilioretinal artery supplies the fovea, potentially preserving central vision {{caption_text}} Other Diagnostic Tests Reveals retinal edema, structural changes, and possibly an embolic plaque within the retinal artery and other systemic causes. Cranial MRI or CT Carotid duplex scanning Echocardiography Thrombophilia screening Incorrect Options: Central retinal venous occlusion (CRVO) (Option B) occurs when the central retinal vein, becomes blocked. It typically presents with sudden, painless vision loss and may be associated with retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and retinal edema. Branched retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) (Option C) occurs when one of the branches of the central retinal artery becomes blocked, leading to a localized area of retinal ischemia. The affected area of the retina may appear pale, with associated retinal hemorrhages. Branched retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) (Option D) occurs when one of the branches of the central retinal vein becomes blocked, resulting in impaired venous drainage from a particular area of the retina. It can lead to retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and macular edema. @Neet_pg_bot

f7">occlusion (CRAO)

Explanation:

  • The presentation of sudden, painless vision loss with a cherry-red spot at the macula is suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO).

  • Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)

    • The central retinal artery is blocked, causing widespread retinal ischemia. Sometimes, if a cilioretinal artery is present, it can continue to supply the macula, preserving central vision even when the central retinal artery is occluded.

Clinical features:

Symptoms:

  • Sudden, painless, profound vision loss
  • Painless, except in GCA: GCA-associated CRAO may present with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and/or pain around the temple

Clinical Signs:

  • Visual Acuity (VA): severely reduced, often to counting fingers or worse
  • Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD): Profound and sometimes total (amaurotic pupil)

Fundus Examination:

  • Retinal Whitening: Pale and opaque retina , particularly in the posterior pole
  • Cherry-Red Spot): Bright red area at the fovea due to the contrast between pale retina and underlying choroidal circulation
  • Cattle truck appearance: Due to segmentation of blood column in retinal veins
  • Attenuated Arteries: Narrowed and segmented retinal arterioles
  • Optic Disc Changes: Pale optic disc over time due to optic atrophy from prolonged ischemia is seen in chronic cases.
