  • Arterial Filling: Delayed
  • Masking of Background Fluorescence: Edematous retina blocks normal fluorescence from the choroid
  • Patent Cilioretinal Artery: Area of normal perfusion if a cilioretinal artery supplies the fovea, potentially preserving central vision

Other Diagnostic Tests

Reveals retinal edema, structural changes, and possibly an embolic plaque within the retinal artery and other systemic causes.

  • Cranial MRI or CT
  • Carotid duplex scanning
  • Echocardiography
  • Thrombophilia screening

Central retinal venous occlusion (CRVO) (Option B) occurs when the central retinal vein, becomes blocked. It typically presents with sudden, painless vision loss and may be associated with retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and retinal edema.

Branched retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) (Option C) occurs when one of the branches of the central retinal artery becomes blocked, leading to a localized area of retinal ischemia. The affected area of the retina may appear pale, with associated retinal hemorrhages.

Branched retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) (Option D) occurs when one of the branches of the central retinal vein becomes blocked, resulting in impaired venous drainage from a particular area of the retina. It can lead to retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and macular edema.

Sympathetic ophthalmitis (SO)

Definition

Bilateral, granulomatous, panuveitis (Option A) occurring after penetrating trauma where uveal prolapse may have been a feature of the trauma

Etiology and pathogenesis
  • Trauma to one eye (exciting eye) — 2 weeks to 3 months — Uveitis in the uninjured eye (sympathizing eye).
  • T-cell mediated autoimmune hypersensitivity reaction to Retinal S antigen.
  • Maximum risk upon injury to the ciliary body.

Histopathology
  • Diffuse lymphocytic infiltration of the choroid.
  • Scattered aggregates of epithelioid cells are seen, many of which contain fine granules of melanin.
  • Dalen–Fuchs nodules - granulomas located between Bruch membrane and the RPE (also seen in VKH syndrome)

Clinical features
  • The exciting eye is frequently red and irritable.
  • The sympathizing eye develops irritation, blurred vision, photophobia and loss of accommodation causing difficulty in near vision (first symptom)
  • Anterior uveitis develops in both eyes, which may be mild or severe and is usually granulomatous

Investigations
  • Fundus exam: Dalen–Fuchs nodules, Exudative retinal detachment, vasculitis and optic disc swelling.
  • As inflammation settles, residual chorioretinal scarring may confer a ‘sunset glow’ appearance similar to VKH.
  • B-scan ultrasonography: Choroidal thickening and retinal detachment

Treatment
  • Enucleation of a severely injured eye within 10 to 14 days of the injury is effective in preventing or reducing the severity of SO
  • Steroids are the basis of initial treatment. Intravenous methylprednisolone followed by high-dose oral prednisolone is given for several months and gradually tapered according to response. Supplementary topical steroids and cycloplegics may be given

Options B, C, and D are incorrect.

Key features of Karyotyping: A karyotype is a visual representation of an individual's chromosomes, arranged in pairs by size and position of the centromere. Klinefelter syndrome is characterized by tall stature, infertility, and delayed puberty. questions.solution: 7ce71">hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH) is characterized by mutations in the PHEX gene. This gene encodes the phosphate-regulating endopeptidase homolog X-linked (PHEX) protein , which plays a crucial role in phosphate homeostasis. When the PHEX gene is mutated, it leads to increased FGF-23 levels , resulting in impaired phosphate reabsorption in the renal tubules and subsequent hypophosphatemia. XLH is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern and presents with characteristic features including lower limb deformities, dental abnormalities, and skeletal manifestations without typical hypocalcemic symptoms. Most common among genetic disorders causing rickets Inheritance X-linked dominant Gene Mutated PHEX (phosphate-regulating gene with homology to endopeptidases on X chromosome) Normally, product of this gene appears to have an indirect role in inactivating FGF-23 Pathophysiology Clinical Manifestations Lower limb deformities: Coxa vara Genu valgum Genu varum Poor growth Maxillofacial abnormalities Skull deformities: Due to premature fusion of cranial sutures Delayed dentition Short stature Laboratory Findings High renal phosphate excretion Hypophosphatemia Elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) Normal PTH and serum calcium Low or inappropriately normal levels of 1,25-D Treatment Phosphorus Supplementation: 1-3 g elemental phosphorus daily, divided into 4-5 doses Can be given in the form of Joulie solution (30.4 mg phosphate/mL) or as neutral phosphate effervescent tablets Frequent dosing helps to prevent prolonged decrements in serum phosphorus because there is rapid decline after each dose Calcitriol: 30-70 ng/kg/day in 2 doses Burosumab-twza: Monoclonal antibody targeting FGF-23, an alternative for children >1 year Prognosis Generally good response to therapy, though frequent dosing can affect compliance FGF-23 levels decreased (Option A) : This is incorrect because XLH is characterized by elevated levels of FGF-23, not decreased levels. The increased FGF-23 leads to phosphate wasting and decreased active vitamin D production, which are hallmark features of the condition. It is the most common cause of rickets (Option C) : This statement is incorrect because while XLH is the most common inherited form of rickets, nutritional deficiencies, particularly vitamin D deficiency, remain the most common overall cause of rickets worldwide. Excretion of phosphorus is decreased (Option D) : This statement contradicts the pathophysiology of XLH, where there is increased renal phosphate wasting leading to elevated urinary phosphorus excretion.     •  

    X-Linked Hypophosphatemic (XLH) Rickets

    Prevalence

    1 in 20,000. Most common among genetic disorders causing rickets

    Inheritance

    X-linked dominant

    Gene Mutated
    • PHEX (phosphate-regulating gene with homology to endopeptidases on X chromosome)
    • Normally, product of this gene appears to have an indirect role in inactivating FGF-23

    Pathophysiology

     

     

    Clinical Manifestations
    • Lower limb deformities:
      • Coxa vara
      • Genu valgum
      • Genu varum
    • Poor growth
    • Maxillofacial abnormalities
    • Skull deformities: Due to premature fusion of cranial sutures
    • Delayed dentition
    • Short stature

    Laboratory Findings
    • High renal phosphate excretion
    • Hypophosphatemia
    • Elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
    • Normal PTH and serum calcium
    • Low or inappropriately normal levels of 1,25-D

    Treatment
    • Phosphorus Supplementation:
      • 1-3 g elemental phosphorus daily, divided into 4-5 doses
      • Can be given in the form of Joulie solution (30.4 mg phosphate/mL) or as neutral phosphate effervescent tablets
      • Frequent dosing helps to prevent prolonged decrements in serum phosphorus because there is rapid decline after each dose
    • Calcitriol: 30-70 ng/kg/day in 2 doses
    • Burosumab-twza: Monoclonal antibody targeting FGF-23, an alternative for children >1 year

    Prognosis

    Generally good response to therapy, though frequent dosing can affect compliance

     

    FGF-23 levels decreased (Option A): This is incorrect because XLH is characterized by elevated levels of FGF-23, not decreased levels. The increased FGF-23 leads to phosphate wasting and decreased active vitamin D production, which are hallmark features of the condition.

    It is the most common cause of rickets (Option C): This statement is incorrect because while XLH is the most common inherited form of rickets, nutritional deficiencies, particularly vitamin D deficiency, remain the most common overall cause of rickets worldwide.

    Excretion of phosphorus is decreased (Option D): This statement contradicts the pathophysiology of XLH, where there is increased renal phosphate wasting leading to elevated urinary phosphorus excretion. This increased phosphate excretion is a direct result of elevated FGF-23 levels and is a key diagnostic feature of the condition.

clinical presentation of blurred vision, severe pain after swimming in a pond with ring like lesion on examination is suggestive of Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Acanthamoeba keratitis:

It is caused by Acanthamoeba, a free-living amoeba found in water, causes severe corneal infections

Risk Factors:

  1. Contact Lens Use (Primary Risk Factor)
  2. Exposure to Contaminated Water
  3. Trauma
  4. Immunosuppression
  5. Use of Homemade Saline Solutions.
  6. Poor Lens Storage Conditions

Examination Findings in Acanthamoeba Keratitis:

Symptoms:

  • Blurred Vision: Common in corneal conditions due to the disruption of the cornea's transparent surface.
  • Discomfort: Significant discomfort in the affected eye.
  • Severe Pain: Pain is often out of proportion to clinical signs, a key clinical clue.

Signs:

Early Disease:

  • Irregular and Greyish Epithelium: Early sign indicating amoebic invasion.
  • Pseudodendrites: Lesions resembling herpetic keratitis
  • Limbitis and Stromal Infiltrates: Inflammation at the corneal-scleral junction with diffuse or focal infiltrates in the anterior stroma.
  • Perineural Infiltrates (Radial Keratoneuritis): Hallmark sign, radial streaks extending towards the cornea's centre, pathognomonic for Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Advanced Disease:

  • Ring Abscess: Characteristic of advanced infection, where infiltrates form a ring-shaped abscess.
  • Stromal Opacification and Vascularisation: Corneal opacity and new blood vessel growth, leading to significant vision impairment.
  • Corneal Melting: Serious complication where corneal tissue breaks down, often at the infiltrate edges.
  • Scleritis: Reactive inflammation of the sclera, not a direct infection extension.

Options A, B, and C are incorrect.

finition: Most common type of uveitis affecting the anterior segment of the eye.

Clinical Features:

  • Pain
  • Redness
  • Photophobia (sensitivity to light)
  • Blepharospasm (involuntary blinking)
  • Serous discharge
  • Blurring and diminished vision

Examination Findings:

  • Keratic Precipitates (KPs) (Option B):
    • Non-Granulomatous: Fine, grey deposits; composed of lymphocytes
    • Granulomatous: Large, greasy-looking deposits known as "mutton fat KPs"; composed of macrophages
    • Location: Typically found in the lower cornea due to convection currents in aqueous humor; this area is known as Arlt's triangle
  • Aqueous Cells:
    • Indicator of active inflammation
  • Aqueous Flare:
    • Haziness in the anterior chamber due to leakage of proteins from inflamed tissues
  • Muddy Iris:
    • Edema in the iris caused by protein leakage
  • Miosis:
    • Constricted pupil due to toxins released from inflamed tissue
  • Nodules on the Iris:
    • Koeppe's Nodules: At the pupillary border; seen in both granulomatous and non-granulomatous uveitis
    • Busacca Nodules: At the base of the iris; seen in granulomatous uveitis

Complications: (Findings)

  • Posterior Synechiae: Iris adheres to the lens; may lead to festooned-shaped pupil
  • Secclusio Pupil/Ring Synechiae: Adhesion along the entire pupillary border; can lead to Iris Bombe and peripheral anterior synechiae, causing angle closure glaucoma
  • Occlusio Pupil: Covers the whole surface of the lens
  • Cyclitic Membrane
  • Rubeosis Iridis: New vessel formation on the iris

Incorrect Options:

Aqueous flare (Option A) refers to the presence of protein and inflammatory cells in the aqueous humor, which may be seen in anterior uveitis.

Festooned pupil (Option C) is a characteristic feature of posterior synechiae in chronic uveitis.

Bussaca’s nodules (Option D) are larger, granulomatous nodules that are seen in conditions like chronic anterior uveitis, especially in sarcoidosis or tuberculosis.

Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario of a patient with history of chickenpox and cutaneous lesions seen along the course of trigeminal nerve is suggestive of Herpes zoster ophthalmicus.

Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO)

  • Affects the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve.
  • Anterior uveitis occurs in 40-50% of cases, usually within 2 weeks of skin rash onset.
  • Symptoms: mild iritis, vesicular rash on the nose, small KPs, mild aqueous flare, possible hemorrhagic hypopyon.
  • Complications: iris atrophy, secondary glaucoma, complicated cataracts.

Incorrect Options:

Chicken pox exacerbation (Option A), caused by the varicella-zoster virus, usually occurs in children and presents with a generalized vesicular rash. Reactivation of the virus in adults leads to herpes zoster rather than an exacerbation of chickenpox.

Drug allergy to acyclovir (Option B), a common antiviral medication used to treat herpes zoster, would typically present with skin rashes, itching, or swelling after drug exposure.

Herpes zoster oticus (Option D) (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) involves the facial nerve and affects the ear, causing pain, vesicular rash in the ear canal, and facial paralysis. It does not primarily affect the eye or lead to keratitis.

    • Neuroblastoma

    Definition & Epidemiology
    • Neural crest-derived tumor
    • Most common extracranial solid tumor in children
    • 7-8% of all childhood cancers
    • Most common in first year of life
    • Median age at diagnosis: 19 months

    Genetic Features
    • MYCN amplification (~20% of cases)
    • Loss of heterozygosity: 1p, 11q, 14q, 17q
    • TERT and chromatin remodeling genes
    • 1-2% show family history
    • Higher MYCN copy number indicates worse prognosis

    Clinical Presentation

    Primary Sites:

    • Abdominal (65%)
    • Mediastinal (40%)
    • Paraspinal (19%)
    • Head/neck (5%)

     

    Symptoms:

    • Pain, fever, irritability
    • Weight loss
    • Abdominal distension
    • Periorbital ecchymosis
    • Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome (rare)

    International Staging

    Stage L1: Localized tumor, complete excision

    Stage IIA: Incomplete gross excision

    Stage IIB: Complete/incomplete excision with positive lymph nodes

    Stage III: Midline crossing or bilateral involvement

    Stage IV: Distant metastasis (Bone marrow (MC), bone, liver, regional lymph nodes)

    Stage IVS: Localized primary with limited dissemination (infants)

    Diagnostic Markers

    Immunohistochemistry:

    • Synaptophysin
    • Tyrosine hydroxylase
    • PHOX2B
    • Neuron-specific enolase

     

    Other Markers:

    • Desmin
    • Myogenin
    • Keratin
    • CD99

    Treatment Options

    Primary Treatments:

    • Surgery
    • Chemotherapy
    • Radiation therapy

     

    Chemotherapy Regimens:

    • OPEC (vincristine, cyclophosphamide, cisplatin)
    • CADO (vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin)
    • PECADO (cisplatin, etoposide)

     

    Additional Therapies:

    • 13-cis retinoic acid
    • Autologous bone marrow transplantation

     

    Wilms tumor (Option A) primarily metastasizes to the lungs, liver, and regional lymph nodes. While it is the most common renal tumor in children, bone marrow involvement is not a characteristic feature. The typical pattern of spread follows hematogenous routes to the lungs and liver.

    Adrenal gland tumors (Option C), such as adrenocortical carcinomas, typically spread to local lymph nodes, liver, and lungs. Bone marrow metastasis is not a common feature of these tumors.

    Granulosa cell tumor of ovary (Option D) typically spreads within the peritoneal cavity and to regional lymph nodes. It is rare in children, and bone marrow metastasis is not a characteristic feature. These tumors are more commonly seen in adults.

Signs of active trachoma

Signs of cicatricial trachoma

Conjunctival signs:

  • Conjunctival congestion
  • Follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva: Look like sago-grains
  • Papillary enlargement: red, velvety

Conjunctival signs:

  • Scarring
    • It may be irregular, star-shaped, or linear
    • Linear scar in the sulcus subtarsalis is called Arlt’s line (Option C)
  • accumulation of dead epithelial cells and inspissated mucus in the glands of Henle
  • Pseudocyst
  • Xerosis
  • Symblepharon

Corneal signs:

  • Superficial keratitis on slit lamp and fluorescein
  • Herbert’s follicles
  • Progressive pannus/Trachomatous pannus: The upper part of the cornea is cloudy
  • Corneal ulcers are common at the advancing edge of the pannus
    • Shallow, little infiltrated
    • Cause lacrimation and photophobia

Corneal signs:

  • Regressive pannus or pannus siccus:
    • Receding infiltration
    • Vessels extend beyond the area of infiltration and haze
  • Herbert pits: oval or circular pitted scars formed after the healing of Herbert’s follicles in the limbal area
  • Vascularized and opaque cornea.
  • Corneal xerosis
  • Corneal ectasia
  • Total corneal pannus (blinding sequelae)

 

 

Lid signs:

  • Distortion of the lids
  • Tylosis : Thickening of the tarsal plate/lid margin
  • Trichiasis due to rubbing of lashes on the cornea
  • Trachomatous ptosis (sleepy appearance)
  • Entropion
  • Madarosis
  • Ankyloblepharon

Lacrimal apparatus sequelae:

  • Chronic dacryocystitis
  • Chronic dacryoadenitis

findings of clubbing of fingers, seen in various cardiopulmonary conditions. Clubbing is not always irreversible and can be reversible in certain conditions.

Clubbing of fingers

Definition
  • Enlargement of distal segments of fingers and toes
  • Proliferation of connective tissue
  • Particularly on the dorsal surface
  • Changes at the base of clubbed nail

Pathophysiology
  • Connective tissue proliferation
  • Exact mechanism unknown
  • Platelet-derived growth factors implicated

Clinical Signs
  • Bulbous Enlargement of the Distal Phalanges
  • Loss of the Normal Angle Between the Nail and the Nailbed (Lovibond’s Angle)
  • Increased Sponginess of the Soft Tissue at the Base of the Nail
  • Nail Changes:
  • Nail flattening/nail curvature
  • Hippocratic fingers: The tips of the fingers become enlarged, and the nails curve downward

Clinical tests

Schamroth’s Sign:

  • Normal: A small diamond-shaped window should be visible between the nails when the fingers are positioned in this way.
  • Positive Schamroth’s Sign: The window disappears, and there is no gap between the nails, indicating the loss of the normal angle at the nail bed.

Associated Conditions
  • Cyanotic congenital heart disease
  • Infective endocarditis
  • Bronchiectasis
  • Cystic Fibrosis
  • Lung cancer
  • Tuberculosis
  • Inflammatory bowel disease

Key Features
  • Can be hereditary or acquired
  • May be reversible in certain circumstances
  • Associated with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy
  • Can cause pain and arthritis-like changes

 

Spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia) (Option A): The nail abnormality is characterized by thin, fragile nails with a concave appearance, either horizontally or vertically oriented. The nail plate appears to be depressed in the centre and bent outward at the edges.

Raynaud's phenomenon (Option B) presents as repeated constriction of blood vessels in the fingers and toes, typically triggered by cold temperatures or stress.

Pallor (Option C) refers to a noticeable decrease in the normal colour and tone of the skin or mucous membranes, which may occur due to changes in blood flow, anaemia, or other unclear factors.

  • Cardiovascular: Hypertension, hypokalemia, and oedema.

angiography:

Principle: Based on the detection of fluorescent light emitted by fluorescein dye in circulation.

  • Absorption & Emission Wavelengths:
    • Irradiating light: 420–490 nm.
    • Emitted fluorescence: 510–530 nm.
  • Retinal pigments and red blood cells can absorb fluorescent light, masking deeper structures. Pigment migration allows visibility of deeper layers.

Diagnostic uses:

  • Diabetic Retinopathy: Reveals neovascularization, and assesses vascular tree integrity.
  • Fundus Disorders: Identifies depth of pathological involvement.
  • Optic Nerve Pathologies: Useful in detecting optic nerve issues such as papilloedema.
  • Neovascularization of Iris: Detects leakage from iris vessels, an early sign of rubeosis.

Normal Study

Abnormalities Detected by Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA)

Fluorescence Type

Cause

Examples

Hyperfluorescence

Window defect in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)

Atrophy showing background choroidal fluorescence

Pooling of dye under detached RPE

Age-related macular degeneration (ARMD)

Pooling of dye under sensory retina

Central serous retinopathy (CSR)

Leakage into the neurosensory retina due to the breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier

Cystoid macular edema (CME)

Leakage from choroidal or retinal neovascularization

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy, subretinal neovascular membrane in ARMD

Staining (long retention of dye by tissues)

Drusen, normal optic disc

Leakage from optic nerve head

Papilloedema

Hypofluorescence

Blockage of background fluorescence

Retinal hemorrhage, hard exudates, pigmented clumps

Occlusion of retinal/choroidal vasculature

Central retinal artery occlusion , diabetic retinopathy capillary occlusion

Loss of vasculature

Choroideremia, myopic degeneration

Incorrect Options:

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) (Option B) is a non-invasive imaging technique that uses light waves to produce cross-sectional images of the retina.It is particularly useful in assessing conditions like macular edema, macular holes, and retinal detachment.

Retinal CT (Option C) is not a recognized imaging modality in ophthalmology, as computed tomography (CT) is generally not suitable for the detailed visualization of retinal layers.

Retinal MR (Option D) can be used to assess orbital or optic nerve conditions, it does not provide the level of detail required for retinal imaging

he history of alcohol abuse point to the diagnosis of alcohol liver disease.

Alcohol liver disease

Pathophysiology

Alcohol Metabolism
  • Ethanol is primarily metabolized in the liver by enzymes, particularly alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) and cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1).
  • This metabolism produces acetaldehyde, a toxic intermediate, which can cause cellular damage.

Oxidative Stress
  • The metabolism of alcohol generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) and increases oxidative stress within liver cells.
  • This oxidative damage leads to lipid peroxidation, protein modifications, and DNA damage, contributing to hepatocyte injury and inflammation.

Inflammatory Response
  • Alcohol consumption stimulates the activation of immune cells (e.g., Kupffer cells) leading to the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6).
  • These cytokines promote inflammation and can further damage hepatocytes.

Altered Lipid Metabolism
  • Alcohol disrupts normal lipid metabolism, leading to fat accumulation in liver cells (steatosis).
  • This accumulation can progress to steatohepatitis, where inflammation and liver cell injury occur.

Fibrosis and Cirrhosis
  • Chronic inflammation and injury stimulate the activation of hepatic stellate cells, which produce collagen and lead to fibrosis.
  • Over time, repeated injury can result in cirrhosis, characterized by scarring and loss of normal liver architecture.

 

Clinical features:

General
  • Usually asymptomatic
  • Fever, malaise, jaundice, history of alcohol intake + (at least within last 8 weeks before symptom onset)

Abdominal
  • Right upper quadrant pain, tender hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites
  • Caput medusae: enlarged veins radiating from the umbilicus
  • Bleeding varices (portal hypertension)

Dermatological
  • Spider angioma, palmar erythema, ecchymosis

Reproductive
  • Gynaecomastia, gonadal atrophy, loss of libido, amenorrhea

Neurological
  • Peripheral neuropathy: tingling and numbness usually over feet
  • Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: Ophthalmoplegia, confusion, ataxia + anterograde amnesia
  • Hepatic encephalopathy: Asterixis (most prominent finding), altered sensorium, sleep disturbances, lethargy

Others
  • Dupuytren’s contracture, temporal muscle wasting, parotid gland enlargement

 

Alcoholic liver disease LFT:

AST (Aspartate aminotransferase)

Non-specific ; ↑ (<300-400)

ALT (Alanine aminotransferase)

Specific for liver injury ; ↑ (<300-400)

AST/ALT ratio: ≥ 2: 1

Specific for ALD

ALP (Alkaline phosphatase)

Elevated in bile duct pathologies

GGT (γ-glutamyl transferase)

Non-specific marker of ALD

5’-Nucleotidase

Specific marker for bile duct pathologies

S.Bilirubin

Usually normal/mildly ↑

S.Albumin

↓ in chronic liver disease (cirrhosis)

Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT)

Best serum marker for alcoholic liver disease.

questions.solution: mage represents the patient suffering from hemispatial neglect where there are missing details in the left side of the line drawing. Hemispatial Neglect : Hemispatial neglect is the inability to report, respond, and orient to stimuli in one-half of the space despite having no motor or sensory deficits. Types and location of lesions: Contralesional Hemispatial Neglect: Result of damage to cortical or subcortical components of the spatial attention network. Not always caused by parietal lobe lesions, as traditionally believed. Spatial Attention Model: Right hemisphere: Directs attention to the entire extrapersonal space. Left hemisphere: Directs attention mostly to the right hemispace (contralateral). Left hemisphere lesions: Minor neglect, as the right hemisphere compensates. Right hemisphere lesions: Severe neglect of the left hemispace due to lack of ipsilateral attentional mechanisms in the left hemisphere. Clinical Examination: Patients may neglect grooming, eating, and reading on the left side. Line drawing and writing often have missing details on the left side. Tests for neglect: Simultaneous Bilateral Stimulation: Patients fail to detect bilateral stimuli and experience extinction (only detecting stimuli from the right side). Target Detection Task: Difficulty detecting targets on the left side, reflecting a motor and attentional deficit rather than sensory input loss (hemianopia). Some patients may deny the existence of hemiparesis or even the paralyzed limb (anosognosia). Clinical Observation: Neglect is more common, severe, and long-lasting after right hemisphere damage. Severe neglect of the right hemispace is rare even with left hemisphere lesions. Confabulation (Option A) is a phenomenon in which the patient fills in memory gaps with made-up stories and inaccurate facts. Kinetic apraxia (Option C) is the inability to perform a fine movement or task despite having the desire and physical capability to do it. The lesion lies in the paracentral cortex. mage represents the patient suffering from hemispatial neglect where there are missing details in the left side of the line drawing.

Hemispatial Neglect:

  • Hemispatial neglect is the inability to report, respond, and orient to stimuli in one-half of the space despite having no motor or sensory deficits.

Types and location of lesions:

  • Contralesional Hemispatial Neglect:
    • Result of damage to cortical or subcortical components of the spatial attention network.
    • Not always caused by parietal lobe lesions, as traditionally believed.
  • Spatial Attention Model:
    • Right hemisphere: Directs attention to the entire extrapersonal space.
    • Left hemisphere: Directs attention mostly to the right hemispace (contralateral).
    • Left hemisphere lesions: Minor neglect, as the right hemisphere compensates.
    • Right hemisphere lesions: Severe neglect of the left hemispace due to lack of ipsilateral attentional mechanisms in the left hemisphere.

Clinical Examination:

  • Patients may neglect grooming, eating, and reading on the left side.
  • Line drawing and writing often have missing details on the left side.
  • Tests for neglect:
    • Simultaneous Bilateral Stimulation: Patients fail to detect bilateral stimuli and experience extinction (only detecting stimuli from the right side).
    • Target Detection Task: Difficulty detecting targets on the left side, reflecting a motor and attentional deficit rather than sensory input loss (hemianopia).
  • Some patients may deny the existence of hemiparesis or even the paralyzed limb (anosognosia).

Clinical Observation:

  • Neglect is more common, severe, and long-lasting after right hemisphere damage.
  • Severe neglect of the right hemispace is rare even with left hemisphere lesions.

 

Confabulation (Option A) is a phenomenon in which the patient fills in memory gaps with made-up stories and inaccurate facts.

Kinetic apraxia (Option C) is the inability to perform a fine movement or task despite having the desire and physical capability to do it. The lesion lies in the paracentral cortex.

Asterixis (Option D) is a type of negative myoclonus where irregular lapses of the posture of body parts are noted.

questions.solution: n and the next step of management is defibrillation since this is a shockable rhythm. Shockable Conditions Non-Shockable Conditions Ventricular Fibrillation Asystole Ventricular Tachycardia Pulseless Electrical Activity Shockable Conditions Non-Shockable Conditions Immediate Recognition Identify Shockable Rhythm: Recognize VF or pulseless VT. Activate Emergency Response: Call for advanced life support. ↓ Initiate CPR Start High-Quality CPR: Perform chest compressions at a rate of 100-120/min, with a depth of 5-6 cm. Continue CPR for 2 minutes. ↓ Defibrillation (Option A) After 2 minutes of CPR, deliver a Non-Synchronized DC Shock to restore normal rhythm. If no change, administer a second shock immediately. ↓ Continue CPR Resume CPR for 2 Minutes Place an intravenous or intraosseous line for drug administration. ↓ Administer Epinephrine Epinephrine 1 mg (Option C) (1:10,000): Given IV/IO after 2 minutes of CPR to enhance coronary perfusion pressure. ↓ Advanced Airway Management Secure Airway: Perform endotracheal intubation if necessary. Capnography: Monitor end-tidal CO2 levels. Ventilation: Provide 1 breath every 6 seconds post-intubation. ↓ Further Defibrillation Third Shock: If VF or pulseless VT persists, deliver a third non-synchronized shock. Continue CPR for 2 More Minutes: Follow with additional CPR. ↓ Administer Antiarrhythmic Medication Amiodarone 300 mg IV: Administer for shock-refractory VT to stabilize heart rhythm. ↓ Identify and Treat Reversible Causes Immediate Recognition Identify Non-Shockable Rhythm: Recognize asystole or pulseless electrical activity (PEA). Activate Emergency Response: Call for advanced life support. ↓ Initiate CPR Start High-Quality CPR: Perform chest compressions at a rate of 100-120/min, with a depth of 5-6 cm. Continue CPR for 2 minutes. ↓ Establish intravenous or intraosseous lines for medication administration. ↓ Administer Epinephrine Epinephrine 1 mg (1:10,000): Administer IV/IO after the first 2 minutes of CPR. ↓ Identify Rhythm Non-Shockable Rhythm: Continue CPR and administer epinephrine every 3-5 minutes. Pheochromocytoma

Description
  • Pheochromocytomas are rare tumours arising from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.
  • The clinical features result from excessive secretion of catecholamines.

Epidemiology
  • Estimated to occur in 2 to 8 of 1 million persons per year.
  • The mean age at diagnosis is 40 years, although the tumours can occur from early childhood until late in life.
  • The classic ‘rule of tens’ is 10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal (Paragangliomas), and 10% metastatic. It is not used nowadays.

Etiopathogenesis
  • These tumors can be benign or malignant and are frequently associated with familial syndromes like
    • Neurofibromatosis type 1,
    • multiple endocrine neoplasia type II, and
    • Von-Hippel Lindau disease.
  • Catecholamines are produced in the chromaffin cells starting with the rate-limiting step of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), regulating the conversion of tyrosine to dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA).
  • Pheochromocytomas release these catecholamines in various patterns ranging from paroxysmal, continuous, and mixed patterns. Norepinephrine is released continuously and can result in persistent hypertension, while epinephrine is released in a paroxysmal pattern resulting in tachyarrhythmias.
    • Ryanodine-2 receptors (RyR2).
    • Beta-2 adrenoceptors
    • Alpha(1)-adrenoreceptors

Histopathology
  • Histology of the lesion characteristically shows zellballen nests of chromaffin cells with strong positivity to chromogranin, synaptophysin, CD56, and focally to S100.
  • The presence of chromaffin cells in the extra-adrenal tissue is the only pathognomonic characteristic of the malignant form of the entity.

Clinical features
  • Classical triad
    • Episode of palpitation
    • Headache
    • Profuse sweating
  • The dominant sign is Hypertension
  • Tachycardia
  • Anxiety
  • Subcutaneous neurofibromas
  • Cafe-au-lait macules
  • Thyroid mass
  • Axillary freckling
  • Lisch nodules on the iris
  • Retinal angiomas
  • Abdominal mass

Diagnosis
  • Diagnosis of pheochromocytoma can be established by biochemical confirmation of hypersecretion of metanephrines and catecholamines.

24-hour urine test

  • Catecholamines
  • Fractionated metanephrines
  • Total metanephrines

Imaging:

  • CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis to locate the tumour.
  • 18F-FDG PET scanning is recommended for metastatic disease.
  • MIBG scintigraphy
  • Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy
  • Gallium DOTATATE PET scanning

Differential Diagnosis
  • Hyperthyroidism
  • Renal artery stenosis
  • Hyperaldosteronism
  • Cardiomyopathy
  • Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS)

Treatment
  • The definitive treatment of pheochromocytoma is surgical resection.
  • Preoperative preparation of the patient has to be considered, and blood pressure should be consistently < 160/90 mm Hg.
  • Blood pressure is controlled by alpha-adrenergic blockers(phenoxybenzamine 0.5-4 mg/kg of body weight)
  • Oral Prazosin or IV phentolamine can be used to control paroxysm.

 

Unilateral Pheochromocytoma:

  • Minimally invasive adrenalectomy: Preferred treatment for most unilateral adrenal pheochromocytomas.
  • Open adrenalectomy

 

Bilateral pheochromocytomas:

  • Bilateral total adrenalectomy is associated with a lifelong need for steroid replacement with long-term side effects.
  • Bilateral partial or cortical sparing adrenalectomy (open or laparoscopic)

Complications
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Cardiogenic shock
  • Renal Failure
  • Pulmonary edema
  • Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
  • Lactic acidosis
  • Hypertensive retinopathy
  • Hypertensive encephalopathy

 

Fibromuscular dysplasia (Option A) is a systemic vascular disease that is the cause of 10% to 20% of renal artery stenosis. This presents with resistant hypertension, hematuria, flank pain, renal infarct, hypokalemia, and abdominal bruit.

Renal artery stenosis (Option C) can cause hypertension, but it does not typically present with sudden-onset headaches, palpitations, and profuse sweating.

Hyperthyroidism (Option D) can cause symptoms such as palpitations and sweating. However, sudden-onset headaches and episodes of high blood pressure are not typical features of this condition.

Dermal Manifestations of Systemic Sclerosis (SSc)

  • Bilateral Symmetrical Skin Thickening: Begins distally in the fingers and progresses proximally.
  • Skin Pigmentation Changes:
    • Early diffuse tanning without sun exposure.
    • Hypopigmentation with a "salt-and-pepper" appearance on the scalp, upper back, and chest is common in dark-skinned individuals.
  • Sclerosis of Skin and Loss of Appendages:
    • Leads to hair loss, reduced sweating, xerosis, and itching.
    • Disappearance of transverse finger creases and fixed flexion contractures causing muscle atrophy.
  • Fixed Contractures: Affects wrists, elbows, and knees due to skin and tendon fibrosis.
  • Neck Skin Ridges: Firm adherence to platysma muscle limits neck extension.
  • Facial Changes ("Mauskopf"):
    • Taut, shiny skin with loss of wrinkles and reduced mobility.
    • Thinned lips, prominent perioral radial furrows, and microstomia.
    • Pinched, beak-like nose.
  • Telangiectasia: Dilated capillaries on face, hands, lips, and oral mucosa; correlated with microvascular disease severity.
  • Skin Ulcerations:
    • Chronic ulcers on fingertips, PIP joints, and bony prominences heal slowly and may become infected.
    • Fingertip ischemia leaves fixed digital "pits."
  • Acro-Osteolysis: Resorption of terminal phalanges due to ischemia.
  • Calcinosis Cutis:
    • Dystrophic calcifications in the skin and soft tissues, commonly in patients with anti-centromere antibody–positive lcSSc.
    • Calcific deposits vary in size and may ulcerate, causing pain, infections, or nerve compression.

 

Rheumatoid arthritis (Option A) has symmetrical involvement of small joints, morning stiffness lasting for more than 1 hour, and classical deformities in severe cases. The given scenario does not include symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option C) presents with fatigue, joint pain, photosensitive rash, mouth ulcers, and hair loss. The given clinical scenario is not of SLE.

Pneumonia (Option D) is an infection of the pulmonary parenchyma, classified into community-acquired (CAP), hospital-acquired (HAP) and ventilator-associated (VAP). Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA) Defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction due to the focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without acute infarction or tissue injury. A TIA typically lasts less than an hour, more often minutes. Usually resolves within 24 hours. Risk is highest in the first 48 hours following a transient ischemic attack. Etiology: Common risk factors for all TIA include diabetes, hypertension, age, smoking, obesity, alcoholism, unhealthy diet, psychosocial stress, and lack of regular physical activity. A previous history of stroke or TIA will increase substantially the subsequent risk of recurrent stroke or TIA. Pathophysiology: TIA subtypes, classified according to the pathophysiological mechanisms Large artery atherothrombosis (M/C): This may be intracranial or extracranial atherothrombosis. The mechanism may be a lack of blood flow distal to the site of arterial stenosis or an artery-to-artery embolism. Small vessel ischemic diseases: The underlying pathology is either lipohyalinosis or small vessel arteriolosclerosis. The commonest risk factor is hypertension, followed by diabetes and age. Cardiac embolism: A clot in the cardiac chamber, most commonly in the left atrium , is secondary to atrial fibrillation. Cryptogenic : This is usually a cortical pattern of ischemia without any identifiable large artery atherothrombosis or cardiac source of emboli. More recently it is often referred to as ESUS (embolic stroke of unknown source). Other uncommon causes such as arterial dissection or vasculitis. Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA)

  • Defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction due to the focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without acute infarction or tissue injury.
  • A TIA typically lasts less than an hour, more often minutes.
  • Usually resolves within 24 hours.
  • Risk is highest in the first 48 hours following a transient ischemic attack.

Etiology:

  • Common risk factors for all TIA include diabetes, hypertension, age, smoking, obesity, alcoholism, unhealthy diet, psychosocial stress, and lack of regular physical activity.
  • A previous history of stroke or TIA will increase substantially the subsequent risk of recurrent stroke or TIA.

Pathophysiology:

TIA subtypes, classified according to the pathophysiological mechanisms

  • Large artery atherothrombosis (M/C): This may be intracranial or extracranial atherothrombosis. The mechanism may be a lack of blood flow distal to the site of arterial stenosis or an artery-to-artery embolism.
  • Small vessel ischemic diseases: The underlying pathology is either lipohyalinosis or small vessel arteriolosclerosis. The commonest risk factor is hypertension, followed by diabetes and age.
  • Cardiac embolism: A clot in the cardiac chamber, most commonly in the left atrium, is secondary to atrial fibrillation.
  • Cryptogenic: This is usually a cortical pattern of ischemia without any identifiable large artery atherothrombosis or cardiac source of emboli. More recently it is often referred to as ESUS (embolic stroke of unknown source).
  • Other uncommon causes such as arterial dissection or vasculitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following leads to a continuous murmur?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following leads to a continuous murmur?
questions.solution: >Peripheral Pulmonic stenosis produces a characteristic continuous murmur due to persistent turbulent blood flow through narrowed pulmonary artery branches. This congenital condition creates turbulence in blood flow that begins in systole, peaks near the second heart sound, and continues through diastole. The continuous nature of the murmur occurs because the pressure gradient between the pulmonary artery and its branches remains throughout the cardiac cycle, maintaining constant turbulent flow. Continuous murmur Definition Murmur that persists across systole and diastole Begins in at S1, continues through second heart sound (S2) and tapers at next S1 Causes Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) Peripheral Pulmonic stenosis Valsalva aneurysm Aortopulmonary window Great vessel arteriovenous fistula Coronary to pulmonic fistula Severe Pulmonary artery hypertension (Option B) typically causes leakage of blood into the RV during the diastole due to the high pressure in the pulmonary arteries, characteristically producing a diastolic murmur. Type A aortic dissection (Option C) is a medical emergency and the presentation mainly accompanies classical signs like blood pressure discrepancies between the upper extremities, pulse deficits & hypotension. Murmur is rarely seen and if seen its mostly diastolic murmur. Rupture of cardiac chamber (Option D) is a medical emergency. Continuous murmur

Definition
  • Murmur that persists across systole and diastole
  • Begins in at S1, continues through second heart sound (S2) and tapers at next S1

Causes

Type A aortic dissection (Option C) is a medical emergency and the presentation mainly accompanies classical signs like blood pressure discrepancies between the upper extremities, pulse deficits & hypotension. Murmur is rarely seen and if seen its mostly diastolic murmur.

Rupture of cardiac chamber (Option D) is a medical emergency. The hemodynamic compromise would be severe and acute, leading to cardiogenic shock and unrecordable BP. No murmur will be heard.

questions.solution: complement activation is primarily initiated by the spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 to form C3(H2O) , which then binds to factor B. This activates the pathway and leads to the formation of the C3 convertase , which plays a key role in the amplification of the complement cascade. In the alternative pathway , C3 is crucial for both the activation and amplification of the complement system, as it is cleaved to form C3a and C3b , which further participate in opsonization, inflammation, and cell lysis. Complement System: Definition : A complex network of at least 30 proteins in the blood, crucial for innate and acquired immunity. Functions : Lysis : Directly kills pathogens by forming membrane pores. Opsonization : Coats pathogens to enhance recognition and uptake by phagocytes. Immune Clearance : Removes immune complexes from circulation. Inflammation : Triggers release of mediators, recruiting immune cells. Pathways of Complement Activation: Pathway Trigger Mechanism Key Components Involved Classical Pathway Binding of C1q to antigen-antibody complexes C1q (Option A ruled out) , C3 convertase, Membrane Attack Complex (MAC) Alternative Pathway Direct binding of complement proteins to pathogens C3, factors B and D, C3 convertase Lectin Pathway Binding of mannose-binding lectin (MBL) to mannose MBL, MASP1, MASP2, C4 (Option D ruled out) , C2 (Option B ruled out) , C3 convertase {{caption_text}} Key Points: Convergence : All pathways converge at the formation of the C3 convertase. C3 Convertase : Cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b, leading to the formation of C5 convertase and, ultimately, MAC. Regulation : The complement system is tightly regulated to prevent excessive activation and damage to host tissues. Regulatory Proteins : Include inhibitors and inactivators that control the cascade. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is amplified in an RT-PCR test for the COVID-19 virus?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is amplified in an RT-PCR test for the COVID-19 virus?
questions.solution: trong> In an RT-PCR (Reverse Transcription PCR) test for COVID-19, the RNA of the virus is first reverse-transcribed into DNA by the enzyme reverse transcriptase . This step is essential because PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) works with DNA , not RNA. The RNA is converted into complementary DNA (cDNA), which is then amplified in the PCR process to detect the presence of the virus. Real-Time RT-PCR for COVID-19 Diagnosis Real-time reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) is the gold standard for diagnosing COVID-19. Turnaround Time : The average time from sample receipt to result generation is approximately 4-5 hours. Capacity : Can process up to 90 samples in a single run, making it efficient for frontline testing. Gene Targets : Screening (Genus Specific) : Spike protein (S) Envelope protein (E) Membrane protein (M) Nucleocapsid protein (N) Confirmation (Species Specific for SARS-CoV-2) : RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) Open reading frames (ORF1a/b) N2 nucleocapsid Principle of Testing : Qualitative real-time PCR amplifies target genes in the specimen using a thermocycler. Fluorescence is generated when the amplicon binds to the probe, with the cycle threshold (Ct) indicating positivity. A sample is considered positive if both screening and confirmatory genes are detected with a Ct value ≤ 40 cycles. Detectability : NAAT can be positive as early as day 1 of symptom onset (usually 5 days post-infection) and generally declines by the third week, often becoming undetectable thereafter. Automated Real-Time RT-PCR Systems include Truenat and CBNAAT (Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test, e.g., GeneXpert). Widely accessible Turnaround Time : Quick results in 30-60 minutes. Automation : Fully automated with minimal handling, reducing biosafety hazards. Gene Targets : CBNAAT : E gene for screening, N2 gene for confirmation. Truenat : E gene for screening, RdRp gene for confirmation. Disadvantages : Limited to 1-4 samples per run, suitable for low sample loads (24-48 samples/day). Antigen Detection Rapid chromatographic immunoassay (SD Biosensor) for qualitative detection of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein. Sample Collection : Nasopharyngeal swab immersed in viral extraction buffer to inactivate the virus and release the antigen. Point-of-Care Testing : Conducted at the bedside within one hour; antigen stability is limited to one hour. Performance : Highly specific (99–100%) but moderate sensitivity (50–84%); symptomatic but negative patients should be referred for RT-PCR testing. Incorrect Options: RNA (Option A): In an RT-PCR test for COVID-19, the viral RNA is converted into complementary DNA (cDNA) using reverse transcriptase enzyme. This cDNA is then amplified through PCR. Structural Protein (Option C): Structural proteins are components of the virus, but they are not the target of RT-PCR testing. RT-PCR is designed to detect and amplify the genetic material of the virus. Envelope (Option D) : The envelope is a protein that is part of the virus structure. However, the envelope protein itself is not directly amplified in RT-PCR. The test targets the viral RNA, not the proteins. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>
  • In an RT-PCR (Reverse Transcription PCR) test for COVID-19, the RNA of the virus is first reverse-transcribed into DNA by the enzyme reverse transcriptase. This step is essential because PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) works with DNA, not RNA. The RNA is converted into complementary DNA (cDNA), which is then amplified in the PCR process to detect the presence of the virus.

Real-Time RT-PCR for COVID-19 Diagnosis

  • Real-time reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) is the gold standard for diagnosing COVID-19.
  • Turnaround Time: The average time from sample receipt to result generation is approximately 4-5 hours.
  • Capacity: Can process up to 90 samples in a single run, making it efficient for frontline testing.
  • Gene Targets:
    • Screening (Genus Specific):
      • Spike protein (S)
      • Envelope protein (E)
      • Membrane protein (M)
      • Nucleocapsid protein (N)
    • Confirmation (Species Specific for SARS-CoV-2):
      • RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)
      • Open reading frames (ORF1a/b)
      • N2 nucleocapsid
  • Principle of Testing:
    • Qualitative real-time PCR amplifies target genes in the specimen using a thermocycler.
    • Fluorescence is generated when the amplicon binds to the probe, with the cycle threshold (Ct) indicating positivity.
    • A sample is considered positive if both screening and confirmatory genes are detected with a Ct value ≤ 40 cycles.
  • Detectability: NAAT can be positive as early as day 1 of symptom onset (usually 5 days post-infection) and generally declines by the third week, often becoming undetectable thereafter.

Automated Real-Time RT-PCR

  • Systems include Truenat and CBNAAT (Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test, e.g., GeneXpert).
  • Widely accessible
  • Turnaround Time: Quick results in 30-60 minutes.
  • Automation: Fully automated with minimal handling, reducing biosafety hazards.
  • Gene Targets:
    • CBNAAT: E gene for screening, N2 gene for confirmation.
    • Truenat: E gene for screening, RdRp gene for confirmation.
  • Disadvantages: Limited to 1-4 samples per run, suitable for low sample loads (24-48 samples/day).

Antigen Detection

  • Rapid chromatographic immunoassay (SD Biosensor) for qualitative detection of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein.
  • Sample Collection: Nasopharyngeal swab immersed in viral extraction buffer to inactivate the virus and release the antigen.
  • Point-of-Care Testing: Conducted at the bedside within one hour; antigen stability is limited to one hour.
  • Performance: Highly specific (99–100%) but moderate sensitivity (50–84%); symptomatic but negative patients should be referred for RT-PCR testing.

Incorrect Options:

RNA (Option A): In an RT-PCR test for COVID-19, the viral RNA is converted into complementary DNA (cDNA) using reverse transcriptase enzyme. This cDNA is then amplified through PCR.

Structural Protein (Option C): Structural proteins are components of the virus, but they are not the target of RT-PCR testing. RT-PCR is designed to detect and amplify the genetic material of the virus.

Envelope (Option D): The envelope is a protein that is part of the virus structure. However, the envelope protein itself is not directly amplified in RT-PCR. The test targets the viral RNA, not the proteins.

a-dictid="9864ad42b21692777191febeee1002">lamina layer defect

Explanation:

  • Berry aneurysms primarily develop due to disruption of the internal elastic lamina of cerebral blood vessels. The internal elastic lamina is a critical structural component that provides tensile strength and elasticity to blood vessels. When this layer is compromised, the vessel wall becomes weakened and less able to withstand normal hemodynamic stresses, leading to outward bulging and eventual aneurysm formation.

Berry Aneurysm

Definition
  • Saccular outpouching of intracranial arterial wall
  • Represents 90% of cerebral aneurysms
  • Primary location: Circle of Willis
  • Most common sites:
    • Anterior communicating/anterior cerebral junction
    • Posterior communicating/internal carotid junction
    • Middle cerebral artery bifurcation
    • Basilar apex

Pathophysiological Mechanisms

Structural Changes:

  • Most important- Internal elastic lamina disruption
  • Media layer thinning
  • Adventitial layer remodeling

Molecular Mechanisms:

  • Inflammatory mediator activation
  • Matrix metalloproteinase upregulation
  • Vessel wall extracellular matrix degradation

Hemodynamic Factors:

  • Wall shear stress elevation
  • Flow-related endothelial injury
  • Intramural stress distribution alterations

Histopathological Classification

1. Mycotic:

  • Infectious arterial wall damage
  • Distal vessel predilection
  • Inflammatory cell infiltration

2. Arteriosclerotic:

  • Intimal hyperplasia
  • Media degeneration
  • Elastic fiber fragmentation

3. Traumatic:

  • Transmural disruption
  • False lumen formation
  • Adventitial hemorrhage

Rupture Risk Stratification

Morphological Criteria:

  • Size >7mm: high risk
  • Aspect ratio >1.6
  • Daughter sac presence
  • Wall irregularity

Hemodynamic Factors:

  • Systolic BP >140 mmHg
  • Flow pattern alterations
  • Intrasaccular pressure gradients

Genetic Markers:

  • Collagen deficiency
  • Elastic fiber abnormalities
  • Matrix metalloproteinase polymorphisms

Clinical Manifestations

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage:

  • Hunt-Hess grading scale correlation
  • Fisher scale for CT findings
  • Modified Rankin Scale outcomes

Mass Effect:

  • Cranial nerve compression syndromes
  • Brainstem compression sequelae
  • Hydrocephalus development

Thromboembolic Events:

  • Watershed infarction patterns
  • Perforator occlusion syndromes
  • Distal embolization phenomena

 

Endothelial injury due to HTN (Option A) while hypertension can exacerbate aneurysm formation and increase rupture risk, it is not the primary underlying cause of berry aneurysms. Hypertension acts as a contributing factor rather than the initiating defect.

Endothelial layer defect (Option C) although the endothelium can be involved in aneurysm progression, the primary defect occurs in the internal elastic lamina rather than the endothelial layer. The endothelial dysfunction is usually secondary to the underlying structural abnormality.

Adventitia defect (Option D) the adventitial layer is the outer layer of blood vessels and is not the primary site of berry aneurysm formation. The key pathology begins in the internal elastic lamina and medial layer of the vessel wall.

questions.stem: A 45-year patient working in a factory for the past 20 years presents with breathlessness. HRCT chest shows pleural thickening and fibrosis. Diagnosis is?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year patient working in a factory for the past 20 years presents with breathlessness. HRCT chest shows pleural thickening and fibrosis. Diagnosis is?
questions.solution: rong> The clinical presentation indicates asbestosis , a form of pneumoconiosis caused by prolonged asbestos exposure. The key diagnostic features in this case include the patient's 20-year occupational exposure in a factory setting, presenting symptom of breathlessness, and most importantly, the HRCT findings of pleural thickening and fibrosis . Pleural involvement i s a characteristic feature of asbestos-related lung disease , distinguishing it from other occupational lung diseases. Workers in the shipbuilding and construction trades, including pipe fitters and boilermakers, are occupationally exposed to asbestos. Asbestosis is a diffuse interstitial fibrosing disease of the lung . Past exposure to asbestos is specifically indicated by pleural plaques on chest radiographs, which are characterized by either thickening or calcification along the parietal pleura, particularly along the lower lung fields. Pulmonary function testing in asbestosis reveals a restrictive pattern with a decrease in both lung volumes and diffusing capacity. Complications include carcinoma of lung and mesothelioma . Coal worker pneumoconiosis (Option B) is characterized by small nodules diffusely distributed throughout the lungs, with upper lobe predominance and eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes. The presence of pleural thickening rather than nodular opacities makes this diagnosis less likely. Silicosis (Option C) typically presents with multiple small nodules in the upper lung zones with a characteristic "ground-glass" appearance. The absence of these findings and the presence of pleural thickening make silicosis an unlikely diagnosis. Berylliosis (Option D) presents with early-stage parenchymal nodules and later develops lymphadenopathy and interstitial fibrosis. The prominent pleural involvement seen in this case is not typical of berylliosis, and the exposure history doesn't suggest beryllium exposure. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 10-year-old male child presents with headache and cola-colored urine. His parents report throat pain 2 weeks ago. On examination, red blood cells are present in urine and his KFT is increased two fold. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 10-year-old male child presents with headache and cola-colored urine. His parents report throat pain 2 weeks ago. On examination, red blood cells are present in urine and his KFT is increased two fold. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: an infection, most commonly caused by Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus . The diagnosis is supported by the classic presentation of cola-colored urine and recent history of throat infection . The condition develops due to formation of immune complexes by streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B (SPEB) , which get distributed in renal parenchyma and damage blood vessels, leading to increased protein excretion and hematuria. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) Cause Group A β-Hemolytic streptococci Pathogenesis Immune-complex mediated ( Type III hypersensitivity reaction) Clinical manifestations It is more common in children and young adults. History of impetigo (2-6 weeks) or pharyngitis (1-3 weeks ). {{caption_text}} Pulmonary oedema (shortness of breath, cough, chest pain) Periorbital and pedal oedema Hypertensive encephalopathy: Abrupt rise in BP Headache Loss of consciousness Features of uremia include fatigue, weakness, confusion, swelling over body parts, shortness of breath, abnormal urine output, nausea, and vomiting. Test for antibodies Anti- DNAse Anti-Hyaluronidase ASO (antistreptolysin O) titer Lab findings Urine analysis: Red-colored urine, which turns dark ( cola-colored ) on standing ( hematuria ). {{caption_text}} Raised values of renal function test (serum creatinine, urea, etc). Raised serum potassium Low serum levels of C3, IgG & CH50 Normal serum C4 level. Pathological findings Gross findings: Flea-bitten appearance of kidneys {{caption_text}} Light microscopy: Hypercellular glomeruli (increased number of neutrophils, macrophages, endothelial and mesangial cells). {{caption_text}} Electron microscopy: Subepithelial humps (due to immune complex deposition) {{caption_text}} Immunofluorescence study: A starry-sky appearance (Granular) is observed (due to immune complex deposition). {{caption_text}} Management Self-limiting disorder Conservative and supportive management involves: HTN crisis : Labetalol (IV), sodium nitroprusside Pulmonary edema: Furosemide Antibiotics (Benzathine penicillin) Dialysis if needed Minimal change disease (Option A) is characterized by minimal changes in the glomeruli on microscopic examination and commonly presents in children with proteinuria, edema, and hypoalbuminemia. The absence of significant proteinuria and presence of hematuria rules out this diagnosis. Membranous Glomerulonephritis (Option B) typically presents with thickening of the glomerular basement membrane due to immune complex deposits, causing proteinuria, edema, and hypoalbuminemia. The acute onset and recent history of throat infection makes this diagnosis less likely. IgA nephropathy (Option D) is characterized by IgA deposits in the mesangium and typically develops within 48 hours after an upper respiratory tract infection. The timing of symptoms (2 weeks after throat pain) and the classic cola-colored urine presentation makes this diagnosis less likely. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
an infection, most commonly caused by Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus. The diagnosis is supported by the classic presentation of cola-colored urine and recent history of throat infection. The condition develops due to formation of immune complexes by streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B (SPEB), which get distributed in renal parenchyma and damage blood vessels, leading to increased protein excretion and hematuria.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)

Cause

Group A β-Hemolytic streptococci

Pathogenesis

Immune-complex mediated (Type III hypersensitivity reaction)

Clinical manifestations
  • It is more common in children and young adults.
  • History of impetigo (2-6 weeks) or pharyngitis (1-3 weeks).
  • Pulmonary oedema (shortness of breath, cough, chest pain)
  • Periorbital and pedal oedema
  • Hypertensive encephalopathy:
    • Abrupt rise in BP
    • Headache
    • Loss of consciousness
  • Features of uremia include fatigue, weakness, confusion, swelling over body parts, shortness of breath, abnormal urine output, nausea, and vomiting.

Test for antibodies
  • Anti- DNAse
  • Anti-Hyaluronidase
  • ASO (antistreptolysin O) titer

Lab findings

  • Urine analysis: Red-colored urine, which turns dark (cola-colored) on standing (hematuria).
  • Raised values of renal function test (serum creatinine, urea, etc).
  • Raised serum potassium
  • Low serum levels of C3, IgG & CH50
  • Normal serum C4 level.

Pathological findings
  • Gross findings: Flea-bitten appearance of kidneys

 

  • Light microscopy: Hypercellular glomeruli (increased number of neutrophils, macrophages, endothelial and mesangial cells).

 

  • Electron microscopy: Subepithelial humps (due to immune complex deposition)

 

  • Immunofluorescence study: A starry-sky appearance (Granular) is observed (due to immune complex deposition).

Management

  • Self-limiting disorder
  • Conservative and supportive management involves:
    • HTN crisis: Labetalol (IV), sodium nitroprusside
    • Pulmonary edema: Furosemide
    • Antibiotics (Benzathine penicillin)
    • Dialysis if needed

 

Minimal change disease (Option A) is characterized by minimal changes in the glomeruli on microscopic examination and commonly presents in children with proteinuria, edema, and hypoalbuminemia. The absence of significant proteinuria and presence of hematuria rules out this diagnosis.

Membranous Glomerulonephritis (Option B) typically presents with thickening of the glomerular basement membrane due to immune complex deposits, causing proteinuria, edema, and hypoalbuminemia. The acute onset and recent history of throat infection makes this diagnosis less likely.

IgA nephropathy (Option D) is characterized by IgA deposits in the mesangium and typically develops within 48 hours after an upper respiratory tract infection. The timing of symptoms (2 weeks after throat pain) and the classic cola-colored urine presentation makes this diagnosis less likely.

Definition

questions.stem: In a village with a given population, the total number of live births in a year is 4000. 40 newborns died within the first 7 days of life whereas 40 died due to various causes between 8 to 28 days of life. There were 50 deaths between the age of 1 month to 6 months of life and O of them died in utero. What is the neonatal mortality rate in this population?
questions.stemHtml: In a village with a given population, the total number of live births in a year is 4000. 40 newborns died within the first 7 days of life whereas 40 died due to various causes between 8 to 28 days of life. There were 50 deaths between the age of 1 month to 6 months of life and O of them died in utero. What is the neonatal mortality rate in this population?
questions.solution: g>Neonatal mortality rate (NMR) calculation: NMR = (Number of neonatal deaths/Total number of live births) x 1,000 Given: Total live births = 4,000, Deaths (0-7 days) = 40 Deaths (8-28 days) = 40 NMR ((40+40)/4,000) x 1,000 = (80/4,000) x 1,000 = 0.02 x 1,000 = 20 Interpretation: The NMR in this population is 20 per 1,000 live births, indicating 20 deaths within the first 28 days of life per 1,000 live births. Causes of Neonatal deaths: Most common cause - Birth Asphyxia or Hypoxia Other causes : Prematurity and low birth weight, neonatal pneumonia, sepsis, congenital anomalies, diarrhea, injuries, and other non-communicable diseases. Danger Signs: Refusal to feed, lethargic, cold to touch, difficult or rapid breathing, convulsions, persistent vomiting, jaundice at birth, blue color of extremities. Other Neonatal Mortality Indicators: Early neonatal mortality rate (No. of deaths of children (neonate) 0 – 7 days of life / live births) x 1000) Late neonatal mortality rate (No. of deaths of children (neonate) 8th – 28 days of life / live birth) x 1000) Post neonatal mortality rate (No. of deaths of children (neonate) 29th day - 1 year of life / live births) x 1000) @Neet_pg_bot

g>Neonatal mortality rate (NMR) calculation:
  • NMR = (Number of neonatal deaths/Total number of live births) x 1,000
  • Given:

  • Interpretation: The NMR in this population is 20 per 1,000 live births, indicating 20 deaths within the first 28 days of life per 1,000 live births.

Most common cause - Birth Asphyxia or Hypoxia

Other causes: Prematurity and low birth weight, neonatal pneumonia, sepsis, congenital anomalies, diarrhea, injuries, and other non-communicable diseases.

questions.solution: dictid="b29a1a16ab1692777199ede1c6e28b">stain (A type of negative stain) is specifically used to visualize the capsule surrounding Cryptococcus neoformans in CSF samples. A clear halo around the yeast cells indicates the presence of the capsule, which is an important virulence factor. Urease test positive Maltese cross appearance under polarising microscope Cryptococcus Spp. Cryptococcus is a true yeast. Capsule Polysaccharide capsule - helps in serotyping and protection against phagocytosis . Serotypes A, D, AD serotypes - Cryptococcus variety neoformans B, C serotypes -Cryptococcus variety gattii Virulence factors Polysaccharide Capsule : The primary virulence factor. It helps the pathogen evade phagocytosis and suppresses the host’s local immune responses, enabling the organism to survive and spread. Melanin Production : Cryptococcus produces melanin via the enzyme phenol oxidase, which contributes to its virulence by protecting the pathogen from oxidative stress and immune defenses. Enzyme Production : The fungus secretes several enzymes, including: Phospholipase : Aids in tissue invasion and damage. Urease : Helps the fungus survive in the host environment by neutralizing acidic conditions, enhancing its ability to colonize and spread. Risk of infection Immunocompromised States: HIV/AIDS, cancer, organ transplant recipients, those on immunosuppressive therapies, extremes of age are at higher risk. Geographic Location: Exposure to environments where Cryptococcus gattii is endemic, such as tropical and subtropical regions Environmental Exposure: Exposure to bird droppings or decaying wood can increase the likelihood of infection, especially with C. neoformans. Management of cryptococcosis Microscopy India ink - Demonstrates the capsule, which appears as clear space surrounding the round budding yeast cells Mucicarmine stain: It stains the carminophilic cell wall of C. neoformans Culture Sabouraud Dextrose Agar , forming smooth, mucoid, cream-coloured colonies. Niger seed agar and bird seed agar : Demonstrates melanin production (brown colored colonies) due to phenol oxidase/laccase enzyme. The ability to grow at 37°C and hydrolyse urea differentiates C. neoformans from non-pathogenic cryptococci {{caption_text}} Antigen detection tests Demonstration of the capsular antigen by Precipitation and Latex agglutination test Treatment Initial Treatment with liposomal Amphotericin B and Flucytosine Maintenance Therapy with Fluconazole for 6-12 months, depending on immune status. Monitoring: Regularly check CSF for fungal clearance, renal function, and electrolytes. Management of Underlying Conditions: Optimize ART to reduce recurrence risk. Incorrect Options: Aspergillus (Option A) : Aspergillus species are molds, not yeasts, and they do not have a thick capsule. They do not stain well with India ink. Penicillium (Option B) : Penicillium is also a mold, and like Aspergillus , it lacks a thick capsule and is not typically identified using India ink. Candida (Option D) : While Candida species are yeasts, they do not have the same thick, gelatinous capsule that would be visible with India ink staining. Candida is typically diagnosed using other methods like Gram staining or culture. @Neet_pg_bot

dictid="b29a1a16ab1692777199ede1c6e28b">stain (A type of negative stain) is specifically used to visualize the capsule surrounding Cryptococcus neoformans in CSF samples.

  • A clear halo around the yeast cells indicates the presence of the capsule, which is an important virulence factor.

  • Urease test positive

  • Maltese cross appearance under polarising microscope

    • Cryptococcus Spp.

    Cryptococcus is a true yeast.

    Capsule

    Polysaccharide capsule - helps in serotyping and protection against phagocytosis .

    Serotypes

    A, D, AD serotypes - Cryptococcus variety neoformans

    B, C serotypes -Cryptococcus variety gattii

    Virulence factors

    • Polysaccharide Capsule: The primary virulence factor. It helps the pathogen evade phagocytosis and suppresses the host’s local immune responses, enabling the organism to survive and spread.

    • Melanin Production: Cryptococcus produces melanin via the enzyme phenol oxidase, which contributes to its virulence by protecting the pathogen from oxidative stress and immune defenses.

    • Enzyme Production: The fungus secretes several enzymes, including:

      • Phospholipase: Aids in tissue invasion and damage.

      • Urease: Helps the fungus survive in the host environment by neutralizing acidic conditions, enhancing its ability to colonize and spread.

    Risk of infection

    Immunocompromised States:

    • HIV/AIDS, cancer, organ transplant recipients, those on immunosuppressive therapies, extremes of age are at higher risk.

    Geographic Location:

    • Exposure to environments where Cryptococcus gattii is endemic, such as tropical and subtropical regions

    Environmental Exposure:

    • Exposure to bird droppings or decaying wood can increase the likelihood of infection, especially with C. neoformans.

     

    Management of cryptococcosis

    Microscopy

    • India ink- Demonstrates the capsule, which appears as clear space surrounding the round budding yeast cells

    • Mucicarmine stain: It stains the carminophilic cell wall of C. neoformans

    Culture

    • Sabouraud Dextrose Agar, forming smooth, mucoid, cream-coloured colonies.

    • Niger seed agar and bird seed agar: Demonstrates melanin production (brown colored colonies) due to phenol oxidase/laccase enzyme.

    • The ability to grow at 37°C and hydrolyse urea differentiates C. neoformans from non-pathogenic cryptococci

    Antigen detection tests

    Demonstration of the capsular antigen by Precipitation and Latex agglutination test

    Treatment

    • Initial Treatment with liposomal Amphotericin B and Flucytosine

    • Maintenance Therapy with Fluconazole for 6-12 months, depending on immune status.

    • Monitoring: Regularly check CSF for fungal clearance, renal function, and electrolytes.

    • Management of Underlying Conditions: Optimize ART to reduce recurrence risk.

    Incorrect Options:

    Aspergillus (Option A): Aspergillus species are molds, not yeasts, and they do not have a thick capsule. They do not stain well with India ink.

    Penicillium (Option B): Penicillium is also a mold, and like Aspergillus, it lacks a thick capsule and is not typically identified using India ink.

    Candida (Option D): While Candida species are yeasts, they do not have the same thick, gelatinous capsule that would be visible with India ink staining. Candida is typically diagnosed using other methods like Gram staining or culture.

The eggs are colorless and not bile-stained

Enterobius vermicularis / Pinworm / Threadworm

Epidemiology:

  • The most common age group being school children.
  • Infections can persist for years due to auto-infective cycles.
  • Factors contributing to infection include:
    • Overcrowding
    • Impaired hygiene
    • Poor personal care practices (such as nail-biting and inadequate handwashing).

Morphology

Adult worm

 
  • The adults are short, white, and fusiform, resembling bits of white thread.
  • The mouth is surrounded by three wing-like structures called cervical alae, which are transversely striated.

Female worm

 
  • Females are long.
  • The posterior third tapers into a thin, pointed, pin-like tail.
  • Females are oviparous.

Male worm
  • The posterior end is tightly curved ventrally, sharply truncated, and has a prominent copulatory spicule.

Eggs

 
  • The eggs are colorless and not bile-stained
  • They float in saturated salt solution and have an elongated ovoid shape.
  • Each egg contains a tadpole-shaped, coiled embryo that becomes infectious only 6 hours after being deposited.

Scotch-tape test:

  • A piece of clear tape is pressed against the skin around the anus to collect eggs, typically overnight. The tape is then examined under a microscope for pinworm eggs.

Life cycle:

  • Enterobius vermicularis spends the entire lifecycle in humans.
  • It has no intermediate hosts and does not undergo systemic migration.
  • The eggs hatch in the intestine, and the larvae enter the caecum and mature into adults.
  • The male worm does not migrate and most often dies after mating and is passed in the feces.
  • The female worm migrates to the rectum from the colon and travels to the perianal skin at night to lay its sticky eggs and dies after laying all eggs or gets crushed due to scratching.

 

Pathogenicity:

  • The embryonated egg is the infective form.
  • The disease thus caused is called enterobiasis, which is more common in children than in adults.
  • It affects females > males.
  • The infection occurs in two ways:
    • Exogenous autoinfection is where the eggs are transferred from the perianal region to the mouth by nails after scratching the region.
    • Endogenous autoinfection/retro-infection is where the larva migrates retrograde and travels back into the colon after hatching in the perianal skin.

Incorrect Options:

Trichuris trichiura (Option B) (whipworm): While whipworms can infect the intestines, they are not typically associated with perianal itching or the nocturnal symptoms described. Their main symptoms involve abdominal pain, diarrhea, and occasionally rectal prolapse.

Trichinella spiralis (Option C): This parasite causes trichinosis, which is typically associated with consuming undercooked pork or wild game. The primary symptoms are muscle pain and swelling, not perianal itching.

Strongyloides stercoralis (Option D): This parasite causes strongyloidiasis, which typically presents with symptoms like abdominal pain, diarrhea, and skin rashes, but not specifically with perianal itching.
