questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy developed bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps. The bacteria isolated from the stool specimen was non motile and did not ferment lactose or mannitol. Which of the following organisms is implicated here?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy developed bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps. The bacteria isolated from the stool specimen was non motile and did not ferment lactose or mannitol. Which of the following organisms is implicated here?
questions.solution: ng>Shigella dysenteriae is a key pathogen that can cause bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps , typical of shigellosis . This organism is non-motile, does not ferment lactose or mannitol, and typically produces bloody diarrhea due to the invasion of the intestinal mucosa and resulting ulceration . Clinical Presentation of Shigella: Diarrhea: Typically acute and often bloody (dysentery). Incubation Period: 1-3 days after exposure. Prodromal Period: 1-2 days after the incubation period. Abdominal Pain: Severe cramping. Fever: Often high-grade. Tenesmus: Painful straining with defecation. Systemic Symptoms: Malaise, headache, and sometimes vomiting. Complications Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS): Particularly associated with Shigella dysenteriae type 1. Reactive Arthritis: More commonly seen after infection with Shigella flexneri . Neurological Complications: Including seizures, especially in young children. Diagnosis Clinical Evaluation: Based on symptoms such as bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever, along with a recent history of exposure (e.g., travel to endemic areas). Laboratory Tests: Stool Culture: Gold standard for diagnosis; Shigella species identified on selective media like MacConkey agar or XLD (xylose lysine deoxycholate) agar. Biochemical Tests: Confirmatory tests include lactose non-fermentation and indole production, among other specific biochemical characteristics. Serotyping: Identification of specific Shigella species and serotypes using agglutination tests with specific antisera. PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction): Rapid detection of Shigella -specific genes and virulence factors. Stool Microscopy: Presence of leukocytes and erythrocytes in stool samples indicative of invasive diarrhea. Treatment Fluid Replacement: Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT): Recommended for mild to moderate dehydration. Intravenous Fluids: Necessary for severe dehydration or if the patient cannot tolerate oral fluids. Antibiotic Therapy: Recommended for severe cases, young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised patients. First-line Antibiotics: Include fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin), third-generation cephalosporins (e.g., ceftriaxone), or azithromycin based on susceptibility testing. Increasing antibiotic resistance necessitates periodic updates on local resistance patterns. Symptomatic Treatment: Antipyretics for managing fever. Avoidance of antimotility agents like loperamide, which can worsen the infection. Incorrect Options: E. coli (Option B) : While E. coli (especially E. coli O157:H7) can cause bloody diarrhea, it is lactose fermenting and typically motile . Furthermore, E. coli infections are associated with hemorrhagic colitis and may present with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) in severe cases. The stool culture results indicating non-motility and no lactose or mannitol fermentation are not typical of E. coli . Salmonella (Option C) : Salmonella species can cause gastroenteritis with bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. However, Salmonella is typically motile and lactose non-fermenting , so it could appear similar to Shigella , but it typically presents with non-bloody diarrhea in many cases and a longer incubation period. Shigella sonnei (Option D) : Like Shigella dysenteriae , Shigella sonnei can cause bloody diarrhea but is often less virulent and typically produces a milder infection . While it is non-motile and lactose non-fermenting , the severity of symptoms with Shigella sonnei usually doesn't match that of Shigella dysenteriae , which is often associated with more severe disease like dysentery . @Neet_pg_bot

  • Often high-grade.

  • Painful straining with defecation.

  • Malaise, headache, and sometimes vomiting.

  • Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS): Particularly associated with Shigella dysenteriae type 1.
  • Reactive Arthritis: More commonly seen after infection with Shigella flexneri.
  • Neurological Complications: Including seizures, especially in young children.

Diagnosis

Clinical Evaluation:

  • Based on symptoms such as bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever, along with a recent history of exposure (e.g., travel to endemic areas).

Laboratory Tests:

  • Stool Culture: Gold standard for diagnosis; Shigella species identified on selective media like MacConkey agar or XLD (xylose lysine deoxycholate) agar.
  • Biochemical Tests: Confirmatory tests include lactose non-fermentation and indole production, among other specific biochemical characteristics.
  • Serotyping: Identification of specific Shigella species and serotypes using agglutination tests with specific antisera.
  • PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction): Rapid detection of Shigella-specific genes and virulence factors.
  • Stool Microscopy: Presence of leukocytes and erythrocytes in stool samples indicative of invasive diarrhea.

Treatment

Fluid Replacement:

  • Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT): Recommended for mild to moderate dehydration.
  • Intravenous Fluids: Necessary for severe dehydration or if the patient cannot tolerate oral fluids.

Antibiotic Therapy:

  • Recommended for severe cases, young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised patients.
  • First-line Antibiotics: Include fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin), third-generation cephalosporins (e.g., ceftriaxone), or azithromycin based on susceptibility testing.
  • Increasing antibiotic resistance necessitates periodic updates on local resistance patterns.

Symptomatic Treatment:

  • Antipyretics for managing fever.
  • Avoidance of antimotility agents like loperamide, which can worsen the infection.

Incorrect Options:

E. coli (Option B): While E. coli (especially E. coli O157:H7) can cause bloody diarrhea, it is lactose fermenting and typically motile. Furthermore, E. coli infections are associated with hemorrhagic colitis and may present with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) in severe cases. The stool culture results indicating non-motility and no lactose or mannitol fermentation are not typical of E. coli.

Salmonella (Option C): Salmonella species can cause gastroenteritis with bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. However, Salmonella is typically motile and lactose non-fermenting, so it could appear similar to Shigella, but it typically presents with non-bloody diarrhea in many cases and a longer incubation period.

Shigella sonnei (Option D): Like Shigella dysenteriae, Shigella sonnei can cause bloody diarrhea but is often less virulent and typically produces a milder infection. While it is non-motile and lactose non-fermenting, the severity of symptoms with Shigella sonnei usually doesn't match that of Shigella dysenteriae, which is often associated with more severe disease like dysentery.

questions.solution: 777194239a21b52c">pararenal space lies between the posterior parietal peritoneum & the perirenal fat, and it contains the head, neck, and body of the pancreas (the tail of the pancreas is within the splenorenal ligament), ascending and descending colon, and the duodenum (except for the proximal first segment). The retroperitoneum divides into three main anatomical spaces: Retroperitoneal spaces Anterior pararenal space It contains the head, neck, and body of the pancreas (the tail of the pancreas is within the splenorenal ligament), the ascending and descending colon, and the duodenum (except for the proximal first segment). Perirenal space This includes the adrenal gland, kidney, ureters, and renal vessels. (Statement 2 ruled out) Posterior pararenal space It is surrounded by the posterior leaf of the renal fascia and muscles of the posterior abdominal wall , contains no major organs and is composed primarily of fat, blood vessels, and lymphatics. As there is a history of renal problems in his brother and father, he requested an abdominal ultrasound, which revealed the presence of multiple renal and pancreatic cysts. 24-hour urinary metanephrine was sent, which was elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?Multiple endocrine neoplasia type I
questions.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man came to the clinic with a headache, palpitations, and sweating. As there is a history of renal problems in his brother and father, he requested an abdominal ultrasound, which revealed the presence of multiple renal and pancreatic cysts. 24-hour urinary metanephrine was sent, which was elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?Multiple endocrine neoplasia type I
questions.solution: li>The most likely diagnosis is Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease , a hereditary condition characterised by the development of multiple cysts in the kidneys, pancreas, and other organs. VHL is an autosomal dominant disorder due to VHL gene mutation on chromosome 3. Patients often have an increased risk of developing pheochromocytomas, which can cause symptoms like headaches, palpitations, and sweating. The elevated urinary metanephrines further support this diagnosis, as they are markers for pheochromocytomas. It is also associated with the development of various tumours like Hemangioblastomas in the CNS (cerebellum and retina) Cysts of the pancreas, liver, and kidneys Renal cell carcinomas Multiple endocrine neoplasia type I (Option A) is a genetic condition characterised by the development of tumours in multiple endocrine glands, and it typically features hyperparathyroidism, pituitary adenomas, and pancreatic tumours, rather than the renal and pancreatic cysts as seen in VHL. Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome (Option C) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder clinically manifested by fibrofolliculomas, renal cell carcinoma, lung cysts, and spontaneous pneumothorax. It is caused by mutations in the FLCN gene. Though they develop renal tumours, they do not commonly cause pancreatic cysts , pheochromocytomas , or elevated metanephrines . Tuberous sclerosis (Option D), also called Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), is an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in either the TSC1 or TSC2 gene. It causes benign tumours in various organs, including the brain, kidneys, heart, and skin. It also leads to skin lesions like ash-leaf spots, shagreen patches, and facial angiofibroma. However, pancreatic cysts and pheochromocytomas are not typically associated with tuberous sclerosis. @Neet_pg_bot

General Fertility rate

Definition

Disadvantages and advantages

It is a common postoperative condition where the normal peristalsis of the intestines is temporarily reduced or absent, leading to a buildup of gas and fluid in the intestines, often seen on X-ray, which is frequently associated with hypokalemia . Paralytic ileus Etiology Abdominal surgery. Uremia. Mesenteric ischemia. Retroperitoneal hematoma. Intra-abdominal sepsis. Dyselectrolytemia (e.g. hypokalemia) (Option B) Drugs affecting intestinal motility: Opiates. Antipsychotics. Clinical Features Abdominal distension. Abdominal discomfort. Non-colicky pain. Vomiting. Non-passage of feces and flatus. Absence of bowel sounds. Investigations IOC: Abdominal X-ray. Findings: Dilated bowel loops. Gas in the colon and rectum. Multiple air-fluid levels. Management Decompression: Nasogastric aspiration. Diet: Restrict oral intake until bowel sounds return or the patient starts passing faeces and flatus. Treatment of Underlying Cause: Correct dyselectrolytemia (e.g., hypokalemia). Discontinue medications affecting motility (e.g., opiates). Hypocalcemia (Option A) can cause muscle cramps and other symptoms, but it is not typically associated with paralytic ileus. Hyperkalemia (Option C) does not commonly result in paralytic ileus. Hypercalcemia (Option D) is not associated with paralytic ileus. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male presents with diffuse abdominal pain. He has a past history of peptic ulcer disease. Physical examination reveals rigidity. An X-ray of the abdomen is shown below. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old male presents with diffuse abdominal pain. He has a past history of peptic ulcer disease. Physical examination reveals rigidity. An X-ray of the abdomen is shown below. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.solution: rong> Explanation: The presence of air under the diaphragm on an X-ray (pneumoperitoneum) is a classic sign of perforated viscus , most commonly due to a perforated peptic ulcer which is a surgical emergency. Physical examination findings of rigidity and past history of peptic ulcer disease also support this diagnosis. Hence, the most appropriate next step in management is urgent surgical exploration to repair the perforation and address any potential complications, such as peritonitis. Delaying the surgery can lead to potential complications. Antibiotics and NPO (nothing by mouth) (Option A) are part of the supportive treatment; they are not sufficient alone in this case. The presence of free air under the diaphragm indicates a perforation that requires immediate surgical intervention. Upper GI endoscopy (Option B) is useful for identifying ulcers in the non-perforated stage, but this patient already shows signs of perforation, including rigidity and free air; hence, surgery is the immediate priority. CT abdomen (Option D) of the abdomen can provide valuable information in many cases of abdominal pain, including suspected perforation, but it is not the next best step when there are signs of peritonitis, such as rigidity during physical examination. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male presents with a low backache and weight loss. He has progressive difficulty in urination and had an episode of urinary retention two days back, which was relieved by catheterisation. PSA was done, which was 5.2 ng/ml, and an x-ray of the LS spine showed osteoblastic changes. What is the clinical diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old male presents with a low backache and weight loss. He has progressive difficulty in urination and had an episode of urinary retention two days back, which was relieved by catheterisation. PSA was done, which was 5.2 ng/ml, and an x-ray of the LS spine showed osteoblastic changes. What is the clinical diagnosis?
questions.solution: strong> The combination of urinary symptoms , elevated PSA , and osteoblastic changes on the x-ray strongly points to prostate cancer. Osteoblastic changes in the lumbar spine are a characteristic feature that suggests bone metastasis, which is common in prostate cancer, as it frequently metastasises to bone. Investigations for Prostate Cancer DRE Physical examination detects nodules but is limited in early-stage PSA Test Measures PSA levels; elevated levels suggest cancer TRUS Imaging with the rectal probe detects abnormalities mpMRI Advanced imaging; superior for staging and capsular spread Prostate Biopsy The gold standard for diagnosis; tissue sampling for cancer cells Benign prostatic hypertrophy (Option A) can also cause urinary symptoms like difficulty urinating and urinary retention , but it does not cause weight loss or osteoblastic bone changes on an x-ray. Additionally, the PSA in BPH is usually mildly elevated but not to the degree seen in prostate cancer. Carcinoma bladder (Option B) can cause urinary symptoms like hematuria, dysuria, or obstructive voiding symptoms, but it is less likely to cause osteoblastic changes in the bones, and the PSA elevation is also not characteristic of bladder cancer. Renal cell cancer (Option D) presents with symptoms such as hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable abdominal mass. The symptoms described by the patient, along with the elevated PSA level and osteoblastic changes on the X-ray, are not characteristic of renal cell cancer. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: NITI Aayog has replaced the?
questions.stemHtml: NITI Aayog has replaced the?

options.label: B
options.text: National institute of health & family welfare (NIHFW)

questions.solution: trong>Explanation: The full form of NITI Aayog is National Institution for Transforming India. It replaced the planning commission on January 1, 2015. NITI Aayog is the organization responsible for developing the Health Index in India . The Health Index is a composite measure that tracks the performance of Indian states and Union Territories on various health indicators. Eg. Neonatal Mortality Rate, Under-5 Mortality Rate, etc. NITI Aayog replaced Planning Commission of India in 2015 , acts as a think tank to the central and state governments on policy matters, including health. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare collaborates with NITI Aayog and provides data but is not the primary organization for evaluating and releasing the Health Index. The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) focuses on biomedical research and is not involved in creating the Health Index. The World Health Organization (WHO) is an international body that provides health-related guidelines and support but does not develop the Health Index for India. Medical Council of India (MCI) (Option A): The MCI was a statutory body that regulates medical education. The MCI has been replaced by by the National Medical Commission (NMC) to enhance transparency and improve medical education standards. National Institute of Health & Family Welfare (NIHFW) (Option B): The NIHFW is an autonomous organization under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in India, the NIHFW has not been replaced by NITI Aayog. National Board of Examinations (NBE) (Option D): The NBE is an autonomous body responsible for conducting postgraduate medical examinations in India. The NBE has not been replaced by NITI Aayog. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 54-year-old farmer from Ohio presents to a physician with a chronic cough. A chest x-ray demonstrates a cavitary lesion with hilar lymphadenopathy. Biopsy of the lymph node and staining with lactophenol cotton blue demonstrates the following characteristics as shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old farmer from Ohio presents to a physician with a chronic cough. A chest x-ray demonstrates a cavitary lesion with hilar lymphadenopathy. Biopsy of the lymph node and staining with lactophenol cotton blue demonstrates the following characteristics as shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum . It is commonly found in regions with soil that is enriched with bird or bat droppings, such as the Ohio River Valley . This makes the farmer from Ohio particularly at risk, as he may have been exposed to the fungus while working in environments with high concentrations of bird or bat feces. The key features of histoplasmosis on the chest x-ray (cavitary lesion with hilar lymphadenopathy) are consistent with this diagnosis, as the infection often affects the lungs and can lead to chronic pulmonary disease in immunocompetent individuals. In some cases, it may cause granulomatous lymphadenopathy . The appearance of Histoplasma on lactophenol cotton blue staining typically shows small, round, or oval yeast cells inside macrophages, which is characteristic of this fungal pathogen. Based on the patient’s history, histopathology showing intramacrophagic yeast form and (LPCB) mount showing numerous hyaline hyphae with few tuberculate macroconidia (arrows) and many smooth-walled oval microconidia are pointing towards a diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis. Histoplasmosis Causative Agent Histoplasma capsulatum; thermally dimorphic fungus. H. capsulatum var. capsulatum: Causes classical histoplasmosis. H. capsulatum var. duboisii: Causes African histoplasmosis. Epidemiology Endemic to central and eastern USA; also found in Africa. Route of transmission Thrives in soil, decaying trees, and bird droppings. Inhalation of fungal spores. Clinical manifestations Classical histoplasmosis is often asymptomatic. Calcified lesions. Pulmonary disease mimics tuberculosis. Disseminated histoplasmosis can occur. Infection of the reticuloendothelial system causes: Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, fever, and anaemia Skin and mucous membrane: Granulomatous and ulcerative lesions. African Histoplasmosis: It primarily affects the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and bones Lungs are rarely involved, and disseminated cases are infrequent Specimens for Diagnosis Blood, urine, bone marrow, lesions Diagnosis Microscopy: Stained smears of the specimens show small intra- and extracellular yeast cells {{caption_text}} Culture: Blood agar and Sabouraud agar show characteristic growth White, cottony, mycelial growth with large thick-walled spherical spores with tuberculate (finger-like projections) {{caption_text}} Serodiagnosis: Antibody titers increase in progressive disease Antigen tests on urine and serum, are helpful for immunocompromised individuals Skin Test: Delayed hypersensitivity to histoplasmin confirms exposure Treatment Amphotericin-B for two to four weeks followed by a year of itraconazole Incorrect Options: Coccidioidomycosis (Option B) : Caused by Coccidioides species , this fungal infection is more common in the southwestern United States (California, Arizona, New Mexico) and is characterized by arthroconidia (spores) in sputum or biopsy, not the intracellular yeast forms typical of histoplasmosis. Cryptococcus (Option C) : Cryptococcus neoformans is another fungal pathogen, but it typically presents with meningitis , particularly in immunocompromised patients . It does not usually cause cavitary lung lesions with hilar lymphadenopathy in the manner seen in histoplasmosis. Blastomycosis (Option D) : Caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis , blastomycosis can also cause pulmonary infection with cavitary lesions, but it typically presents with a larger yeast form in tissue, and is more common in areas around the Great Lakes, Mississippi River, and St. Lawrence River regions, rather than Ohio. @Neet_pg_bot

    Causative Agent

    Histoplasma capsulatum; thermally dimorphic fungus.

    • H. capsulatum var. capsulatum: Causes classical histoplasmosis.
    • H. capsulatum var. duboisii: Causes African histoplasmosis.

    Epidemiology

    Route of transmission

    Thrives in soil, decaying trees, and bird droppings.

    Skin and mucous membrane: Granulomatous and ulcerative lesions.

    African Histoplasmosis:

    • It primarily affects the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and bones
    • Lungs are rarely involved, and disseminated cases are infrequent

    Specimens for Diagnosis

    Blood, urine, bone marrow, lesions

    Diagnosis

    Microscopy:

    • Stained smears of the specimens show small intra- and extracellular yeast cells

    Culture:

    • Blood agar and Sabouraud agar show characteristic growth
    • White, cottony, mycelial growth with large thick-walled spherical spores with tuberculate (finger-like projections)

    Serodiagnosis:

    • Antibody titers increase in progressive disease
    • Antigen tests on urine and serum, are helpful for immunocompromised individuals

    Skin Test:

    • Delayed hypersensitivity to histoplasmin confirms exposure

    Treatment

    Amphotericin-B for two to four weeks followed by a year of itraconazole

    Coccidioidomycosis (Option B): Caused by Coccidioides species, this fungal infection is more common in the southwestern United States (California, Arizona, New Mexico) and is characterized by arthroconidia (spores) in sputum or biopsy, not the intracellular yeast forms typical of histoplasmosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following options is considered a high-level disinfectant?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following options is considered a high-level disinfectant?
questions.solution: ed a high-level disinfectant , meaning it is capable of killing most microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses, and fungi, as well as spores (although it may require longer exposure times for spores). It is commonly used to disinfect medical equipment and instruments that cannot withstand the high temperatures required for autoclaving. Glutaraldehyde is effective at sterilizing items when used properly, although it can be toxic, so precautions are necessary during its use. Risk category Recommended method Medical device/Equipment 1. Critical device (high risk): Items that enter a normally sterile site . Sterilisation If heat resistant : Hot air oven or autoclave If heat-sensitive : Ionising radiation or ethylene oxide or plasma sterilisation. Surgical instruments , implants /prostheses, rigid endoscopes , syringes, needles, CuT, Urinary catheter 2. Semi-critical device (intermediate risk): Items in contact with mucous membranes or body fluids . High-level disinfection (HLD) : Such as glutaraldehyde , ortho-phthalaldehyde, formaldehyde and hydrogen peroxide . Respiratory equipment , non-invasive flexible endoscopes, bedpans , urine bottles 3. Non-critical (low-risk) Items in contact with intact skin. Intermediate or Low-level disinfection (ILD or LLD): Such as phenols (Option D ruled out) , chlorhexidine, isopropyl alcohol (Option A ruled out) , povidone-iodine , iodophores (Option C ruled out) , etc Patient items include blood pressure cuffs , ECG electrodes, thermometer and stethoscopes . Environmental surfaces include computers, bed rails , food utensils, bedside tables , patient furniture and floor. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A barber aged 42 years presented with a healed ulcer as below, over the lower medial aspect of the right leg. On examination, he has varicose veins on both his legs. What is the most likely type of ulcer he had?
questions.stemHtml: A barber aged 42 years presented with a healed ulcer as below, over the lower medial aspect of the right leg. On examination, he has varicose veins on both his legs. What is the most likely type of ulcer he had?
questions.solution: st likely diagnosis is venous ulcer , given the ulcer's location on the medial aspect of the leg and the presence of varicose veins , which are indicative of venous insufficiency. These ulcers commonly occur in areas of chronic venous insufficiency , often associated with varicose veins . Venous ulcer (Option C) Arterial ulcer (Option B) Neuropathic ulcer (Option A) Pressure ulcer Site Gaiter’s area (area between malleolus and calf) At distal ends of limbs, such as toes, feet and legs. Over toe joints, under the heel, over malleoli, under the metatarsal head, etc Seen over pressure points, most common are ischium, greater trochanter, sacrum, hee, malleolus, occiput, etc Appearance Vertically oval with a sloping edge and will not penetrate deep fascia. Punched-out edges are seen in this type of ulcer. Ulcers can be associated with gangrene and abscesses; osteomyelitis can be seen here. Punched out ulcer with bone as a base. Cause Caused by ambulatory chronic venous hypertension due to varicose veins. This occurs due to severe arterial insufficiency of digital and medium-sized arteries, leading to ischemia and tissue death in the region. It is caused due to repeated trauma and ischemia due to microangiopathy in diabetic patients . It is tissue necrosis and ulceration due to prolonged pressure on any part of the body. Characteristics It is initially painful, then chronically becomes painless. It heals on rest and treatment but reforms again. It is intensely painful, and distal pulses are not palpable, and associated with shiny skin, brittle nails and loss of hair over the region. It is also known as diabetic ulcer since it is seen in diabetic patients. It is common in bedridden patients with head injuries, neurological deficits, and comatose and stroke-ridden patients. Tuberculous ulcer (Option D) occurs when tuberculosis affecting the lungs spreads to the skin . This type of ulcer is relatively uncommon but can develop in individuals with advanced or untreated TB. These ulcers typically have distinct characteristics like an undermined edge and necrotic base and may show signs like scarring or lymphadenopathy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: What is the underlying cause of the symptoms exhibited by a 55-year-old male, including fever, fatigue, and abnormal vital signs, along with the identification of the causative agent based on the microscopic examination of his peripheral blood smear?
questions.solution: aee08b169277718361438e1a91">causative agent of severe malaria , which can present with symptoms like fever , fatigue , abnormal vital signs (such as hypotension or tachycardia), and in some cases, organ failure or cerebral malaria . It is the most dangerous of the Plasmodium species and can cause life-threatening complications, especially if not treated promptly. The microscopic findings described—infected red blood cells of various sizes, multiple ring forms within single red blood cells, and the presence of crescentic (banana-shaped) gametocytes—are characteristic of Plasmodium falciparum . questions.stem: What is the cause of the following appearance in IVP?
questions.stemHtml: What is the cause of the following appearance in IVP?
questions.solution: ost characteristic of ureterocoele , where there is a cystic dilation of the distal ureter at its insertion into the bladder. Ureterocele is the congenital dilation of the distal ureter within the bladder wall. It can obstruct urine flow, leading to recurrent UTIs and hydronephrosis. Treatment often involves surgical correction to relieve the obstruction. Ureterocoele Types Simple Ureterocele (Intravesical - 20%): Found entirely within the bladder and associated with a single ureter. It is less complex and easier to manage. Ectopic Ureterocele (80%) : Extends beyond the bladder and often involves a duplicated ureter. This is more complicated due to its location, which may involve the bladder, neck, or urethra. Etiology Congenital anomaly is caused by an obstruction in the development of the distal ureter during fetal growth, leading to cystic dilation at the ureteral orifice. Clinical Features Recurrent Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)/ Urosepsis. Unilateral Hydroureteronephrosis. Palpable Abdominal Mass: Particularly in children, where a distended bladder or large ureterocele might be felt as a mass. Investigations Ultrasound (USG): The first-line imaging modality revealing hydroureteronephrosis and a cystic structure in the bladder. Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU): Demonstrates a filling defect in the bladder caused by the ureterocele. Cystoscopy: Allows direct visualisation of the ureterocele as a cystic structure that enlarges and collapses with urine flow in the bladder. Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP): The investigation of choice (IOC) for diagnosing ureterocele, showing the characteristic "adder head" or "cobra head" appearance due to the dilated ureter within the bladder. {{caption_text}} Cobra head or adder head appearance Treatment The treatment approach depends on the type of ureterocele: Intravesical Ureterocele: Typically managed with an incision over the cyst wall to allow free flow of urine into the bladder, relieving the obstruction. Ectopic Ureterocele: More complex, often requiring surgical excision of the ureterocele and reimplantation of the ureter into the bladder to correct the abnormal anatomy. Associated Congenital Abnormalities The most common congenital abnormality of the upper urinary tract is ureteral duplication , which can be associated with ureterocele. Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) , another common congenital abnormality, may occur in conjunction with ureterocele, particularly in cases involving ureteral duplication. Horseshoe kidney (Option A) refers to a congenital fusion of the lower poles of the kidneys, forming a U-shape. IVP here shows characteristic findings, which include medial orientation of calyces (Hand Joining Sign) and high insertion of ureters with anterior transposition ("Flower Vase" appearance of the ureters) . {{caption_text}} {{caption_text}} Bladder tumour (Option C) may cause various structural changes in the bladder, but it normally does not result in the distinct cobra head appearance seen in the ureterocoele. Bladder tumours are more likely to show mass-like lesions or irregularities in the bladder contour. Posterior urethral valve (Option D) Posterior urethral valves are a congenital abnormality in males where there is a flap-like obstruction in the posterior urethra. This condition is typically diagnosed in infancy or childhood. While an IVP may show associated findings, such as bladder distention or bilateral hydronephrosis, it does not typically cause the cobra head appearance seen in the ureterocoele . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Receptor used for the entry of HIV virus into the host cell is?
questions.stemHtml: Receptor used for the entry of HIV virus into the host cell is?
questions.solution: p> CCR5 (C-C chemokine receptor type 5) is one of the primary receptors used by HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) to enter host cells. Specifically, CCR5 is found on the surface of CD4+ T cells and other immune cells, and HIV binds to it along with CD4 (another receptor) in order to gain entry into the host cell. Modes of Transmission of HIV Sexual Transmission : Most common (75% of cases). Heterosexual Route: Male to female via vaginal intercourse is typical; risk per encounter is low (0.1–1%). Higher risk with anal intercourse. Blood Transfusion : Least common (5% of cases) but has a high transmission risk (90–95%). Percutaneous/Mucosal Transmission : Includes needle stick injuries and sharing razors; less effective compared to sexual transmission. Perinatal Transmission : 20–40% risk of mother-to-fetus transmission without intervention; highest risk during delivery. Casual Contact: No evidence of transmission through casual contact, kissing, or insect bites. Viral Load : Highest in blood, genital secretions, and cerebrospinal fluid; minimal in saliva and other body fluids. Saliva : Contains substances that may inhibit HIV transmission. Pathogenesis: Receptor Attachment Main Receptor: HIV binds its gp120 to the CD4 receptor on host cells, primarily expressed on helper T cells and other cells like monocytes and macrophages. Co-Receptors: Fusion requires a second receptor: CXCR4 : Found on T lymphocytes. CCR5 : Present on macrophage lineage cells. (Option B) DC-SIGN: A dendritic cell-specific receptor that binds HIV-1 but does not mediate entry; facilitates transport to lymphoid organs. CCR5 Delta 32 Mutation: Mutation can block HIV entry: Homozygous individuals are resistant to HIV (1% of Northern Europeans). Heterozygous individuals may have delayed progression to AIDS (10–15% of Europeans). Replication {{caption_text}} Options A, C, and D are incorrect. These are not used as a receptor for the entry of HIV into the host cells. @Neet_pg_bot

p>

CCR5 (C-C chemokine receptor type 5) is one of the primary receptors used by HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) to enter host cells. Specifically, CCR5 is found on the surface of CD4+ T cells and other immune cells, and HIV binds to it along with CD4 (another receptor) in order to gain entry into the host cell.

Modes of Transmission of HIV

  • Sexual Transmission:
    • Most common (75% of cases).
    • Heterosexual Route: Male to female via vaginal intercourse is typical; risk per encounter is low (0.1–1%). Higher risk with anal intercourse.
  • Blood Transfusion: Least common (5% of cases) but has a high transmission risk (90–95%).
  • Percutaneous/Mucosal Transmission: Includes needle stick injuries and sharing razors; less effective compared to sexual transmission.
  • Perinatal Transmission: 20–40% risk of mother-to-fetus transmission without intervention; highest risk during delivery.
  • Casual Contact: No evidence of transmission through casual contact, kissing, or insect bites.
  • Viral Load: Highest in blood, genital secretions, and cerebrospinal fluid; minimal in saliva and other body fluids.
  • Saliva: Contains substances that may inhibit HIV transmission.

Pathogenesis:

  • Receptor Attachment
    • Main Receptor:
      • HIV binds its gp120 to the CD4 receptor on host cells, primarily expressed on helper T cells and other cells like monocytes and macrophages.
    • Co-Receptors: Fusion requires a second receptor:
      • CXCR4: Found on T lymphocytes.
      • CCR5: Present on macrophage lineage cells. (Option B)
    • DC-SIGN:
      • A dendritic cell-specific receptor that binds HIV-1 but does not mediate entry; facilitates transport to lymphoid organs.
    • CCR5 Delta 32 Mutation:
      • Mutation can block HIV entry:
        • Homozygous individuals are resistant to HIV (1% of Northern Europeans).
        • Heterozygous individuals may have delayed progression to AIDS (10–15% of Europeans).
  • Replication

Options A, C, and D are incorrect. These are not used as a receptor for the entry of HIV into the host cells.

questions.solution: l> Aedes albopictus , also known as the Asian tiger mosquito , is one of the primary vectors responsible for transmitting the Zika virus . g>intense pain during erection and a deviated penis for the past six months, is most likely suffering from Peyronie’s disease.

Peyronie’s disease

Definition

It is characterised by fibrous plaques in the tunica albuginea of the penis, causing abnormal curvature during erections.

Characteristics

Plaque Location: Typically on the dorsolateral aspect of the penis.

Curvature: Resulting from plaque contraction.

 

Causes
  • Trauma/Injury: Repeated minor trauma to the penis.
  • Genetic Factors: Possible genetic predisposition.
  • Connective Tissue Disorders: Associated with conditions like Dupuytren’s contracture.

Associated Conditions

Galezia’s Triad:

  • Dupuytren’s Contracture: Thickening and shortening of connective tissue in fingers.
  • Retroperitoneal Fibrosis: Fibrosis in the retroperitoneal space.
  • Peyronie’s Disease

Clinical Features
  • Painful Erection
  • Erectile Dysfunction
  • Penile Curvature
  • Palpable Plaques
  • Impotence & Infertility (in severe cases)

Treatment

Observation:

  • Spontaneous Resolution: Often improves without treatment.

Medical Management:

  • Oral Medications: Pentoxifylline, colchicine, vitamin E (efficacy varies).

Surgical Intervention (If Spontaneous Resolution Does Not Occur):

  • Nesbit Operation: Placement of a non-absorbable suture opposite the plaque to correct the curvature.
  • Plication Surgery: Shortens the longer side of the penis.
  • Plaque Excision and Grafting: Removes plaque and replaces it with graft material.
  • Penile Prosthesis: For severe cases.

 

Priapism (Option B) is a condition where a prolonged and often painful erection occurs unrelated to sexual stimulation. It is typically unrelated to penile curvature and is caused by abnormal blood flow in the penis, leading to stagnant blood in the erectile tissues. It is considered a urological emergency and requires immediate medical attention.

Marion’s disease (Option C) is also known as bladder neck stenosis or primary bladder neck obstruction (PBNO). Marion described diseases affecting the bladder and neck as causing urinary disturbances resembling those caused by prostate enlargement. However, these disturbances result from changes in the bladder neck itself, without any visible abnormalities.

Erectile dysfunction (Option D) is the inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for sexual intercourse. It is not associated with pain or penile curvature. In some cases, pain or discomfort may accompany an erection, but it is not the primary symptom of ED.

questions.solution: rong> involving a lymph node. The most characteristic finding is a “starry sky” pattern. At high-power magnification, the neoplastic cells are of intermediate size, similar to the size of benign histiocyte nuclei. The neoplastic cells have round nuclear contours, multiple nucleoli, frequent mitoses, and basophilic cytoplasm. Macrophages with engulfed pyknotic nuclei and nuclear debris are also present. Burkitt's lymphoma Aspects Description Definition An aggressive form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterised by the proliferation of mature B-cells. Epidemiology Endemic (African) form : Common in children, associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection. Sporadic form : Worldwide distribution, more common in children and young adults. Immunodeficiency-related : Often seen in HIV/AIDS patients. Etiology Strong association with EBV (especially in the endemic form). Translocations involving the MYC gene (chromosome 8). Genetic Abnormality t(8;14): MYC gene translocated next to the IgH locus (most common). t(2;8) or t(8;22) : Less common, involving MYC and Ig light chain loci. Clinical Features Endemic form : Presents with jaw or facial bone tumours. Sporadic form : Often involves the abdomen (e.g., ileum, cecum) and may cause bowel obstruction. Systemic symptoms : Fever, night sweats, weight loss. Pathology Histology : "Starry-sky" appearance due to numerous apoptotic cells and macrophages. Tumor cells are medium-sized with round nuclei, coarse chromatin, and high mitotic activity. Immunophenotype Positive for CD19 , CD20 (B-cell markers), and CD10 . Expresses surface IgM . High proliferation index (Ki-67 > 95%). Diagnosis Biopsy : Histological examination showing "starry-sky" appearance. Cytogenetics : Detection of MYC translocations. Immunohistochemistry : Positive for B-cell markers (CD19, CD20). Prognosis Highly aggressive but potentially curable with prompt treatment. Favorable response to chemotherapy in many cases. Treatment Chemotherapy : Intensive regimens like cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and methotrexate (CODOX-M) . CNS prophylaxis : Methotrexate or cytarabine. Supportive care for tumour lysis syndrome. Complications Risk of tumour lysis syndrome due to rapid tumour breakdown. It may progress to involve bone marrow or CNS if untreated. Differential Diagnosis Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Other high-grade B-cell lymphomas. Lymphoblastic lymphoma. Hodgkin lymphoma (rarely resembles). Kikuchi disease (Option A) is a subacute necrotising lymphadenopathy affecting young adults, predominantly women, especially in Japan and neighbouring Asian countries. It presents with painless lymphadenopathy, moderate fever, chills, myalgia, sore throat, and skin rashes . Histopathology reveals necrotising lymphadenitis with histiocyte proliferation and reactive germinal centres. Infectious mononucleosis (Option B) presents with a triad of fever, pharyngitis, and cervical or generalised lymphadenopathy. Histopathology reveals Paracortical hyperplasia with a mottled ("moth-eaten") lymph node architecture. Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) (Option C) is characterised by a heterogeneous cellularity comprising a minority of specific neoplastic cells—the Hodgkin cells, the Reed-Sternberg cells, and a majority of reactive non-neoplastic cells. {{caption_text}} @Neet_pg_bot

    Burkitt's lymphoma

    Aspects

    Description

    Definition

    An aggressive form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterised by the proliferation of mature B-cells.

    Epidemiology
    • Endemic (African) form: Common in children, associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection.
    • Sporadic form: Worldwide distribution, more common in children and young adults.
    • Immunodeficiency-related: Often seen in HIV/AIDS patients.

    Etiology
    • Strong association with EBV (especially in the endemic form).
    • Translocations involving the MYC gene (chromosome 8).

    Genetic Abnormality
    • t(8;14): MYC gene translocated next to the IgH locus (most common).
    • t(2;8) or t(8;22): Less common, involving MYC and Ig light chain loci.

    Clinical Features
    • Endemic form: Presents with jaw or facial bone tumours.
    • Sporadic form: Often involves the abdomen (e.g., ileum, cecum) and may cause bowel obstruction.
    • Systemic symptoms: Fever, night sweats, weight loss.

    Pathology
    • Histology: "Starry-sky" appearance due to numerous apoptotic cells and macrophages.
    • Tumor cells are medium-sized with round nuclei, coarse chromatin, and high mitotic activity.

    Immunophenotype
    • Positive for CD19, CD20 (B-cell markers), and CD10.
    • Expresses surface IgM.
    • High proliferation index (Ki-67 > 95%).

    Diagnosis
    • Biopsy: Histological examination showing "starry-sky" appearance.
    • Cytogenetics: Detection of MYC translocations.
    • Immunohistochemistry: Positive for B-cell markers (CD19, CD20).

    Prognosis
    • Highly aggressive but potentially curable with prompt treatment.
    • Favorable response to chemotherapy in many cases.

    Treatment
    • Chemotherapy: Intensive regimens like cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and methotrexate (CODOX-M).
    • CNS prophylaxis: Methotrexate or cytarabine.
    • Supportive care for tumour lysis syndrome.

    Complications
    • Risk of tumour lysis syndrome due to rapid tumour breakdown.
    • It may progress to involve bone marrow or CNS if untreated.

    Differential Diagnosis
    • Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
    • Other high-grade B-cell lymphomas.
    • Lymphoblastic lymphoma.
    • Hodgkin lymphoma (rarely resembles).

    Kikuchi disease (Option A) is a subacute necrotising lymphadenopathy affecting young adults, predominantly women, especially in Japan and neighbouring Asian countries. It presents with painless lymphadenopathy, moderate fever, chills, myalgia, sore throat, and skin rashes. Histopathology reveals necrotising lymphadenitis with histiocyte proliferation and reactive germinal centres.

    Infectious mononucleosis (Option B) presents with a triad of fever, pharyngitis, and cervical or generalised lymphadenopathy. Histopathology reveals Paracortical hyperplasia with a mottled ("moth-eaten") lymph node architecture.

    Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) (Option C) is characterised by a heterogeneous cellularity comprising a minority of specific neoplastic cells—the Hodgkin cells, the Reed-Sternberg cells, and a majority of reactive non-neoplastic cells.

questions.stem: What is the term for a stone obstructing the cystic duct, causing dilation of the common hepatic duct, resulting in CBD obstruction and jaundice?
questions.stemHtml: What is the term for a stone obstructing the cystic duct, causing dilation of the common hepatic duct, resulting in CBD obstruction and jaundice?
questions.solution: Mirizzi's syndrome is seen in 1% of all cholecystectomies, where a gallstone impacts the gallbladder wall, leading to compression and pressure necrosis. This often results in adherence to the common hepatic duct (CHD) or common bile duct (CBD) wall and can occasionally lead to a cholecystocholedochal fistula. It leads to biliary obstruction , which can result in jaundice and dilation of the bile ducts (CHD and CBD). Mirizzi’s syndrome Pathophysiology The gallstone usually impacts from the Hartmann's pouch, leading to compression of the CHD/CBD. Can also occur from the fundus of the gallbladder into the CBD. Clinical features Fever Abdominal pain Obstructive jaundice Upper abdominal tenderness on the right side Possible palpable soft, enlarged liver Csendes Classification Type I - Extrinsic compression of the CBD/CHD by a large impacted stone in Hartmann's pouch; IA- the presence of cystic duct IB- is obliterated cystic duct Type II - The stone has eroded the CBD/CHD less than 1/3rd of the circumference of the CBD/CHD, forming a fistula Type III - Involving up to 2/3rd of the circumference of CBD/ CHD Type IV - Cholecystocholedochal fistula (>2/3rd) involving the entire circumference of the CBD/CHD Type V - Cholecystocholedochal fistula with cholecystoenteric fistula without gallstone ileus (VA) or with gallstone ileus (VB) {{caption_text}} Investigations Ultrasonography (USG): Initial imaging to assess gallbladder and ducts. CT Scan: Provides detailed imaging of the biliary system. ERCP/ MRCP: Essential for delineating duct anatomy and identifying the site of obstruction. HIDA Scan: Useful for functional assessment of the biliary system. Findings: Dilatation of the intrahepatic biliary system with a block at the common hepatic duct (CHD). Acute cholecystitis (Option A) is inflammation of the gallbladder, typically due to gallstone obstruction of the cystic duct. While this condition can cause pain and tenderness in the right upper quadrant , it does not commonly cause dilation of the common hepatic duct or jaundice unless there is a secondary obstruction of the CBD or cystic duct. Porcelain gallbladder (Option B) refers to calcification of the gallbladder wall, usually due to chronic cholecystitis . This condition is associated with an increased risk of gallbladder cancer but does not cause biliary obstruction or jaundice due to stone impaction in the cystic duct. Cholesterolosis (Option C), also called strawberry gallbladder, involves lipid deposits in the gallbladder mucosa, leading to a characteristic appearance on imaging. It is often asymptomatic and does not typically cause biliary obstruction or jaundice . @Neet_pg_bot

    Pathophysiology
    • The gallstone usually impacts from the Hartmann's pouch, leading to compression of the CHD/CBD.

    Clinical features

    • Upper abdominal tenderness on the right side

    Csendes Classification

    Type I - Extrinsic compression of the CBD/CHD by a large impacted stone in Hartmann's pouch;

    • IA- the presence of cystic duct
    • IB- is obliterated cystic duct

    Type II - The stone has eroded the CBD/CHD less than 1/3rd of the circumference of the CBD/CHD, forming a fistula

    Type IV - Cholecystocholedochal fistula (>2/3rd) involving the entire circumference of the CBD/CHD

    • CT Scan: Provides detailed imaging of the biliary system.
    • ERCP/ MRCP: Essential for delineating duct anatomy and identifying the site of obstruction.
    • HIDA Scan: Useful for functional assessment of the biliary system.
    • Findings: Dilatation of the intrahepatic biliary system with a block at the common hepatic duct (CHD).

questions.solution: des tumour Explanation: The clinical features and HPE show increased stromal cellularity and overgrowth, giving rise to the typical leaf-like architecture, suggesting phyllodes tumour. Phyllodes tumours, also called cystosarcoma phyllodes, are stromal tumours developing from the breast's connective tissue. It occurs in middle-aged women (40 - 50 years). Most phyllodes tumours are benign (noncancerous) , but a small number (about 10% to 15%) can be borderline or malignant (cancerous). They present as a lump in the breast, which may be firm, smooth, and well-defined. It may also grow quickly from a few centimetres to massive lesions involving the entire breast. Phyllodes tumour is differentiated from fibroadenoma based on its overgrowth of stroma, increased mitotic activity and cellularity, and nuclear pleomorphism. (Option B ruled out) Inflammatory carcinoma (Option C) presents with redness, swelling, warmth, and often skin changes (such as peau d’orange). It also presents with more aggressive symptoms like axillary lymphadenopathy and is often accompanied by pain. Ductal carcinoma (Option D) usually presents with irregular masses , skin changes , and often axillary lymphadenopathy . Histologically, it is characterised by the proliferation of malignant epithelial cells in the ducts, not the stromal cellularity and leaflike pattern seen in phyllodes tumours. @Neet_pg_bot

Genetics Autosomal recessive disorder, caused by mutations in the β-globin gene leading to defective hemoglobin synthesis. Pathophysiology Reduced or absent β-globin chains lead to excess α-globin chains, which form unstable precipitates, causing ineffective erythropoiesis, hemolysis, and severe anaemia. Clinical Features Symptoms appear around 6 months of age (as fetal haemoglobin declines); severe anaemia, growth retardation, hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal deformities (crew-cut appearance on skull X-ray, frontal bossing), jaundice, and delayed puberty. Thalassemia Major (β-Thalassemia Major)

Features

Description

Definition

A severe form of β-thalassemia caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the β-globin gene (HBB) on chromosome 11, leading to absent or markedly reduced β-globin chain production.

Genetics

Autosomal recessive disorder, caused by mutations in the β-globin gene leading to defective hemoglobin synthesis.

Pathophysiology

Reduced or absent β-globin chains lead to excess α-globin chains, which form unstable precipitates, causing ineffective erythropoiesis, hemolysis, and severe anaemia.

Clinical Features

Symptoms appear around 6 months of age (as fetal haemoglobin declines); severe anaemia, growth retardation, hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal deformities (crew-cut appearance on skull X-ray, frontal bossing), jaundice, and delayed puberty.

Hematological Findings

  • Peripheral smear: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia, target cells, anisopoikilocytosis, nucleated RBCs.
  • Bone marrow: Erythroid hyperplasia with expansion of marrow cavities.

Hemoglobin Electrophoresis

Absent or very low HbA, markedly increased HbF (>90%), variable HbA2.

Complications

  • Iron overload (due to repeated transfusions leading to secondary hemochromatosis)
  • Cardiac failure (due to iron deposition)
  • Endocrinopathies (diabetes, hypothyroidism, hypogonadism)
  • Osteopenia/osteoporosis
  • Increased infection risk (especially from Yersinia and viral infections).

Diagnosis

Blood tests (CBC, peripheral smear), Hb electrophoresis/HPLC, Serum ferritin (for iron overload), Genetic testing (HBB gene mutations), Prenatal diagnosis (chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis).

Treatment

Regular blood transfusions, iron chelation therapy (deferoxamine, deferasirox, deferiprone), splenectomy (in refractory cases), and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) (only curative option).

Prevention

Carrier screening, genetic counselling, prenatal diagnosis, preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) in high-risk couples.

41a2">neonate presenting with the mentioned complaints and the barium swallow showing a “string sign” suggests Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS).

Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS)

Definition

It is a condition involving hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle, leading to gastric outlet obstruction in male infants, typically between 2 and 6 weeks of age.

Clinical Presentation
  • Symptoms: Projectile, non-bilious vomiting after feeds, starting around 2 to 6 weeks of age.
    • Persistent vomiting leads to dehydration, hypokalemia and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis because the body loses hydrochloric acid (HCl) in the vomitus.
  • Physical Examination: Visible gastric peristalsis from left to right and a palpable “olive-shaped” mass in the epigastric region.

Diagnosis
  • Ultrasound (USG) is the Investigation of choice for CHPS, characterised by
    • Pyloric muscle thickness of > 3 mm
    • Pyloric length > 14 mm
    • The pyloric channel appears elongated and thickened (10-14 mm)

  • Contrast Studies (Upper GI Series): Less frequently used, demonstrating the classic ¸ with a thin line of contrast through the elongated and narrowed pyloric channel and delayed gastric emptying without duodenal dilation.

 

 

Hirschsprung’s disease (Option A) is characterized by the absence of ganglion cells in the distal intestine, which can present as delayed passing of meconium or constipation. Barium enema shows the dilated proximal segment and the transition zone. Forceful vomiting without bile and visible stomach movements are not typical of Hirschsprung's disease.

Jejunal atresia (Option C) is a condition where there is a congenital obstruction in the jejunum, often presenting with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. It is characterised by multiple dilated loops of the small bowel and a "triple bubble sign" on X-ray. In this case, the vomiting is non-bilious, which rules out this diagnosis.

Duodenal atresia (Option D) is another congenital condition where there is a complete or partial obstruction of the duodenum, which results in bilious vomiting. It often presents with a "double bubble" sign on the X-ray.

questions.solution: 472d4a">swelling will decrease automatically Explanation: In the case of a nasal fracture with no involvement of the septum , the most appropriate approach is to wait for the swelling to subside before proceeding with closed reduction . questions.stem: What is the probable diagnosis for a 5-year-old child with abdominal swelling, mild discomfort, no pain or vomiting, and a fluctuant soft swelling that moves freely in a plane perpendicular to the mesentery attachment, as seen in the outpatient department?
questions.stemHtml: What is the probable diagnosis for a 5-year-old child with abdominal swelling, mild discomfort, no pain or vomiting, and a fluctuant soft swelling that moves freely in a plane perpendicular to the mesentery attachment, as seen in the outpatient department?
questions.solution: The description of the abdominal swelling , which is fluctuant , soft , and moves freely in a plane perpendicular to the mesentery attachment , strongly points toward a Chylolymphatic cyst . It is a type of mesenteric cyst, which is a rare, benign cystic lesion that typically contains chyle (lymph fluid mixed with fat). These cysts are often seen in children and are related to lymphatic malformations . (Congenitally misplaced lymphatics) Pathophysiology: absence of efferent lymphatics → collection of chyle→ progressive increase in the size of the cyst. The cyst is usually soft , fluctuant , and non-tender, aligning with the clinical presentation. The cyst moves freely in a plane perpendicular to the mesentery attachment, which is characteristic of cysts within the mesentery or mesenteric root . Peritoneal cysts (Option A) are also fluid-filled sacs within the peritoneal cavity, but they tend to be less common in children and often do not exhibit the same characteristic free movement seen in chylolymphatic cysts . Lipoma (Option B) is a benign fatty tumour , typically firm and mobile but not fluctuating in consistency. They are solid masses and do not show the fluctuating and soft characteristics described here. They also typically don't show distinct movement in relation to mesenteric attachment. Pseudocysts (Option D) are more commonly associated with acute or chronic pancreatitis and would typically present with symptoms such as abdominal pain or other signs of pancreatic pathology. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Best way to localise extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma:
questions.stemHtml: Best way to localise extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma:
questions.solution: 2">Nucleotide scan Explanation: The best method to localise extra-adrenal pheochromocytomas is through a Nucleotide scan (such as MIBG or PET scan), which allows for accurate identification of the tumour's location. MIBG is a radiopharmaceutical that is selectively absorbed by neuroendocrine tumours, such as pheochromocytomas. When radioactive iodine-labelled MIBG is administered intravenously, the tumour cells take it up due to their affinity for norepinephrine. Once the MIBG is taken up by the tumour, a whole-body scan is performed using a gamma camera , allowing for the precise localization of pheochromocytomas, including extra-adrenal tumours . X-ray (Option A) is not suitable for visualising soft tissue tumours like pheochromocytomas or detecting abnormal growths. It is better suited for visualising bones or detecting larger, more obvious structural abnormalities. VMA excretion (Option C) is a metabolite of catecholamines and can be measured in urine to help diagnose pheochromocytoma . However, while increased VMA (Vanillyl mandelic acid) excretion is suggestive of pheochromocytoma, it does not help localise the tumor . Clinical examination (Option D) can reveal signs and symptoms of pheochromocytoma, but it is not reliable for localising an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma. Symptoms like hypertension, sweating, and tachycardia suggest the presence of pheochromocytoma, but further imaging studies (like the nucleotide scan) are required for accurate localisation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A patient, after heavy drinking of alcohol presents with multiple episodes of vomiting and hematemesis. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.solution: multiple episodes of vomiting, and hematemesis , the most likely diagnosis is Mallory-Weiss syndrome , where the vomiting-induced tear leads to bleeding from the oesophagus . Mallory-Weiss syndrome Definition It is defined as mucosal lacerations in the gastric mucosa at the gastroesophageal (GE) junction that are caused by forceful vomiting, retching, coughing, or straining. Epidemiology It accounts for 10-15% of acute upper gastrointestinal haemorrhages. The greatest risk for massive haemorrhage is alcoholic patients with preexisting portal hypertension. Risk Factors Alcoholic patients with intense vomiting after binge drinking. Forceful abdominal contractions against a closed cardia. Any patient with repeated episodes of emesis. Portal hypertension in alcoholic patients. Diagnosis The patient's history is crucial. It can be confirmed with endoscopy. Retroflexion manoeuvre during endoscopy is used to view the area below the gastroesophageal junction. Symptoms Vomiting, hematemesis, upper abdominal pain, hypotension, tachycardia Complications Rarely massive bleeding associated with portal hypertension Treatment Endoscopic methods (multipolar electrocoagulation, epinephrine injection, band ligation), angiographic transarterial embolisation, rarely surgery Prognosis Generally good with appropriate endoscopic treatment Esophageal carcinoma (Option B) can present with dysphagia , weight loss , and anorexia . It may cause hematemesis in advanced stages, but it is less likely to be associated with acute episodes of vomiting or retching, as seen in this patient. Achalasia cardia (Option C) is a disorder of the lower esophageal sphincter , causing difficulty in swallowing and regurgitation of food, but it doesn't usually present with hematemesis or the tears caused by vomiting. Boerhaave's syndrome (Option D) involves a rupture of the oesophagus due to severe vomiting or retching. It presents with severe chest pain , subcutaneous emphysema , pleural effusions , tachypnea , fever , and hypotension . It is a life-threatening condition often associated with violent vomiting , much more severe than Mallory-Weiss syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: The treatment of choice for inguinal hernia in infants is:
questions.stemHtml: The treatment of choice for inguinal hernia in infants is:
questions.solution: on: The treatment of choice for inguinal hernia in infants is herniotomy , which involves the removal of the hernial sac . This procedure is preferred in infants as it effectively addresses the condition by removing the sac and preventing further complications, such as incarceration or strangulation, without the need for complex repair techniques used in older patients. Herniorrhaphy (Option B) is a more complex procedure involving suturing the defect in the abdominal wall, which is more commonly used in older children and adults but not typically in infants due to the smaller size and risks associated with suturing in such delicate tissues. TRUSS (Option C) is a device used to support a hernia, but it is not a definitive treatment. It does not address the anatomical defect; hence, it is not preferred for managing inguinal hernias and is not recommended for infants. Hernioplasty (Option D) is a procedure that typically involves the use of a mesh to repair a hernia defect. It is usually employed in adults or in complex, large, or recurrent hernias. In infants and younger children, herniotomy is the preferred treatment. Hernioplasty is considered in specific, complex cases but is not the routine treatment for inguinal hernias in infants. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: > hypertrophy. Explanation: The symptoms described- difficulty breathing through the nose, an elongated face, lack of expression, mouth-breathing, high-arched palate, and crowded upper teeth- are classic signs of adenoid hypertrophy . Adenoid hypertrophy occurs when the adenoid tissue, located in the nasopharynx, becomes enlarged, obstructing airflow through the nasal passages. This leads to mouth breathing , sleep disturbances , and characteristic facial features, including an elongated face and a high-arched palate due to the prolonged open-mouth breathing pattern. Adenoid Hypertrophy: Adenoid hypertrophy is common in young children and can cause nasal obstruction , leading to mouth breathing and sleep disturbances (e.g., snoring, sleep apnea). It may also result in facial deformities like the elongated face, high-arched palate, and crowded teeth due to chronic open-mouth breathing. X-ray imaging typically shows enlargement of the adenoid tissue in the nasopharyngeal region. Incorrect Options: Lingual tonsils (Option A) : is incorrect because while the lingual tonsils can contribute to obstructive symptoms, they are located at the base of the tongue, not in the nasopharynx. Quinsy (Option B) : is incorrect because quinsy refers to a peritonsillar abscess , typically presenting with severe throat pain , fever, and trismus , not with chronic nasal obstruction and facial deformities. Tonsillar hypertrophy (Option C) : is incorrect because tonsillar hypertrophy refers to the enlargement of the palatine tonsils , which is more likely to cause throat-related symptoms like difficulty swallowing , rather than the nasal obstruction seen in this case. @Neet_pg_bot

CSF Rhinorrhea: CSF rhinorrhea occurs when cerebrospinal fluid leaks from the brain's subarachnoid space into the nasal cavity. options.label: A

questions.answerText: It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss
questions.solution: trong>Explanation: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) is a non-invasive diagnostic test that measures the auditory pathways' response to sound stimulation. It is primarily used to assess the sensorineural hearing loss , as it evaluates the function of the auditory nerve and brainstem. BERA is particularly helpful in diagnosing hearing loss in infants, young children, and patients who are unable to cooperate with standard hearing tests. BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry): Procedure : During BERA, electrodes are placed on the scalp, and sound stimuli are presented through headphones. The electrical response generated by the brainstem in reaction to the sound is recorded and analyzed. Uses : It is primarily used to assess the function of the auditory pathway up to the brainstem, particularly to detect sensorineural hearing loss , and can help in identifying conditions like auditory neuropathy or brainstem lesions. Incorrect Options: It is an invasive procedure (Option B) : is incorrect because BERA is non-invasive . It does not require any surgical intervention or insertion of instruments inside the body. It can be used for screening for hearing loss (Option A) : While BERA can aid in diagnosing hearing loss, it is not commonly used for general screening in routine practice. It is more useful for confirming and assessing hearing loss, particularly sensorineural types, in specific cases (e.g., infants, patients who cannot cooperate with standard tests). It is a subjective investigation (Option D) : is incorrect because BERA is objective , as it records the brainstem's electrical response to sound stimuli, which is an automated and measurable process, not dependent on patient feedback or subjective interpretation. @Neet_pg_bot

    • Acute stage (few months): Fever, lymphadenitis, epididymo-orchitis.
    • Chronic Obstructive stage (>10 years): Hydrocele, chyluria, elephantiasis
    • Occult stage: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (hypersensitivity reaction) with absent microfilariae

Syphilis (Option A):

  • Syphilis (Treponema pallidum infection) causes painless ulcers (chancre), maculopapular rash, and systemic involvement, but does not lead to massive lymphedema.

Leprosy (Option B):

  • Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) leads to skin lesions, nerve damage, and deformities, but does not cause gross limb swelling like elephantiasis.

Leishmaniasis (Option D):

  • Cutaneous leishmaniasis presents with ulcerative skin lesions, while visceral leishmaniasis causes hepatosplenomegaly and fever. Neither form causes lymphatic obstruction and massive swelling.

Explanation:

  • The Serratus Anterior muscle is located on the lateral aspect of the thorax and attaches to the medial border of the scapula.
  • It is primarily responsible for protracting and stabilizing the scapula against the thoracic wall.
  • Weakness or dysfunction of the Serratus Anterior can result in winged scapula, where the medial border of the scapula protrudes away from the thoracic wall.

Serratus Anterior:

  • Origin: Upper 8 ribs (anterolaterally)
  • Insertion: Costal surface of the scapula
  • Nerve Supply: Long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7 – "Wings to Heaven")
  • Function:
    • Protracts the scapula (pulls it forward)
    • Holds scapula against the thoracic wall (prevents winging)
    • Rotates the scapula laterally (turning the glenoid cavity upwards for full overhead abduction)

Injury to Long Thoracic Nerve:

  • Causes Winging of Scapula
  • Seen in post-mastectomy cases, trauma, weightlifting injuries
  • Patient has difficulty in overhead abduction (arm cannot be fully raised)

 

Trapezius (Option A): Dysfunction of the trapezius (innervated by the spinal accessory nerve, CN XI) causes drooping of the shoulder, but not classic scapular winging.

Latissimus dorsi (Option C): This muscle helps in adduction, extension, and medial rotation of the humerus. It is innervated by the thoracodorsal nerve and does not cause scapular winging.

Supraspinatus (Option D): This muscle initiates arm abduction (first 15°) and is innervated by the suprascapular nerve. It is not responsible for scapular stability. Incorrect.

questions.stem: Which type of cells are implicated in the development of contact dermatitis in a 12-year-old boy who presented to the emergency department?
questions.stemHtml: Which type of cells are implicated in the development of contact dermatitis in a 12-year-old boy who presented to the emergency department?
questions.solution: Meta" data-dictid="fedc53b3161692777186553c8f8d7d">dermatitis is an inflammatory skin condition that occurs when the skin comes into contact with an allergen or irritant. The pathogenesis involves a complex interplay between various immune cells, including antigen-presenting cells (such as dendritic cells), T cells (including helper T cells ), and other immune mediators. Helper T cells are activated upon recognition of the allergen, and they release cytokines that recruit and activate other immune cells, leading to the characteristic inflammation and skin reactions seen in contact dermatitis. The type of hypersensitivity involved in contact dermatitis is Type IV . Mechanisms of Type IV hypersensitivity Description Examples Cytokine-mediated inflammation (mediated by CD4+ T cells) CD4+ T cells recognise protein antigens presented by APCs and differentiate into Th1 and Th17 cells . Th1 cells secrete cytokines like IFN-γ, activating macrophages to cause tissue damage and fibrosis. Th17 cells produce IL-17 to recruit neutrophils, promoting inflammation. Tuberculin test (a classic example of delayed-type hypersensitivity) Granulomas Contact dermatitis Rheumatoid arthritis Multiple sclerosis IBD Psoriasis T cell-mediated cytotoxicity (mediated by CD8+ T cells) Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) directly kill antigen-bearing target cells, including tumour cells, virus-infected cells, and allogeneic tissue, during graft rejection. CTLs use perforin-granzyme-dependent killing and Fas-Fas ligand-dependent killing mechanisms to induce apoptosis in target cells. Type 1 DM Hepatic injury in HBV infection Graft vs host disease Helper T cells play a crucial role in the immune response by coordinating and regulating other immune cells. They release cytokines that activate and recruit other cells to the site of inflammation, including in the case of contact dermatitis. Neutrophils (Option B) are typically involved in acute inflammation and play a major role in fighting bacterial infections. While neutrophils may be recruited to the site of inflammation in some cases of contact dermatitis, they are not the primary cells involved in the pathogenesis of the condition. NK cells (Option C) are a type of cytotoxic lymphocyte that plays a role in the innate immune response. They are primarily involved in recognising and eliminating virally infected and tumour cells. NK cells are not typically the primary cells involved in contact dermatitis. Cytotoxic T cells (Option B) are a type of T lymphocyte that directly kills infected or abnormal cells. They play a critical role in the immune response against viruses and tumour cells. While they may be involved in certain immune responses, they are not the primary cells in contact dermatitis. @Neet_pg_bot

Clinical signs like sensory loss in the lateral arm and posterior forearm support this diagnosis, possibly due to trauma or compression from the fracture. Surgical neck humerus fracture with axillary nerve injury (Option B): Would cause sensory loss over the lateral shoulder (regimental badge area) , not the posterior forearm. Spine fracture with foot drop (Option C): Would involve the common peroneal nerve , leading to sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and foot drop , which is unrelated to the current sensory findings. @Neet_pg_bot

mMeta" data-dictid="4fff084ff9169277719765c9d85a8e">radial nerve palsy

Explanation:

  • The X-ray reveals a fracture in the shaft of the humerus, often accompanied by radial nerve damage, which affects wrist, finger, and thumb extension, along with sensation in the forearm and hand.
  • Clinical signs like sensory loss in the lateral arm and posterior forearm support this diagnosis, possibly due to trauma or compression from the fracture.

Nerve

Root origin

Common causes

Features

Radial

C5-T1
  • Compression in axilla (crutches, "Saturday night palsy")
  • Midshaft fracture of humerus
  • Repetitive pronation/supination (screwdriver use, "finger drop")

Above elbow injury:

  • Loss of sensation over posterior arm/forearm and dorsal hand
  • Wrist drop (loss of elbow, wrist, and finger extension)
  • Decreased grip strength (wrist extension necessary for maximal action of flexors)

Below elbow injury:

  • Distal paresthesias without wrist drop

Midshaft fracture:

  • Tricep function and posterior arm sensation spared

Median

C5-T1
  • Supracondylar fracture of humerus (proximal lesion)
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome and wrist laceration (distal lesion)
  • "Ape hand" and "Hand of benediction"
  • Loss of wrist flexion
  • Loss of function of LOAF muscles (Lumbricals (lateral two), Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis)
  • Loss of sensation over thenar eminence and dorsal and palmar aspects of lateral 3 1/2 fingers with proximal lesion

Ulnar

C8-T1
  • Fracture of medial epicondyle of humerus (proximal lesion)
  • Fractured hook of hamate (distal lesion) from fall on outstretched hand
  • Compression of nerve against hamate during cycling
  • "Ulnar claw" on digit extension
  • Radial deviation of wrist upon flexion (proximal lesion)
  • Decreased flexion of ulnar fingers
  • Loss of abduction and adduction of fingers (interossei)
  • Loss of thumb adduction
  • Loss of action of ulnar 2 lumbrical muscles
  • Loss of sensation over ulnar 1 1/2 fingers including hypothenar eminence

 

Fracture-dislocation of the elbow (Option A): Typically affects the ulnar or median nerve, not the radial nerve.

Surgical neck humerus fracture with axillary nerve injury (Option B): Would cause sensory loss over the lateral shoulder (regimental badge area), not the posterior forearm.

Spine fracture with foot drop (Option C): Would involve the common peroneal nerve, leading to sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and foot drop, which is unrelated to the current sensory findings.

questions.stem: A sexually active male presented with warts on his penis as shown below. Similar lesions were present near the anal canal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A sexually active male presented with warts on his penis as shown below. Similar lesions were present near the anal canal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: a, commonly known as genital warts. Genital warts are caused by certain strains of the human papillomavirus (HPV), which is a sexually transmitted infection. They typically appear as raised, flesh-colored or grayish growths on or around the genitals, including the penis in males. In some cases, they can also be found near the anal canal, as mentioned in the scenario. Condyloma acuminata (anogenital warts): Benign, moist, soft, pedunculated wart found on the external genitalia and has low malignant potential. Site: They may be found in the genital area such as the penile shaft, scrotum, or labia majora of the vagina, or in the anal area. Appearance: They are generally pink and project out from the surface of the skin. Size may vary; they usually appear small but can merge into large masses. Microscopy: A branching villous structure with connective tissue stroma. Epidermis showing hyperkeratosis and acanthosis (thickening). Cytoplasmic vacuolization of the squamous cells ( koilocytosis ) is Characteristic. No evidence of dysplasia. {{caption_text}} The table below shows the clinical features of HPV and the types responsible for various lesions: Clinical lesion Oncogenic potential HPV types Plantar warts Benign 1 Common skin warts Benign 2, 4, 27, 57 Epidermodysplasia verrucosa Mostly benign, rarely progresses to malignancy 5, 8, 9, 12, 17 Anogenital warts Laryngeal papilloma Intraepithelial neoplasia Low malignant potential 6, 11 Palmar warts in butchers Low malignant potential 7 Carcinomas of the cervix & other genital mucosa/larynx/oesophagus High malignant potential 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 68 Penile cancer (Option A): Penile cancer refers to the malignant growth of cells in the penis. It may present as changes in the skin, ulcerations, or lumps, but it is distinct from the appearance of genital warts. Bowen disease (Option C): Bowen disease is an intraepidermal carcinoma that appears as a red, scaly patch on the skin, typically caused by prolonged exposure to sunlight. Hemorrhoids (Option D): Hemorrhoids are swollen blood vessels in the anal canal that can cause discomfort, itching, and pain. @Neet_pg_bot
