data-dictid="e08c004e8f1692777194c9d37e17ad">oxide (NO) is a vital signalling molecule involved in vasodilation and various other physiological processes. Nitric oxide synthesis in blood vessels requires the amino acid arginine, which serves as its precursor.

Steps in Nitric Oxide Synthesis:

  1. Enzyme Involved:
    • Nitric oxide synthase (NOS) converts L-arginine to nitric oxide (NO) and L-citrulline in the presence of oxygen and cofactors like NADPH and tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4).
  2. Physiological Role of NO:
    • NO is a potent vasodilator that relaxes vascular smooth muscle cells, thus regulating blood pressure and improving blood flow.
    • It also has roles in neurotransmission and immune response.

Citrulline (Option A) is a byproduct of nitric oxide synthesis and can be recycled back into arginine via the urea cycle, but it is not directly used in NO production.

Histidine (Option C) is a precursor for histamine and is involved in immune responses, but it does not play a role in NO synthesis.

Tryptophan (Option D) is a precursor for serotonin and melatonin but is not involved in nitric oxide production.

questions.solution: Xeroderma pigmentosum, as the girl has severe sunburns with minimal exposure, freckling, and sun-induced skin damage, which are hallmark features of XP. Xeroderma Pigmentosum: It is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by extreme sensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight. It arises due to genetic mutations affecting genes responsible for the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway. It presents with freckle-like pigmented patches, atrophic areas, and other skin abnormalities in sun-exposed areas. Additionally, patients may experience ocular manifestations such as photophobia, conjunctival injection, and corneal ulcers due to UV-induced damage. Systemic manifestations can include mental retardation and low intelligence. Increased risk of developing skin cancers, including melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, at a young age. {{caption_text}} Bloom Syndrome (Option A): It is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the BLM gene. It presents with short stature, photosensitivity, and characteristic facial features including a long, narrow face and prominent nose, along with other physical anomalies such as micrognathia and cafe-au-lait spots. Increased risk of various cancers, particularly leukaemia and lymphoma, at an early age. Warts (Option C): Warts (caused by HPV) present as localized verrucous lesions, not widespread freckling and sun sensitivity. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) (Option D): SLE can cause photosensitivity, but it presents with a malar rash, systemic symptoms (fatigue, arthritis, renal involvement), and autoantibodies. XP causes DNA repair defects, not an autoimmune reaction. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Xeroderma pigmentosum, as the girl has severe sunburns with minimal exposure, freckling, and sun-induced skin damage, which are hallmark features of XP.

Xeroderma Pigmentosum:

  • It is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by extreme sensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight.
  • It arises due to genetic mutations affecting genes responsible for the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway.
  • It presents with freckle-like pigmented patches, atrophic areas, and other skin abnormalities in sun-exposed areas.
  • Additionally, patients may experience ocular manifestations such as photophobia, conjunctival injection, and corneal ulcers due to UV-induced damage.
  • Systemic manifestations can include mental retardation and low intelligence.
  • Increased risk of developing skin cancers, including melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, at a young age.

Bloom Syndrome (Option A):

  • It is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the BLM gene.
  • It presents with short stature, photosensitivity, and characteristic facial features including a long, narrow face and prominent nose, along with other physical anomalies such as micrognathia and cafe-au-lait spots.
  • Increased risk of various cancers, particularly leukaemia and lymphoma, at an early age.

Warts (Option C):

  • Warts (caused by HPV) present as localized verrucous lesions, not widespread freckling and sun sensitivity.

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) (Option D):

  • SLE can cause photosensitivity, but it presents with a malar rash, systemic symptoms (fatigue, arthritis, renal involvement), and autoantibodies. XP causes DNA repair defects, not an autoimmune reaction.

questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old male patient presents to the OPD complaining of pain in the medial part of the elbow for the past 4-6 weeks. He states that the pain worsens while lifting weights in the gym. On examination, there is tenderness over the medial epicondyle, and reverse Cozen's test is positive. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be injured in this patient?
questions.solution: on: The patient suffers from medial epicondylitis or golfer's elbow. The Ulnar nerve is posterior to the medial epicondyle within the cubital tunnel. The main symptom of medial epicondylitis is the 5 to 10 mm distal tenderness to the medial epicondyle. The pain is generally aggravated with resisted wrist flexion and pronation, known as reverse Cozen's test. Hand and Forearm Deformities: Mallet Finger (Baseball Finger): Permanent flexion of the distal phalanx due to lateral band avulsion of the extensor tendon. Boutonniere Deformity: Flexion of the middle phalanx and hyperextension of the distal phalanx due to central band avulsion of the extensor tendon. Tennis Elbow (Lateral Epicondylitis): Inflammation of extensor tendons from the lateral epicondyle (common in tennis players, violinists). Golfer’s Elbow (Medial Epicondylitis): Inflammation of flexor tendons from the medial epicondyle . Volkmann Ischemic Contracture: Flexion deformity of fingers due to ischemic necrosis of forearm flexor muscles (e.g., tight cast injury). Dupuytren Contracture: Progressive thickening of the palmar aponeurosis , pulling fingers into flexion. Swan Neck Deformity: Hyperextension of the PIP joint with flexion of the DIP joint . Hand and Forearm Deformities:

  • Boutonniere Deformity: Flexion of the middle phalanx and hyperextension of the distal phalanx due to central band avulsion of the extensor tendon.

Common causes

Features

C5-T1

Below elbow injury:

Median (Option A)

C5-T1

Ulnar

C8-T1

questions.stem: At what age is it recommended to introduce solid foods to an infant while continuing breastfeeding?
questions.stemHtml: At what age is it recommended to introduce solid foods to an infant while continuing breastfeeding?
questions.solution: Explanation: According to current recommendations by World Health Organization (WHO) and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), solid foods should be introduced to an infant while continuing breastfeeding at around 6 months of age. At 6 months, infants have typically developed the necessary oral motor skills to handle solid foods, including loss of the tongue-thrust reflex, ability to sit with support, and adequate head and neck control . Breast milk or formula remains the primary source of nutrition during the first year, with complementary foods gradually introduced to meet increasing nutritional demands, especially for iron and zinc. Breastfeeding can go up to 2 years of age or till the time the mother wants. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: ng>Explanation: Bilateral pitting edema is the specific sign of kwashiorkor , distinguishing it from other forms of malnutrition. This characteristic edema develops due to severe protein deficiency, leading to decreased plasma oncotic pressure, which results in fluid accumulation in the interstitial spaces. Kwashiorkor typically affects children between weaning age and 5 years, with the edema being most pronounced in the lower extremities but potentially affecting other body parts, including the face and hands. Features of Kwashiorkar and Marasmus Kwashiorkor Marasmus Pitting Edema: Specific sign of Kwashiorkar Characterized by swelling, often starting in the legs and feet, leaving a persistent indentation when pressed. Severe Wasting: The child appears extremely thin, with prominent bones and little body fat. Sugar Baby Appearance: The child may look deceptively healthy due to oedema, despite being malnourished. Monkey Facies: A sunken appearance of the cheeks due to loss of fat, giving an aged look. Muscle Wasting: Despite the swollen appearance, muscle loss is present, leading to weakness and hypotonia. Baggy Pants Appearance: Loose, sagging skin around the buttocks caused by significant muscle and fat loss. Mental and Neurological Symptoms: The child is apathetic, irritable, and may have feeding difficulties. Alertness: Children with marasmus remain mentally alert. Hair Changes: Hair may lose colour, become thin, and show alternating bands of colour ("flag sign"). Absence of Edema: Unlike kwashiorkor, marasmus does not involve swelling or oedema. Skin Changes: Includes hyperpigmentation, peeling skin ("flaky paint" appearance), and colour changes, particularly in the buttocks, perineum, and thighs. Hypoglycemia Risk: The liver's reduced capacity to produce glucose increases the risk of low blood sugar. Gastrointestinal Issues: Anorexia, vomiting, and abdominal distension. Anaemia is present due to nutritional deficiencies. Hypothermia Risk: The child may struggle to maintain body temperature due to energy depletion. {{caption_text}} {{caption_text}} Weight loss (Option B), while common in malnutrition, is not specific to kwashiorkor. In fact, weight may be masked by the presence of edema, making it an unreliable indicator for this specific condition. Weight loss is a general feature of malnutrition that can occur in various nutritional deficiency states. Flag sign (Option C) is characterized by alternating bands of normal and depigmented hair, is seen in periodic nutritional deficiency but is not specific to kwashiorkor. This sign can be observed in various forms of malnutrition, including marasmus, and can indicate periods of adequate and inadequate nutrition. Muscle wasting (Option D) is a feature of protein-energy malnutrition in general but is not specific to kwashiorkor. While muscle wasting may be present in kwashiorkor, it is often masked by edema and is more prominently seen in marasmus. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
tear in the aorta indicating an Aortic dissection.

Aortic Dissection

  • It occurs when a defect or a flap occurs in the aorta, resulting in blood tracking into aortic tissues, splitting the medial layer and creating a false lumen.

Clinical features:

  • Sudden onset of severe, tearing chest, radiating to the interscapular region
  • Renal pain and renal failure
  • Paraplegia
  • Syncope
  • Weakness
  • Hypotension or shock

Investigations:

  • If the patient is stable, CT angiography is the standard investigation of choice.
  • In the case of unstable patients (SBP<100 mm of HG, HR>100 bpm), the preferred investigation of choice will be TEE (TransEsophageal Echocardiography)
  • MRI can also be done if CT is unequivocal.
  • Chest x-ray reveals widening of mediastinum along with left-sided pleural effusion.

Signs of FALSE LUMEN:

  • Cobweb Sign: Irregularities of False lumen
  • Beak Sign: False lumen forms acute angle with True lumen:

 

Pulmonary embolism (Option B):

  • Filling Defect seen in Pulmonary artery
  • IOC for PE: CT Angiography

Incorrect Options:

Cardiac Myxoma (Option C):

  • Low annotating hypodense lesion on the posterior most chamber of the heart (Left Atrium)
  • MC primary Benign cardiac tumor in adults.

Aortic aneurysm (Option D):

  • Involve either ascending aorta, thoracic aorta & abdominal aorta
  • Represents localized dilation of the aorta; while an aneurysm may predispose to dissection, an intimal tear specifically indicates dissection.
  • M/C cause for abdominal & thoracic aortic aneurysm: Atherosclerosis

It is also used to diagnose posterior urethral valves and neurogenic bladder. questions.solutionHtml:
lass="customMeta" data-dictid="bd478e4ff816927771949528846af9">palpable bladder with recurrent UTIs indicates urinary tract obstruction due to vesicoureteral reflux (VUR).
  • Micturating cystourethrography (MCU) is the most sensitive investigation for diagnosing vesicoureteral reflux (VUR).
  • MCU is a specialized radiological study that involves filling the bladder with contrast material and taking X-ray images during urination, allowing visualization of the bladder outline, urethra, and detection of any retrograde flow of urine into the ureters (vesicoureteral reflux). It is also used to diagnose posterior urethral valves and neurogenic bladder.

    •  

    Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR)

    Definition

    Retrograde flow of urine from the bladder to ureters and pelvis at rest or during micturition

    Epidemiology
    • Present in 30-35% of children with febrile UTI
    • Conventionally considered a major risk factor for acute pyelonephritis and reflux nephropathy
    • Can cause morbidity during pregnancy

    Diagnostic Methods

    Primary Methods:

    • Radionuclide MCU (more sensitive for detecting VUR)
    • Direct or indirect radionuclide cystography
    • Regular radiologic imaging every 24-36 months for grades III-IV VUR

    Additional Techniques:

    • Contrast-enhanced ultrasound
    • MR urography
    • Urinalysis and urine cultures (if symptomatic)

    Follow-up Monitoring:

    • Weight and blood pressure measurements
    • Periodic radiologic cystogram

    Prophylactic Antibiotics

    Medications and Dosages:

    • Amoxiciilin: 10-12.5 mg/kg/day
    • Nitrofurantoin: 1-2 mg/kg/day
    • Cephalexin: 10-12.5 mg/kg/day
    • Cefadroxil: 5 mg/kg/day

    Special Considerations:

    • Avoid cotrimoxazole in infants <3 months, and those with G6PD deficiency
    • Avoid nitrofurantoin in <3 months, G6PD deficiency, renal insufficiency
    • Cephalexin is the drug of choice in the first 3-6 months of life
    • Cefadroxil is an alternative agent in early infancy

    Management Approach

    For Low Grade VUR (I-II):

    • With UTI: Consider antibiotic prophylaxis and Bladder-Bowel dysfunction management
    • Without UTI: No therapy needed

    For High Grade VUR (III-IV):

    • With BBD: Antibiotic prophylaxis until BBD resolves, manage BBD
    • Without BBD: Antibiotic prophylaxis until age 2 and >1-yr UTI-free

    Additional Considerations:

    • Medical therapy based on the principle that VUR resolves over time
    • Prophylactic antibiotics maintain sterile urine and prevent UTI while awaiting resolution
    • Surgical correction indicated for breakthrough infections or parenchymal injury

    Treatment Guidelines
    • Consider dietary modification and medications
    • Some patients require bladder retraining, anticholinergic medications
    • Clean intermittent catheterization may be needed
    • Liberal fluid intake recommended
    • Regular and complete bladder emptying is important
    • Avoid constipation
    • Close follow-up for breakthrough UTI

    Outcomes
    • Tends to resolve by 10 years of age
    • Resolution rate 70-90% for grades I-III
    • 10-35% resolution for higher grades
    • Better outcomes with: younger age, lower grades, unilateral VUR

     

    Ultrasonogram (Option A) is useful as an initial screening tool to visualize kidney size, shape, and hydronephrosis. However, it is not the most sensitive as it cannot provide detailed information about urinary flow dynamics or definitively diagnose vesicoureteral reflux.

    Urine routine examination (Option C) is essential for diagnosing active UTIs and monitoring response to treatment, but it is not the most sensitive investigation as it cannot identify the underlying anatomical or functional abnormalities causing recurrent infections. It provides no information about urinary tract anatomy or voiding dynamics.

    DMSA scan (Option D) is primarily used to detect and evaluate renal scarring from previous UTIs but cannot evaluate bladder and urethral function during voiding. While valuable for assessing renal damage, it doesn't help identify the underlying cause.

ictid="9f524cc9601692777194d19de23a85">parameter for differentiating heart failure with preserved EF (HFpEF) from heart failure with reduced EF (HFrEF).
  • MUGA scan is a non-invasive nuclear imaging test that accurately calculates EF by analyzing the motion of the heart's ventricles using a radioactive tracer and a gamma camera.

    •  

    Purpose

    Scan types

    For Myocardial Perfusion

    • Assess ischemia
    • Cold spot: decreased uptake in ischemic areas.
    • Thallium scan (Commonly used) (Option B)
    • Tetrofosmin
    • Sestamibi scan (Option D)

    For Myocardial Infarction

    • Assess infarct
    • Hot spot in infarct area as pyrophosphate accumulates and is not metabolized.
    • 99m Tc - Pyrophosphate scan.

    For Ventricular Function

    • Evaluate ejection fraction
    • MUGA (Multiple Gated Acquisition) scan (AKA nuclear ventriculography)
      • Radiolabeled RBCs are used
    • Most accurate for ventricular function - Cardiac MRI

    For Myocardial Viability

     
    • Assess the viability of myocardium
    • PETscan - Best investigation for myocardial viability. (Option C)
      • Perfusion and metabolism mismatch are observed in the PET scan.
      • Perfusion Agents:N-13 ammonia and Rubidium chloride.
      • Metabolism Agent:
      • FDG-PET is used for glucose metabolism.
        • No FDG uptake indicates a normal heart or an infarct.
        • FDG uptake is present: In the Ischemic Myocardium
      • FDG-PET is combined with perfusion imaging for comprehensive assessment.
        • Uptake in PET with low perfusion indicates reversible dysfunction (suggestive of hibernation).
        • Irreversible dysfunction indicates the presence of scar tissue.
      • Note: Hibernating myocardium is ischemic but viable.

questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man visited the Suraksha clinic due to an anorectal discharge. Which of the following kits, color-coded for specific purposes, is advised for the syndromic treatment of sexually transmitted infections (STIs)?
questions.solution: Suraksha Clinics: Integrating STI/RTI Treatment and HIV/AIDS Control Government STI/RTI clinics, branded as "Suraksha Clinics," offer free standardized integrated STD and RTI treatment services at district-level and above healthcare facilities. Under National AIDS Control Program (NACP) Referral Centers STD Clinics at district, block, and First Referral Unit (FRU) levels act as referral centers for specialized treatment. Counselling and Condom Distribution Counselling services and high-quality condoms are provided to promote safer sexual practices. Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH):

1. CDH is the intrathoracic herniation of abdominal contents due to congenital defects in the diaphragm.

2. Types of CDH:

  • Bochdalek Hernia: Occurs through the posterolateral pleuroperitoneal canal, most commonly on the left side.
  • Morgagni Hernia: Anterior hernia located at the right cardiophrenic angle.

3. Radiologic Features:

  • Chest Radiograph (CXR):
    • Bochdalek hernia: Dome-shaped soft tissue opacity in the posterolateral thorax, often left-sided.
    • May show gas-filled bowel loops or fat content in the thoracic cavity.
    • Mediastinal shift away from the herniation due to mass effect.
    • On the lateral view, hernias appear above the posterior costophrenic recess.
  • CT/MRI:
    • Visualizes herniation of fat, bowel, spleen, or kidney through a diaphragmatic defect.
    • Important for distinguishing from other masses like cystic adenomatoid malformation or pericardial cyst.
    • CT provides clearer differentiation of soft-tissue or fatty mass protruding through the diaphragm.

4. Complications:

  • Associated with hypoplasia of the ipsilateral lung, leading to respiratory distress, especially in neonates.
  • Neonates may present with respiratory distress and mediastinal deviation.

Incorrect Options:

Intestinal obstruction (Option B):

  • Typically presents with dilated bowel loops confined to the abdominal cavity.
  • Does not involve bowel loops appearing in the chest on imaging.

Pleural effusion (Option C):

  • Characterized by fluid collection in the pleural space.
  • May show blunting of the costophrenic angle or fluid layering but no bowel loops.

Pneumonia (Option D):

  • Presents as patchy or lobar opacities in the lung parenchyma.
  • Does not involve bowel loops in the thoracic cavity.

questions.solution: >The presentation of primary amenorrhea in a 16-year-old girl with absent thelarche (breast development) and a normal stature raises concerns about possible hormonal imbalances affecting her reproductive system. LH (luteinizing hormone) and FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) are the two hormones involved in regulating the menstrual cycle and reproductive function. Abnormal levels of these hormones can provide valuable insights into potential causes of amenorrhea, such as hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis dysfunction, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), or ovarian insufficiency. Diagnostic laparoscopy (Option A) is used to visually examine the pelvic organs for structural issues, but it is not the first step in investigating primary amenorrhea. Hormonal tests are needed initially to assess the endocrine system. Pelvic ultrasound (Option B) provides information about the reproductive organs (e.g., uterus, ovaries), but given the absence of thelarche, a hormonal investigation (LH and FSH levels) should be prioritized to assess the function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. CT brain (Option D) is not the primary investigation for primary amenorrhea unless there are additional symptoms suggesting an intracranial abnormality, such as a pituitary tumor. @Neet_pg_bot

Meckel Diverticulum:

Most common congenital GI anomaly (2-3% of infants) with incomplete obliteration of omphalomesenteric duct.

Characteristics ("Rule of 2s")
  • 2% of population

Clinical Manifestations

Diagnosis

    • Specificity: 95%

  • Plain radiographs and barium studies are less useful

Complications

Intussusception, Volvulus and Perforation.

Appendicitis (Option B) involves inflammation of the appendix, which is consistently located at the cecum, not 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal junction. The appendix is typically 5-10 cm in length and arises from the cecum at the confluence of the teniae coli.

an> findings include obliteration of the costophrenic angle (CP angle) and an upward concave curve on the left side of the lung.
  • These findings are suggestive of a pleural effusion.

Pleural Effusion:

  • Pleural effusion is the accumulation of fluid in the pleural space.
  • Small Pleural Fluid: Often undetectable on PA chest x-rays; ultrasound or CT can detect small subpulmonary effusions.
  • Effusion Progression: Blunting of costophrenic angles starts at 200-500 mL. Classic signs include opacification of the lower chest with a concave superior margin.
  • Massive Effusions: 1000 mL reaches the fourth anterior rib; cause dense opacification of the hemithorax with contralateral mediastinal shift. Diaphragmatic inversion may occur.
  • Lateral decubitus X-rays: Increase sensitivity for small effusions as the pleural fluid moves with gravity and the lung effectively floats on the effusion.
  • Subpulmonary Effusions: Appear as a "high hemidiaphragm" on x-rays, with an unusual contour that peaks laterally than usual. Ultrasound or CT confirms the diagnosis.
  • In an upright PA view, the meniscus sign indicates the presence of a significant amount of pleural fluid, typically exceeding 200 mL and blunting the costophrenic angle.

 

  • Loculated (encysted, encapsulated) pleural fluid:

Consolidation (Option A): This would show more distinct lung tissue involvement with air bronchograms and possible increased density, but it wouldn’t obliterate the costophrenic angle as seen in pleural effusion.

Pneumothorax (Option C) shows a region of lucency (darkness) along the lung margin, typically more pronounced on an erect chest X-ray. In this case symptoms of pleural effusion and x-ray findings suggest fluid rather than air, making pneumothorax unlikely.

Sea-shore sign: On M-mode images, lung sliding manifests as the sea-shore sign, where the pleura and structures above appear as horizontal echogenic lines . The underlying lung presents a grainy or sandy texture. The stratified appearance above the pleural line is due to the motionless chest wall , resembling sea waves , while below the pleural line, the lung movement creates a sandy pattern , akin to the shore . Barcode/stratosphere sign: (Option B, C) In cases where lung sliding is absent , M-mode images show uniform horizontal straight lines known as the stratosphere sign or barcode sign. The lack of a grainy or sandy appearance in these images indicates the absence of motion . The stratosphere sign suggests that pneumothorax may be a likely cause. Lung point sign: The border between the sliding lung and pneumothorax is referred to as the "lung point" sign. This sign can assist in estimating the size of the pneumothorax . It is important to note that the lung point is only observable if part of the lung is still in contact with the chest wall . questions.solution: nation: Cervical ripening refers to the process of softening and dilating the cervix in preparation for labor or a gynecological procedure. One of the methods for cervical ripening involves the use of hygroscopic dilators, which work by absorbing moisture from surrounding tissues to gradually expand and dilate the cervix. Intracervical laminaria tent is a hygroscopic dilator. Laminaria tents are derived from the dried stems of seaweed. When placed in the cervix, they absorb moisture and expand, gradually dilating the cervix. This method is slow and controlled, often preferred for gentle and gradual ripening. Intracervical dinoprostone gel (Option A): Dinoprostone gel (prostaglandin E2) promotes cervical ripening by softening and thinning the cervix, but it does not work through hygroscopic properties. It is a pharmacological agent used for cervical ripening. Foley catheter at internal of cervix (Option C): A Foley catheter is a mechanical method for cervical ripening. It involves the insertion of a balloon-tipped catheter into the cervix, which is inflated with sterile water or saline to apply pressure. This method does not involve hygroscopic properties but instead works through mechanical dilation Misoprostol in posterior fornix (Option D): Misoprostol is a medication used for cervical ripening, but it does not work through hygroscopic mechanisms. It is typically administered orally or vaginally to induce ripening, and its mode of action is through pharmacological pathways rather than absorption of moisture. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
>Explanation:
  • The clinical manifestations indicate Celiac sprue or Gluten-sensitive enteropathy based on the classic presentation of chronic small bowel diarrhea, wheat allergy, villous atrophy, and positive serologic markers (anti-endomysial and TTG IgA antibodies), which is a T-cell mediated autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten ingestion.

 

Celiac sprue / Celiac disease / Gluten-sensitive enteropathy

Clinical manifestations
  • Diarrhoea, growth failure, and anaemia.
  • Temporal association with the introduction of wheat products at weaning.
  • Abdominal distension, vomiting, anorexia, aphthous stomatitis, and bloating.
  • Rickets, osteoporosis, short stature, muscular atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, and irritability might be seen in some cases.
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis can be seen.

Diagnosis:

ESPGHAN (European Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology & Nutrition) guidelines 2020 suggest that in all suspected cases (symptomatic, asymptomatic, and at-risk group), the first test should be total serum IgA and IgAtTG.

 

Serology:

  • Anti-TTG (Tissue Transglutaminase)
  • Anti EMA (Endomysial antibody)
  • Anti-DGP (Deamidated gliadin peptide)

 

Upper GI endoscopy:

  • The endoscopy may be normal or show the absence of folds or scalloped duodenal folds.

 

Histopathology:

  • Villous atrophy/Flat villi
  • Crypt hyperplasia
  • Intraepithelial lymphocyte infiltration.

Treatment:
  • Treatment involves a gluten-free diet (avoid wheat, rye, barley and oats).
  • High-risk groups include type 1 diabetes mellitus, Down syndrome, selective IgA deficiency, autoimmune thyroid disease, Turner syndrome, Williams syndrome, Addison’s disease, autoimmune liver disease and first-degree relatives of patients with celiac disease.
  • A temporal association may be present with the introduction of wheat products at weaning.

 

While cystic fibrosis (Option A) can cause chronic diarrhea, it is typically associated with respiratory symptoms, pancreatic insufficiency, and positive sweat chloride tests. The specific findings of villous atrophy and positive antibodies are not typical of cystic fibrosis.

Whipple's disease (Option B) causes malabsorption and diarrhea but is characterized by PAS-positive macrophages in biopsy. It has no association with wheat allergy and lacks the specific antibodies mentioned in the case. The condition is attributed to Tropheryma whipplei infection.

Tropical sprue (Option C) can cause villous atrophy but occurs specifically in tropical regions. It has no association with wheat allergy and does not produce the specific antibodies seen in celiac disease. The condition typically responds to antibiotics and folate supplementation.

Pathogenesis: Bleeding occurs due to rupture of blood vessels in the decidua basalis. There is an accumulation of blood in the decidua. This causes the separation of the placenta, leading to Further bleeding. planation: Hepatitis A is transmitted by the faecal-oral route. Hence the students can be suspected of acquiring Hepatitis A from the contaminated food. The diagnostic tests for Hepatitis A are a Stool sample, and an Anti HAV IgM antibody performed after 2 weeks of increase in the liver enzyme.

Hepatitis A Virus (HAV)

  • Most Common Cause of viral hepatitis in Children
  • Most Common Cause of Acute Relapsing viral hepatitis

Virus characteristics:

  • HAV is a 27-nm, nonenveloped, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus, resistant to heat, acid, and ether.

Mode of Transmission: Fecal-oral route.

Incubation period: ~3–4 weeks.

Pathogenesis:

  • Replication is limited to the liver but found in the liver, bile, stools, and blood during the late incubation and pre-icteric phases.
  • Faecal shedding, viremia, and infectivity decrease rapidly once jaundice appears.

Clinical presentation:

  • Asymptomatic cases
  • Jaundice
  • Cholestatic hepatitis
  • Fulminant hepatitis - Acute liver failure especially in older adults or those with preexisting liver conditions.
  • Does not lead to chronic liver disease.

Diagnosis:

  • Acute illness - anti-HAV IgM antibodies. (Option B)
  • HAV RNA can persist in stools, liver, and serum for months after acute illness but is not correlated with persistent infectivity.
  • Previous infection: IgG anti-HAV
  • LFT: Elevated bilirubin, serum aminotransferases, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP).

Treatment:

  • Most cases are self-limiting
  • No specific antiviral treatment
  • Symptomatic management (10 % Dextrose)

Prevention:

  • Inactivated vaccination: Single antigen or in combination with hepatitis B
  • Good sanitary conditions and measures

IgA for hepatitis A (Option A): IgA is not specific to Hepatitis A and does not give accurate results.

IgM for hepatitis B (Option C) and IgG for hepatitis B (Option D): Hepatitis A is transmitted by the faecal-oral route. Whereas hepatitis B is transmitted through blood or body fluids.

questions.solution: Untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy can progress to symptomatic urinary tract infections (UTIs), significantly increasing the risk of complications such as pyelonephritis, preterm labor, and low birth weight. Therefore, routine screening and prompt treatment of ASB during pregnancy are essential to ensure maternal and fetal well-being. Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (ASB) ≥10^5 CFU/mL of a single bacterium in urine without UTI symptoms. Causative organisms: E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Proteus. Risk factors: Female sex, age, diabetes, pregnancy, urinary tract abnormalities, catheters, immunosuppressive conditions. Diagnosis: Urine culture: ≥10^5 CFU/mL without symptoms. Management: Pregnant women: Requires treatment (e.g., nitrofurantoin, amoxicillin). Non-pregnant women: Generally, no treatment unless symptomatic. Elderly and catheterized patients: Treatment is usually not recommended unless symptomatic. Complications: Pyelonephritis Preterm delivery Low birth weight Antibiotic resistance Prevention: Pregnancy screening at 12–16 weeks. The prevalence of ASB is 50% (Option A): The prevalence of ASB during pregnancy is not as high as 50%. It is typically estimated to be around 5-10%. It is lower in people with sickle cell trait (Option B): Sickle cell trait does not reduce the risk of UTIs in pregnancy. In fact, individuals with sickle cell trait may have a higher risk of developing infections due to compromised renal function. The preferred antibiotic in pregnancy is amoxicillin (Option C): While amoxicillin is safe in pregnancy and commonly used, the choice of antibiotics is guided by culture sensitivity results and local resistance patterns. Nitrofurantoin and cephalexin are also frequently used. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• Untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy can progress to symptomatic urinary tract infections (UTIs), significantly increasing the risk of complications such as pyelonephritis, preterm labor, and low birth weight. Therefore, routine screening and prompt treatment of ASB during pregnancy are essential to ensure maternal and fetal well-being.

Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (ASB)

  • ≥10^5 CFU/mL of a single bacterium in urine without UTI symptoms.

Causative organisms: E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Proteus.

Risk factors: Female sex, age, diabetes, pregnancy, urinary tract abnormalities, catheters, immunosuppressive conditions.

Diagnosis: Urine culture: ≥10^5 CFU/mL without symptoms.

Management:

  • Pregnant women: Requires treatment (e.g., nitrofurantoin, amoxicillin).
  • Non-pregnant women: Generally, no treatment unless symptomatic.
  • Elderly and catheterized patients: Treatment is usually not recommended unless symptomatic.

Complications:

  • Pyelonephritis
  • Preterm delivery
  • Low birth weight
  • Antibiotic resistance

Prevention: Pregnancy screening at 12–16 weeks.

 

The prevalence of ASB is 50% (Option A): The prevalence of ASB during pregnancy is not as high as 50%. It is typically estimated to be around 5-10%.

It is lower in people with sickle cell trait (Option B): Sickle cell trait does not reduce the risk of UTIs in pregnancy. In fact, individuals with sickle cell trait may have a higher risk of developing infections due to compromised renal function.

The preferred antibiotic in pregnancy is amoxicillin (Option C): While amoxicillin is safe in pregnancy and commonly used, the choice of antibiotics is guided by culture sensitivity results and local resistance patterns. Nitrofurantoin and cephalexin are also frequently used.

questions.solution: xplanation: Superficial inguinal lymph nodes: Vulval cancer primarily drains lymph to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, which are the first-echelon nodes. Sentinel node biopsy in vulval cancer targets these nodes to detect regional metastatic spread early, minimizing the need for extensive lymphadenectomy. Vulval cancer Age Group Most common in elderly women, especially in the 6th and 7th decades, (50-70 years age group) Risk Factors HPV infections, HSV infections, smoking, chronic immunosuppression, chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., lichen sclerosis). Histological Type Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common type. Common Sites Labia majora: Most common site (60%). Clitoris: Second most common site (15%). Presentation Exophytic (outward-growing) growth. Ulcerative lesions. Symptoms Pruritus (most common), often associated with an itch-scratch cycle. Swelling, lump, or ulcer. Cancer cachexia (weight loss and muscle wasting). Cancer pain (late symptom). Spread Primarily through the lymphatic system. Vulvar lymphatics cross midline, especially within 2 cm of the midline. Commonly involved lymph nodes: Inguinofemoral. Lymph node involvement significantly impacts prognosis. Investigations Excisional biopsy: Preferred for lesions < 1 cm, for histological assessment of invasion depth. Incisional biopsy: For lesions ≥ 1 cm. Wedge biopsy, Keyes punch biopsy, and sentinel lymph node biopsy (to assess inguinofemoral node involvement). Treatment Vulvectomy: Partial or total, depending on disease stage. Inguinal lymph node dissection: To evaluate disease spread. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (Superficial inguinal lymph nodes): Determines stage and prognosis. xplanation:

Superficial inguinal lymph nodes:

  • Vulval cancer primarily drains lymph to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, which are the first-echelon nodes.
  • Sentinel node biopsy in vulval cancer targets these nodes to detect regional metastatic spread early, minimizing the need for extensive lymphadenectomy.

 

Vulval cancer

Age Group

Most common in elderly women, especially in the 6th and 7th decades, (50-70 years age group)

Risk Factors

HPV infections, HSV infections, smoking, chronic immunosuppression, chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., lichen sclerosis).

Histological Type

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common type.

Common Sites
  • Labia majora: Most common site (60%).
  • Clitoris: Second most common site (15%).

Presentation
  • Exophytic (outward-growing) growth.
  • Ulcerative lesions.

Symptoms
  • Pruritus (most common), often associated with an itch-scratch cycle.
  • Swelling, lump, or ulcer.
  • Cancer cachexia (weight loss and muscle wasting).
  • Cancer pain (late symptom).

Spread
  • Primarily through the lymphatic system.
  • Vulvar lymphatics cross midline, especially within 2 cm of the midline.
  • Commonly involved lymph nodes: Inguinofemoral.
  • Lymph node involvement significantly impacts prognosis.

Investigations
  • Excisional biopsy: Preferred for lesions < 1 cm, for histological assessment of invasion depth.
  • Incisional biopsy: For lesions ≥ 1 cm.
  • Wedge biopsy, Keyes punch biopsy, and sentinel lymph node biopsy (to assess inguinofemoral node involvement).

Treatment
  • Vulvectomy: Partial or total, depending on disease stage.
  • Inguinal lymph node dissection: To evaluate disease spread.
  • Sentinel lymph node biopsy (Superficial inguinal lymph nodes): Determines stage and prognosis.

 

Pelvic lymph nodes (Option A) are involved in later stages of vulval cancer. They are not first-line nodes for sentinel biopsy.

Cloquet node (Rosenmüller node) (Option B) is a deep inguinal node, located near the femoral canal, may be involved in advanced disease but is not routinely targeted in sentinel node biopsy.

Deep inguinal lymph nodes (Option D) are Though involved in advanced vulval cancer, these nodes are downstream of the superficial inguinal nodes and are not sentinel nodes.

questions.solution: trong> Respiratory alkalosis occurs when there is a decrease in CO2 levels in the blood due to hyperventilation, leading to an elevated pH. Chronic respiratory alkalosis indicates that this process has been ongoing for some time, allowing for partial renal compensation (reduction in bicarbonate). ABG features in pregnancy: pH: Slightly elevated (due to reduced CO2). CO2: Decreased (due to hyperventilation from progesterone). Bicarbonate: Slightly reduced (compensatory renal response). ABG Pattern: Mild respiratory alkalosis with partial compensation (reduced bicarbonate). During pregnancy, women often experience mild hyperventilation due to increased progesterone levels, leading to reduced CO2 and a slightly elevated pH. The body partially compensates over time, but the primary abnormality remains respiratory in nature. Acute metabolic acidosis (Option A) is characterized by a decrease in blood pH due to an accumulation of acids (like lactic acid) or a loss of bicarbonate. Acute metabolic alkalosis (Option B) is characterized by an increase in blood pH due to an excess of bicarbonate or a loss of hydrogen ions (e.g., from vomiting). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A mother of a 5-day-old baby presents with the complaint that her baby is “unable to latch on” for breastfeeding. She also says there is some leakage of milk at times, and on examination, there is bilateral tenderness and swelling. What is the most likely cause of this?
questions.solution: ormation, the most likely cause of the mother's symptoms is breast engorgement. Breast engorgement is a common condition that occurs in the early postpartum period when there is excessive swelling and fullness of the breasts. This often results in difficulty with the baby latching properly. The leakage of milk, as well as the bilateral tenderness and swelling, align with the symptoms of breast engorgement. This condition typically arises in the first few days after childbirth due to hormonal changes that increase blood flow, milk production, and fluid accumulation in the breasts. If the baby is not effectively breastfeeding or emptying the breasts, engorgement can occur. Bacterial mastitis (Option A) usually presents with localized redness, warmth, pain, and swelling of the breast, often accompanied by flu-like symptoms such as fever and body aches. While tenderness and swelling are present in the case, the information provided does not suggest the presence of systemic symptoms commonly associated with bacterial mastitis. A breast abscess (Option B) is a localized collection of pus within the breast tissue. It typically occurs as a complication of untreated mastitis. The presence of bilateral tenderness and swelling is not consistent with a breast abscess, as it usually involves a specific area of the breast and may present with a visible fluctuant mass or localized pain. Lactational mastitis (Option C) refers to inflammation of the breast tissue, often caused by milk stasis or blocked milk ducts. It can lead to redness, pain, and swelling in the affected area. While lactational mastitis is a possibility, the bilateral tenderness and swelling described in the case suggest a more generalized breast engorgement rather than a localized inflammation. @Neet_pg_bot

The constant worry about weight gain may also indicate an underlying thyroid imbalance, as hyperthyroidism can cause disturbances in mood and appetite. Hypocholesterolaemia (Option A) is not typically associated with hyperthyroidism. The symptoms described in this case do not align with those of Cushing's syndrome. Hyperglycaemia (Option D) is not a typical characteristic of hyperthyroidism. This scarring can lead to infertility or an increased risk of ectopic pregnancy. PID is a major cause of infertility in women, especially if left untreated. Pelvic inflammatory disease Pathogenesis Infection ascends from the cervix and endometrium to the fallopian tubes and ovaries, causing inflammation and scarring. Can lead to infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain. Aetiology Acute: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, E. coli, Mycoplasma genitalium, Anaerobes (Bacteroides species), Gardnerella vaginalis, Trichomonas vaginalis, Streptococci, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Actinomyces israelii. Chronic: Same as acute, with possible additional mixed infections. Clinical Features Signs: Fever, Purulent cervical discharge, Cervical motion tenderness, Adnexal tenderness, Abdominal tenderness. Symptoms: Lower abdominal pain, Abnormal vaginal discharge, Dyspareunia (pain during intercourse), Dysuria (pain during urination), Menstrual irregularities, Nausea and vomiting. Complications Infertility: Due to scarring and damage to fallopian tubes. Ectopic Pregnancy Chronic Pelvic Pain Peritonitis Sepsis Laboratory Findings Elevated WBC, Elevated CRP, Elevated ESR. Ultrasound: Thickened, fluid-filled fallopian tubes and free pelvic fluid. Next Step in Diagnosis Endocervical Swab: Detects key pathogens like Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae to guide treatment and prevent complications. Add Doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 14 days, with or without Metronidazole 500 mg PO BD for 14 days. Male Partner Treatment Treat with Cefixime + Azithromycin (Grey kit in India) to prevent reinfection. Out-patient Therapy (India) Yellow kit: Ceftriaxone, Doxycycline, Metronidazole for syndromic management. Uterine cancer (Option B): It arises from the lining of the uterus and is influenced by factors like hormonal imbalances and genetics. Chlamydia infection or PID is not a known cause of uterine cancer. Pelvic organ prolapse (Option C): Although chronic infections can contribute to pelvic floor weakness, pelvic organ prolapse is not a direct long-term consequence of chlamydia or PID.   • This scarring can lead to infertility or an increased risk of ectopic pregnancy. PID is a major cause of infertility in women, especially if left untreated.

    •  

    Pelvic inflammatory disease

    Pathogenesis

    Infection ascends from the cervix and endometrium to the fallopian tubes and ovaries, causing inflammation and scarring. Can lead to infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain.

    Aetiology

    Acute:

    Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, E. coli, Mycoplasma genitalium, Anaerobes (Bacteroides species), Gardnerella vaginalis, Trichomonas vaginalis, Streptococci, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Actinomyces israelii.

     

    Chronic: Same as acute, with possible additional mixed infections.

    Clinical Features

    Signs:

    Fever, Purulent cervical discharge, Cervical motion tenderness, Adnexal tenderness, Abdominal tenderness.

     

    Symptoms:

    Lower abdominal pain, Abnormal vaginal discharge, Dyspareunia (pain during intercourse), Dysuria (pain during urination), Menstrual irregularities, Nausea and vomiting.

    Complications
    • Infertility: Due to scarring and damage to fallopian tubes.
    • Ectopic Pregnancy
    • Chronic Pelvic Pain
    • Peritonitis
    • Sepsis

    Laboratory Findings

    Elevated WBC, Elevated CRP, Elevated ESR.

    Ultrasound: Thickened, fluid-filled fallopian tubes and free pelvic fluid.

    Next Step in Diagnosis

    Endocervical Swab: Detects key pathogens like Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae to guide treatment and prevent complications.

    Treatment

    First-line Therapy:

    Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose, or

    Cefoxitin 2g IM single dose + Probenecid 1g PO single dose, or

    Cefotaxime IV.

    Add Doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 14 days, with or without Metronidazole 500 mg PO BD for 14 days.

    Male Partner Treatment

    Treat with Cefixime + Azithromycin (Grey kit in India) to prevent reinfection.

    Out-patient Therapy (India)

    Yellow kit: Ceftriaxone, Doxycycline, Metronidazole for syndromic management.

     

    Uterine cancer (Option B): It arises from the lining of the uterus and is influenced by factors like hormonal imbalances and genetics. Chlamydia infection or PID is not a known cause of uterine cancer.

    Pelvic organ prolapse (Option C): Although chronic infections can contribute to pelvic floor weakness, pelvic organ prolapse is not a direct long-term consequence of chlamydia or PID.

    Cervical cancer (Option D): While chlamydia infection can increase the risk of acquiring other sexually transmitted infections (such as HPV), which is a known risk factor for cervical cancer, chlamydia itself is not a direct cause of cervical cancer.

options.label: B
options.text: Reassure her that it’s normal to have delayed periods

questions.solution: >Explanation: The first step in a woman with irregular menstrual cycles, especially with a history of regular periods, is to rule out pregnancy. A beta hCG test is used to detect pregnancy, and it is essential to ensure that the irregular cycles are not caused by pregnancy before further investigation or management. Condition Serial beta-hCG Measurement Normal Intrauterine Pregnancy Rising beta-hCG (doubling every 1.4–2 days) Ectopic Pregnancy Plateauing or declining beta-hCG Threatened Abortion Variable beta-hCG changes Early Pregnancy Loss Declining beta-hCG hCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin) hCG is a glycoprotein hormone secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast of the placenta. It can be detected in the maternal blood and urine as early as 8–9 days post-fertilization using techniques like radioimmunoassay. During early pregnancy, hCG levels double every 1.4–2 days. Functions of hCG: Rescue of the Corpus Luteum: The primary role of hCG is to stimulate the secretion of progesterone by the corpus luteum during the first 6 weeks of pregnancy, maintaining the uterine environment. Leydig Cell Stimulation: It stimulates Leydig cells in the male fetus to produce testosterone, crucial for male sexual differentiation. Steroidogenesis: hCG supports steroid hormone production by the adrenal glands and placenta. Thyrotropic Activity: It stimulates the maternal thyroid gland due to its structural similarity to TSH, leading to mild thyroid activation during pregnancy. Relaxin Secretion: hCG promotes the secretion of relaxin from the corpus luteum, which helps in softening the cervix and ligaments in late pregnancy. Clinical Implications of hCG Levels: High hCG levels: Associated with multiple pregnancies, hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma, and Down syndrome (trisomy 21). Low hCG levels: Seen in ectopic pregnancies and impending miscarriages. Transvaginal ultrasound (Option A): While useful for evaluating pelvic organs and identifying conditions like ovarian cysts or fibroids, a transvaginal ultrasound is not the first step when pregnancy is a possibility. Reassure her that it’s normal to have delayed periods (Option B): While occasional menstrual irregularities can occur due to factors like stress or hormonal changes, given the patient’s history of regular cycles, further evaluation is needed to rule out other causes, particularly pregnancy. Serum FSH and LH (Option D): Serum FSH and LH are useful for evaluating the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, especially when conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) are suspected. However, ruling out pregnancy should be the first step in this case. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
>Explanation:
  • The first step in a woman with irregular menstrual cycles, especially with a history of regular periods, is to rule out pregnancy.
  • A beta hCG test is used to detect pregnancy, and it is essential to ensure that the irregular cycles are not caused by pregnancy before further investigation or management.

Condition

Serial beta-hCG Measurement

Normal Intrauterine Pregnancy

Rising beta-hCG (doubling every 1.4–2 days)

Ectopic Pregnancy

Plateauing or declining beta-hCG

Threatened Abortion

Variable beta-hCG changes

Early Pregnancy Loss

Declining beta-hCG

hCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin)

  • hCG is a glycoprotein hormone secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast of the placenta.
  • It can be detected in the maternal blood and urine as early as 8–9 days post-fertilization using techniques like radioimmunoassay. During early pregnancy, hCG levels double every 1.4–2 days.

Functions of hCG:

  • Rescue of the Corpus Luteum: The primary role of hCG is to stimulate the secretion of progesterone by the corpus luteum during the first 6 weeks of pregnancy, maintaining the uterine environment.
  • Leydig Cell Stimulation: It stimulates Leydig cells in the male fetus to produce testosterone, crucial for male sexual differentiation.
  • Steroidogenesis: hCG supports steroid hormone production by the adrenal glands and placenta.
  • Thyrotropic Activity: It stimulates the maternal thyroid gland due to its structural similarity to TSH, leading to mild thyroid activation during pregnancy.
  • Relaxin Secretion: hCG promotes the secretion of relaxin from the corpus luteum, which helps in softening the cervix and ligaments in late pregnancy.

Clinical Implications of hCG Levels:

  • High hCG levels: Associated with multiple pregnancies, hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma, and Down syndrome (trisomy 21).
  • Low hCG levels: Seen in ectopic pregnancies and impending miscarriages.

 

Transvaginal ultrasound (Option A): While useful for evaluating pelvic organs and identifying conditions like ovarian cysts or fibroids, a transvaginal ultrasound is not the first step when pregnancy is a possibility.

Reassure her that it’s normal to have delayed periods (Option B): While occasional menstrual irregularities can occur due to factors like stress or hormonal changes, given the patient’s history of regular cycles, further evaluation is needed to rule out other causes, particularly pregnancy.

Serum FSH and LH (Option D): Serum FSH and LH are useful for evaluating the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, especially when conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) are suspected. However, ruling out pregnancy should be the first step in this case.

Trichomonas Vaginitis

  • Trichomonas vaginitis, caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis, is the most common cause of vaginitis in women of reproductive age, typically transmitted sexually.

Symptoms:

  • Yellowish-Green, Frothy Discharge: Foul-smelling.

Organism:

  • Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated protozoan.
  • It thrives in the vaginal and cervical mucosa, causing inflammation.
  • Infective & Diagnostic Stage: Trophozoite

Diagnosis:

  • Clinical Examination:
    • Profuse, frothy yellow-green discharge.
    • Strawberry cervix.
  • Microscopy (Wet Mount): Motile Trichomonas vaginalis seen under the microscope.
  • Vaginal pH: Elevated (>4.5).
  • Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT): Gold standard for diagnosis.
  • Culture: Less common, but highly accurate.
  • Rapid Antigen Test: Point-of-care, less sensitive than NAAT.

Treatment:

questions.answerText: Patient diagnosed with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids
questions.solution: ated submucous fibroids are fibroids that have hardened and developed a stalk, projecting into the uterine cavity. These fibroids are better managed by surgical removal, such as hysteroscopic resection, rather than uterine artery embolization (UAE). UAE is generally indicated for larger, intramural fibroids or multiple fibroids causing symptoms like heavy menstrual bleeding or pain. Fibroid (Uterine Leiomyoma) Benign smooth muscle tumor of the uterus. Estrogen-dependent growth; typically regresses after menopause. Commonly occurs in reproductive-age women. Types (Based on Location): These fibroids are classified as Type 0 under the FIGO classification of fibroids. {{caption_text}} FIGO Classification of Fibroids. Type Name Submucosal 0 Pedunculated, Intracavity 1 <50% Intramural and rest in cavity 2 ≥ 50% Intramural and a part in cavity 3 100% intramural but contacts endometrium Intramural 4 Intramural Subserosal 5 ≥ 50% Intramural and partly in serosa 6 <50% Intramural and rest in serosa 7 Subserosal Pedunculated Others 8 Other - Cervical, Parasitic 2-5 Hybrid - Present both in the cavity (type 2) and in the serosa (type 5) Symptoms: Menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding). Dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation). Pelvic pain or pressure. Dyspareunia (painful intercourse). Urinary symptoms (frequency, urgency, or retention). Infertility or recurrent miscarriages. Signs: Enlarged, irregular, firm uterus on bimanual examination. Mobility of the uterus may be reduced if fibroids are large. Complications: Severe anemia due to chronic menorrhagia. Infertility and subfertility. Recurrent pregnancy loss. Red degeneration (painful necrosis, often during pregnancy). Torsion of pedunculated fibroids. Malignant transformation (rare; <1% cases to leiomyosarcoma). Diagnosis: Ultrasound: Primary imaging modality; identifies size, number, and location. Hysteroscopy: For evaluation of submucosal fibroids. MRI: Detailed imaging in complex or unclear cases. Sonohysterography: Detects submucosal fibroids and cavity distortion. Treatment Options: Medical: Hormonal therapy (GnRH agonists, progestins). Non-hormonal options (NSAIDs, tranexamic acid). Surgical: Myomectomy: For preserving fertility. Hysterectomy: Definitive treatment for symptomatic fibroids in women who have completed childbearing. Uterine artery embolization (UAE): Minimally invasive, for reducing fibroid size and symptoms. Other Interventions: MRI-guided focused ultrasound (non-invasive ablation). Laparoscopic or hysteroscopic resection. Prognosis: Recurrence possible after myomectomy, especially in younger women. Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) (Option A): Uterine artery embolization is an effective treatment option for postpartum hemorrhage. By blocking the uterine blood supply, it can control bleeding and reduce the need for invasive surgical procedures, such as hysterectomy. Placenta accreta (Option B): In cases of placenta accreta, where the placenta is abnormally adherent to the uterine wall, UAE can be performed pre-operatively to reduce uterine blood flow, thereby minimizing the risk of severe bleeding during placenta removal. Menorrhagia in multiparous women (Option D): For multiparous women with menorrhagia due to fibroids, UAE can be considered. By decreasing blood flow to the fibroids, it alleviates symptoms like heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding. @Neet_pg_bot

ated submucous fibroids are fibroids that have hardened and developed a stalk, projecting into the uterine cavity. These fibroids are better managed by surgical removal, such as hysteroscopic resection, rather than uterine artery embolization (UAE).
  • UAE is generally indicated for larger, intramural fibroids or multiple fibroids causing symptoms like heavy menstrual bleeding or pain.

    • Fibroid (Uterine Leiomyoma)

    • Benign smooth muscle tumor of the uterus.
    • Estrogen-dependent growth; typically regresses after menopause.
    • Commonly occurs in reproductive-age women.

    Types (Based on Location):

    • These fibroids are classified as Type 0 under the FIGO classification of fibroids.

    FIGO Classification of Fibroids.

     

    Type

    Name

    Submucosal

    0

    Pedunculated, Intracavity

    1

    <50% Intramural and rest in cavity

    2

    ≥ 50% Intramural and a part in cavity

    3

    100% intramural but contacts endometrium

    Intramural

    4

    Intramural

    Subserosal

    5

    ≥ 50% Intramural and partly in serosa

    6

    <50% Intramural and rest in serosa

    7

    Subserosal Pedunculated

    Others

    8

    Other - Cervical, Parasitic

    2-5

    Hybrid - Present both in the cavity (type 2) and in the serosa (type 5)

    Symptoms:

    • Menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding).
    • Dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation).
    • Pelvic pain or pressure.
    • Dyspareunia (painful intercourse).
    • Urinary symptoms (frequency, urgency, or retention).
    • Infertility or recurrent miscarriages.

    Signs:

    • Enlarged, irregular, firm uterus on bimanual examination.
    • Mobility of the uterus may be reduced if fibroids are large.

    Complications:

    • Severe anemia due to chronic menorrhagia.
    • Infertility and subfertility.
    • Recurrent pregnancy loss.
    • Red degeneration (painful necrosis, often during pregnancy).
    • Torsion of pedunculated fibroids.
    • Malignant transformation (rare; <1% cases to leiomyosarcoma).

    Diagnosis:

    • Ultrasound: Primary imaging modality; identifies size, number, and location.
    • Hysteroscopy: For evaluation of submucosal fibroids.
    • MRI: Detailed imaging in complex or unclear cases.
    • Sonohysterography: Detects submucosal fibroids and cavity distortion.

    Treatment Options:

    • Medical:
      • Hormonal therapy (GnRH agonists, progestins).
      • Non-hormonal options (NSAIDs, tranexamic acid).
    • Surgical:
      • Myomectomy: For preserving fertility.
      • Hysterectomy: Definitive treatment for symptomatic fibroids in women who have completed childbearing.
      • Uterine artery embolization (UAE): Minimally invasive, for reducing fibroid size and symptoms.
    • Other Interventions:
      • MRI-guided focused ultrasound (non-invasive ablation).
      • Laparoscopic or hysteroscopic resection.

    Prognosis: Recurrence possible after myomectomy, especially in younger women.

     

    Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) (Option A): Uterine artery embolization is an effective treatment option for postpartum hemorrhage. By blocking the uterine blood supply, it can control bleeding and reduce the need for invasive surgical procedures, such as hysterectomy.

    Placenta accreta (Option B): In cases of placenta accreta, where the placenta is abnormally adherent to the uterine wall, UAE can be performed pre-operatively to reduce uterine blood flow, thereby minimizing the risk of severe bleeding during placenta removal.

    Menorrhagia in multiparous women (Option D): For multiparous women with menorrhagia due to fibroids, UAE can be considered. By decreasing blood flow to the fibroids, it alleviates symptoms like heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding.

questions.stemHtml: What is the likely diagnosis for a 45-year-old woman who is a mother of three, experiencing discomfort and a mass in her lower abdomen? During examination, her uterus appears uniformly enlarged and the adnexa is unaffected. An MRI reveals the presence of a cyst within the uterine muscle.
questions.solution: tissue into the myometrium (muscle layer of the uterus). This condition leads to a uniformly enlarged and tender uterus and can present with symptoms such as pelvic discomfort, heavy menstrual bleeding, and dysmenorrhea. The presence of a myometrial cyst seen on MRI is a hallmark finding in adenomyosis, making it the most likely diagnosis in this case. Adenomyosis Definition Presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, leading to uterine enlargement. Epidemiology Common in parous women over 40 years of age. Clinical Features Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB). Chronic pelvic pain. Globally enlarged and globular uterus (if diffuse). Investigations Primary Investigation: TVS with Color Doppler. Key Signs on USG: Shutter/Venetian Blind sign (echogenic striations). Central vascularity on Doppler. Diagnostic Criteria: Asymmetrical uterine wall thickness (posterior > anterior). Heterogeneous myometrial echotexture. Hypoechoic myometrial cysts (honeycomb appearance). Striated projections from endometrium to myometrium. Poorly defined endometrial echo. J-Zone thickening ≥12 mm. Secondary Investigation: MRI (if USG is i nconclusive). {{caption_text}} {{caption_text}} Thickened junctional zone (>12 mm). High-intensity myometrial foci on T2-weighted images. Histopathology Myometrial infiltration by endometrial glands and stroma. {{caption_text}} Medical Management Combined OCPs and progestin-only regimens (for dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia). NSAIDs (for pain and menorrhagia). LNG-IUS (for menorrhagia). GnRH agonists (for subfertility or pre-surgical symptom relief). Danazol (for menorrhagia and pain). Surgical Management Conservative: Adenomyomectomy (risk of recurrence). Uterine mass reduction (laparotomy/laparoscopy). Uterine artery embolization (UAE). Definitive: Total hysterectomy. Endometriosis (Option A) refers to the growth of endometrial tissue outside the uterus, often leading to symptoms like pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility. While it can coexist with adenomyosis, the myometrial cyst described in this scenario is more characteristic of adenomyosis. Leiomyoma (Option C) , or fibroids, are benign tumors of the uterine smooth muscle. They typically present as localized masses within the uterus, leading to an irregularly enlarged uterus rather than a uniformly enlarged one. The presence of a myometrial cyst is not commonly associated with fibroids. Endometrial hyperplasia (Option D) involves excessive thickening of the endometrial lining due to hormonal imbalance, often leading to abnormal uterine bleeding. It does not cause a uniformly enlarged uterus or myometrial cysts, making it an unlikely diagnosis in this scenario. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
tissue into the myometrium (muscle layer of the uterus).
  • This condition leads to a uniformly enlarged and tender uterus and can present with symptoms such as pelvic discomfort, heavy menstrual bleeding, and dysmenorrhea.
  • The presence of a myometrial cyst seen on MRI is a hallmark finding in adenomyosis, making it the most likely diagnosis in this case.

    • Adenomyosis

    Definition

    Presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, leading to uterine enlargement.

    Epidemiology

    Common in parous women over 40 years of age.

    Clinical Features
    • Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB).
    • Chronic pelvic pain.
    • Globally enlarged and globular uterus (if diffuse).

    Investigations

    Primary Investigation: TVS with Color Doppler.

    Key Signs on USG:

    • Shutter/Venetian Blind sign (echogenic striations).
    • Central vascularity on Doppler.

    Diagnostic Criteria:

    • Asymmetrical uterine wall thickness (posterior > anterior).
    • Heterogeneous myometrial echotexture.
    • Hypoechoic myometrial cysts (honeycomb appearance).
    • Striated projections from endometrium to myometrium.
    • Poorly defined endometrial echo.
    • J-Zone thickening ≥12 mm.

    Secondary Investigation: MRI (if USG is inconclusive).

     

    • Thickened junctional zone (>12 mm).
    • High-intensity myometrial foci on T2-weighted images.

    Histopathology

    Myometrial infiltration by endometrial glands and stroma.

     

    Medical Management
    • Combined OCPs and progestin-only regimens (for dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia).
    • NSAIDs (for pain and menorrhagia).
    • LNG-IUS (for menorrhagia).
    • GnRH agonists (for subfertility or pre-surgical symptom relief).
    • Danazol (for menorrhagia and pain).

    Surgical Management

    Conservative:

    • Adenomyomectomy (risk of recurrence).
    • Uterine mass reduction (laparotomy/laparoscopy).
    • Uterine artery embolization (UAE).

    Definitive: Total hysterectomy.

     

     

    Endometriosis (Option A) refers to the growth of endometrial tissue outside the uterus, often leading to symptoms like pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility. While it can coexist with adenomyosis, the myometrial cyst described in this scenario is more characteristic of adenomyosis.

    Leiomyoma (Option C), or fibroids, are benign tumors of the uterine smooth muscle. They typically present as localized masses within the uterus, leading to an irregularly enlarged uterus rather than a uniformly enlarged one. The presence of a myometrial cyst is not commonly associated with fibroids.

    Endometrial hyperplasia (Option D) involves excessive thickening of the endometrial lining due to hormonal imbalance, often leading to abnormal uterine bleeding. It does not cause a uniformly enlarged uterus or myometrial cysts, making it an unlikely diagnosis in this scenario.

questions.stem: Which among the following regions is free from rabies?
questions.stemHtml: Which among the following regions is free from rabies?
questions.solution: ually not found in areas bound on all sides with water. In India, rabies is not found in islands such as Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep. Epidemiological Determinants of Rabies: Agent factor Zoonotic disease with a 100% fatality rate Lyssavirus type 1 Bullet-shaped RNA virus (Rhabdoviridae family). Two Types of Viruses: Street virus: Cause natural infection (Rabies) Variable incubation period (7 days-months) Fixed virus: Fixed incubation period (5-7 days) For vaccine production. It does not demonstrate Negri bodies. Host factors Occupation Dog handlers Forest workers Veterinarians. Transmission Incubation period: 2-8 weeks Animal bite: Dog, Cat, Monkey or Wild animal (all need vaccination) Licks on abraded skin are considered as the route of transmission. Rodent bites don't require vaccination. Human bite is a very dangerous bite (no documented cases yet) In India: Urban Rabies is very common. Rabies is not found around water-bounded areas (Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar Islands) (Option C) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ually not found in areas bound on all sides with water. In India, rabies is not found in islands such as Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep.

 

Epidemiological Determinants of Rabies:

Agent factor
  • Zoonotic disease with a 100% fatality rate
  • Lyssavirus type 1
    • Bullet-shaped RNA virus (Rhabdoviridae family).
  • Two Types of Viruses:
    • Street virus:
      • Cause natural infection (Rabies)
      • Variable incubation period (7 days-months)
    • Fixed virus:
      • Fixed incubation period (5-7 days)
      • For vaccine production.
      • It does not demonstrate Negri bodies.

Host factors
  • Occupation
    • Dog handlers
    • Forest workers
    • Veterinarians.

Transmission
  • Incubation period: 2-8 weeks
  • Animal bite: Dog, Cat, Monkey or Wild animal (all need vaccination)
  • Licks on abraded skin are considered as the route of transmission.
  • Rodent bites don't require vaccination.
  • Human bite is a very dangerous bite (no documented cases yet)
  • In India:
    • Urban Rabies is very common.
    • Rabies is not found around water-bounded areas (Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar Islands) (Option C)

What is the probable diagnosis?

She occasionally smokes but does not consume alcohol or recreational drugs. On examination, her pulse rate is 80 bpm, BP is 150/90 mmHg, and her abdomen is tense on palpation. questions.solution: data-dictid="797686400a16927771956b27d401ff">placental abruption, is the premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall before delivery. Abruptio placenta is a form of antepartum haemorrhage, where the bleeding occurs due to premature separation of the normally situated placenta. Pathogenesis: Bleeding occurs due to rupture of blood vessels in the decidua basalis. There is an accumulation of blood in the decidua. This causes the separation of the placenta, leading to Further bleeding. Thrombin generation from haemorrhage triggers the action of matrix metalloproteinases, inflammatory cytokines, and coagulation cascade (high risk of DIC). Fetal distress. Clinical features: Mild to moderate vaginal bleeding Abdominal pain Uterine tenderness Back pain Fetal distress Hypovolemic shock Frequent contractions Types of abruptio placenta: Revealed Most common type, where the bleeding from the placental detachment is visible and exits through the vagina. This is often associated with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain. Concealed Bleeding is hidden behind the placenta and is not visible externally. Blood collects within the uterus, causing increased pressure and pain without visible bleeding. Mixed Involves both concealed and revealed bleeding. There is both internal and external bleeding, with some blood exiting through the vagina and some collecting behind the placenta. The diagnosis is made after inspection of the placenta following delivery. 1 Bleeding PV + Abdominal pain (Uterine tenderness ±) Fetal heart sounds are normal 2 Bleeding PV + Abdominal pain (Uterine tenderness always +) Fetal distress 3 Bleeding PV + Abdominal pain (marked uterine tenderness) + Shock ± Coagulopathy Fetal death Comparison of findings in placenta previa and abruptio placentae: Placenta previa Abruptio placentae Clinical features Nature of bleeding Painless, causeless, and recurrent. Painful , often attributed to Pre-eclampsia or trauma, and continuous. Character of blood Bleeding is always revealed. Revealed, concealed, or usually mixed. General condition & anaemia Proportionate to visible blood loss. Out of proportion to the visible blood loss in the concealed or mixed variety. Features of eclampsia Not relevant. Present in one-third of the cases. Abdominal examination Height of the uterus Proportionate height to the gestational age. It may be disproportionately enlarged in concealed type. The feel of the uterus Soft and relaxed. It may be tense, tender, and rigid. Malpresentation Common (the head is high floating). Unrelated, the head may be engaged. Fetal heart sounds Usually present. Usually absent, especially in the concealed type. USG, MRI Placenta in the lower segment. Placenta in the upper segment. Vaginal examination The placenta is felt on the lower segment (not to be done in a suspected case). The placenta is not felt on the lower segment. Blood clots should not be confused with placenta. Placenta previa (Option B) occurs when the placenta covers the cervix partially or completely. It typically presents with painless vaginal bleeding in the third trimester and no abdominal pain or tense uterus, making it unlikely in this scenario. Hydramnios (polyhydramnios) (Option C) is an excessive accumulation of amniotic fluid. It may cause abdominal discomfort or uterine distension but does not present with vaginal bleeding, loss of fetal movements, or a tense abdomen. Preterm labor (Option D) involves uterine contractions before 37 weeks of gestation. questions.stem: How should a patient be managed if a 30-year-old woman, using an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) for contraception, presents to the emergency department after experiencing two episodes of painless vaginal bleeding following 8 weeks of missed periods? She also complains of dizziness, and her blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg, with a pulse rate of 138 beats per minute. A urine pregnancy test is positive.
questions.stemHtml: How should a patient be managed if a 30-year-old woman, using an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) for contraception, presents to the emergency department after experiencing two episodes of painless vaginal bleeding following 8 weeks of missed periods? She also complains of dizziness, and her blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg, with a pulse rate of 138 beats per minute. A urine pregnancy test is positive.

options.label: A
options.text: IV fluids followed by oral methotrexate

options.label: C
options.text: Stabilizing the patient followed by suction evacuation

questions.answerText: Stabilizing the patient followed by suction evacuation
questions.solution: ical presentation is highly suggestive of an ectopic pregnancy, which is a medical emergency. Key features in this case include: Missed periods and positive pregnancy test indicating pregnancy. Painless vaginal bleeding and dizziness, raising suspicion of ectopic pregnancy. Hemodynamic instability (BP 80/50 mmHg, pulse 138 bpm), suggesting significant blood loss, possibly due to a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Management Stabilize the patient: Immediate resuscitation with intravenous (IV) fluids to address hypovolemia and maintain blood pressure. Stabilization is critical to ensure the patient is safe for the next steps. Suction evacuation: This minimally invasive procedure removes the ectopic tissue and is the preferred treatment for hemodynamically stable patients. Further imaging or diagnostic laparoscopy may be used to confirm ectopic pregnancy location before intervention if the diagnosis is unclear. IV fluids followed by oral methotrexate (Option A): Methotrexate is suitable only for hemodynamically stable patients with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy and no signs of imminent rupture. This patient is unstable, requiring immediate surgical intervention, making methotrexate inappropriate. Immediate laparotomy (Option B): Laparotomy is indicated for life-threatening cases of ectopic pregnancy rupture with massive intra-abdominal bleeding or when other interventions fail. In this case, suction evacuation after stabilization is sufficient if the diagnosis is confirmed and bleeding is manageable. Dilatation and curettage (D&C) (Option D): D&C is used to manage intrauterine pregnancies or miscarriages but is not suitable for treating ectopic pregnancies, as the pregnancy is outside the uterus. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman who has never given birth and is undergoing hormone replacement therapy (HRT) presents with abdominal pain. On examination, a non-painful palpable mass is detected in the right adnexa. Following further investigation, she undergoes laparotomy, and her ovaries are observed as described. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old woman who has never given birth and is undergoing hormone replacement therapy (HRT) presents with abdominal pain. On examination, a non-painful palpable mass is detected in the right adnexa. Following further investigation, she undergoes laparotomy, and her ovaries are observed as described. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.solution: ul> Ovarian carcinoma is a common cause of adnexal masses in postmenopausal women. The patient’s history of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and a non-tender right adnexal mass raise suspicion, as HRT may stimulate tumor growth and increase the risk of ovarian carcinoma in postmenopausal women. “ Nodular carcinoma of ovary” (Option A) is not a recognized medical term or specific diagnosis. It might be used to describe a solid tumor, but it is not a common or accurate term to describe ovarian malignancy. Ovarian carcinoma is the preferred and more precise diagnosis for malignant ovarian tumors in this context. A chocolate cyst (endometrioma) (Option B) is an ovarian cyst filled with old blood, typically associated with endometriosis. This condition is more common in premenopausal women. In postmenopausal women, especially those on HRT, ovarian carcinoma is more likely, as hormonal therapy can influence the growth of ovarian tumors. Ovarian fibroids (Option C) are not a recognized medical entity. Fibroids, or leiomyomas, are smooth muscle tumors that occur in the uterus, not the ovaries. A mass in the adnexa that is associated with a postmenopausal woman, especially with HRT use, is more consistent with ovarian carcinoma. @Neet_pg_bot
