questions.stem: A 29-year-old female complains of foul-smelling vaginal discharge. A Giemsa stained smear of the discharge is shown below. Which of the following is not seen in this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 29-year-old female complains of foul-smelling vaginal discharge. A Giemsa stained smear of the discharge is shown below. Which of the following is not seen in this condition?
questions.solution: n> is a hallmark of vaginal candidiasis (yeast infection), which is caused by an overgrowth of Candida species. The discharge appears thick and white, often resembling cottage cheese. However, the condition described in this case is Trichomoniasis, which is caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. Trichomoniasis typically results in a frothy, yellow-green discharge that may be foul-smelling, not a curdy white discharge. Trichomonas Vaginitis Trichomonas vaginitis, caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis, is the most common cause of vaginitis in women of reproductive age, typically transmitted sexually. Symptoms: Yellowish-Green, Frothy Discharge: Foul-smelling. Vulvar Irritation & Itching : Around the vaginal opening. (Option D ruled out) Painful Urination (Dysuria): Burning sensation during micturition (Option C ruled out) Dyspareunia: Pain during intercourse. "Strawberry Cervix": Punctate hemorrhages on the cervix. (Option A ruled out) Recurrent Infections. Organism: Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated protozoan. It thrives in the vaginal and cervical mucosa, causing inflammation. Infective & Diagnostic Stage: Trophozoite Diagnosis: Clinical Examination: Profuse, frothy yellow-green discharge. Strawberry cervix. Microscopy (Wet Mount): Motile Trichomonas vaginalis seen under the microscope. Vaginal pH: Elevated (>4.5). Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT): Gold standard for diagnosis. strong>

Types of Tonometry:

1. Indentation Tonometry:

  • Concept: Measures IOP by how much a plunger indents the eye; softer eyes indent more than harder eyes.
  • Schiotz Tonometer (Option A):
    • Most widely used tonometer in the world.
    • Advantages: Inexpensive, simple, and reliable.
    • Disadvantages: Gives false readings in eyes with abnormal scleral rigidity (e.g., high myopes, post-surgery).

2. Applanation Tonometry:

  • Concept: Measures IOP based on the force needed to flatten the cornea's surface (Imbert-Fick Law: P = W/A).
  • Goldmann Tonometer (Option B):
    • Most popular and accurate; uses a double prism on a slit lamp.
    • Technique:
      • Cornea is anesthetized and stained with fluorescein.
      • Cornea and biprisms are illuminated with cobalt blue light.
      • The prism touches the cornea, and the inner edges of two semicircles are adjusted to just touch.
      • IOP is read by multiplying the dial reading by ten.

Variable force tonometers:

  • Goldmann applanation tonometer → Gold standard
  • Perkins tonometer (hand held version of goldmann)
  • Draeger tonometer (measures wide range of IOP)
  • Draeger tonometer is similar to Perkins
    • It has a different set of prisms
    • It operates with a motor
  • Pulsair (non-contact tonometer)
  • Airpuff (non-contact tonometer)
  • Grolman (non-contact tonometer)
  • Tonopen (based on both indentation and applanation)
  • MacKay Marg (based on both indentation and applanation)
  • Rebound tonometer
  • Transpalpebral Tonometer

Fixed force tonometer:

  1. Maklakov tonometer
  2. Barraquer tonometer

Tonopen (Option C) is a handheld electronic tonometer that measures IOP by using both applanation and indentation method..

Pascal dynamic contour (Option D) tonometer is a newer technology that measures IOP by analyzing the contour of the cornea during gentle deformation.

This irregularity in corneal shape prevents light rays from focusing on a single point on the retina, causing blurred or distorted vision. Astigmatism: A refractive error where different meridia of the eye have different refractive errors . Divided into 2 types: Regular and irregular I. Regular Astigmatism: When refraction error changes uniformly from one meridian to the other. ( 2 principle meridians present) Type Description With-the-Rule (WTR) The vertical meridian has greater curvature than the horizontal meridian. Against-the-Rule (ATR) The horizontal meridian is more curved than the vertical meridian. Oblique Astigmatism Principal meridians are at oblique angles (e.g., 45° and 135°), still perpendicular to each other. Bi-oblique Astigmatism Principal meridians are not perpendicular to each other (e.g., 30° and 100°). Regular Astigmatism Based on Focal Lines: Type Description Simple Astigmatism One meridian focuses on the retina; the other focuses in front (simple myopic) or behind (simple hypermetropic). Compound Astigmatism Both meridians focus light either in front (compound myopic) or behind (compound hypermetropic) the retina. Mixed Astigmatism One meridian focuses in front of the retina (myopic), and the other behind (hypermetropic). II. Irregular Astigmatism Involves multiple, changing meridians of refractive power, making it geometrically complex.Usually due to Corneal scars. Excessive eye rubbing (Option B) can irritate the eyes and potentially lead to infections like keratoconjunctivitis. Prolonged exposure to bright light (Option C) can cause eye strain and discomfort. questions.solution: y found in a region, brought from abroad. Scenario: Disease brought to India by 25-year-old male. Classification: Disease is considered exotic due to its foreign origin. Term Definition Examples Epidemic (Option B ruled out) Occurrence of disease clearly in excess of normal expectancy (Mean + 2SD or >80% expected frequency). Occurrence of even a single case of a previously eliminated disease. Occurrence of a single case of an exotic disease. (Option D) Seasonal influenza outbreaks during winter months. Endemic (Option A ruled out) Constant presence of a disease within a specific population. Epidemiologically linked cases in terms of time, place, or person. Malaria in Africa, TB in India Pandemic Global spread of a disease. Defined as an epidemic in a large population. Requires crossing 2 continents and 2 WHO-specific regions. HIV/AIDS, COVID-19. Sporadic They occur randomly and unpredictably, without any discernible pattern in time, location, or individual. There's no epidemiological link between the cases. Tetanus Zoonotic (Option C): Disease transmitted under natural conditions from animal to humans. This option is incorrect. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
y found in a region, brought from abroad.
  • Scenario: Disease brought to India by 25-year-old male.
  • Classification: Disease is considered exotic due to its foreign origin.

    Term

    Definition

    Examples

    Epidemic (Option B ruled out)
    • Occurrence of disease clearly in excess of normal expectancy (Mean + 2SD or >80% expected frequency).
    • Occurrence of even a single case of a previously eliminated disease.
    • Occurrence of a single case of an exotic disease. (Option D)

    Seasonal influenza outbreaks during winter months.

    Endemic (Option A ruled out)

     
    • Constant presence of a disease within a specific population.
    • Epidemiologically linked cases in terms of time, place, or person.

    Malaria in Africa, TB in India

    Pandemic
    • Global spread of a disease.
    • Defined as an epidemic in a large population.
    • Requires crossing 2 continents and 2 WHO-specific regions.

    HIV/AIDS, COVID-19.

    Sporadic
    • They occur randomly and unpredictably, without any discernible pattern in time, location, or individual.
    • There's no epidemiological link between the cases.

    Tetanus

     

    Zoonotic (Option C): Disease transmitted under natural conditions from animal to humans. This option is incorrect.

questions.stemHtml: Installation and usage of sanitary latrines by general public constitutes which level of prevention:
questions.solution: g sanitary latrines promotes hygiene and prevents diseases. Primary prevention includes: Health promotion: (Option A) Health education camps on exercise and lifestyle diseases. Mental health promotion and counselling in schools and colleges. Implementing strict laws against drinking and driving to prevent road traffic accidents due to impaired driving Specific protection: (Option B ruled out) Administration of MR vaccination to children prevents measles and rubella infection via active immunisation, as the risk of infection is high during childhood Iodisation of salt helps prevent endemic goitre, especially in the Himalayan region, as they lack iodine in their diet Level of Prevention Goals Examples Primordial To prevent the establishment of risk factors Lifestyle modification Health promotion Primary Interventions to prevent the onset of disease Vaccinations Health education Family planning Use of mosquito nets Pre-placement examinatio Secondary Early detection and prompt treatment of disease to prevent complications (Option C ruled out) Screening tests (e.g., mammograms, PAP smears) Self-examinations Health camps with screening DOTS for TB; ART for HIV; MDT for leprosy. questions.solutionHtml:
g sanitary latrines promotes hygiene and prevents diseases.

Primary prevention includes:

  • Health promotion: (Option A)
    • Health education camps on exercise and lifestyle diseases.
    • Mental health promotion and counselling in schools and colleges.
    • Implementing strict laws against drinking and driving to prevent road traffic accidents due to impaired driving
  • Specific protection: (Option B ruled out)
    • Administration of MR vaccination to children prevents measles and rubella infection via active immunisation, as the risk of infection is high during childhood
    • Iodisation of salt helps prevent endemic goitre, especially in the Himalayan region, as they lack iodine in their diet

 

 

Level of Prevention

Goals

Examples

Primordial

To prevent the establishment of risk factors

  • Lifestyle modification
  • Health promotion

Primary

Interventions to prevent the onset of disease
  • Vaccinations
  • Health education
  • Family planning
  • Use of mosquito nets
  • Pre-placement examinatio

Secondary

Early detection and prompt treatment of disease to prevent complications (Option C ruled out)
  • Screening tests (e.g., mammograms, PAP smears)
  • Self-examinations
  • Health camps with screening DOTS for TB; ART for HIV; MDT for leprosy.

Tertiary

Interventions to manage and reduce complications of existing disease to prevent disability or death (Option D ruled out)
  • Rehabilitation
  • Physical therapy
  • Chronic disease management programs
  • Reconstructive surgery
